name: Brawl Stars
full_sequence:
Six landscape shots (2208x1242), all built on one template: a 3D hero on the left, a slightly tilted gameplay card on the right, and a two-line caption at bottom right. I studied them at 1100x619. Shot 6 was downloaded to shots/1229016807_6.jpg and larger copies are in shots_big/.
1) Edgar (dark bowl-cut hair, striped scarf) on a violet gradient. The card shows a teal-grass map on a pink hex floor, caught on a cyan super blast hitting a cluster of enemies. The caption ("Rank up / and customize") sells progression and cosmetics before the core loop. Its job is the brand hook: a strong face plus the promise of long-term goals.
2) Shelly (pink hair, skull eyepatch) on teal. The card is a dark night map showing a small skirmish with an emote bubble. The caption sells fast 3v3 play. Its job is the core loop and a promise of short sessions.
3) El Primo in a tuxedo skin on electric blue. The card is a desert map with smoke-ring explosions. The caption is a content count ("60+ brawlers" plus a skin count). Its job is depth of content. The alternate skin the hero wears is the visual proof of the skin claim.
4) Mandy (candy-queen outfit, peace sign) on blue. The card is a green battle royale map. Unlike the others it keeps the timer, emote bubbles and the super button as authenticity cues. The caption names the mode ("Epic / battle royale"). Its job is the headline mode.
5) Willow (green skin, holding a lantern creature) on magenta. The card is a green map with a pink poison-cloud effect. The caption is "Discover / special events". Its job is to show fresh live events.
6) Jacky (yellow hard hat, jackhammer) on blue. The card is a maroon industrial map. The caption is "Create / game maps". Its job is creativity (player-made maps), and a builder hero is cast for the creation claim.
Across the set: a different hero, map biome and effect moment in every shot. The arc runs hook/progression, core loop, content count, main mode, live events, then creation. Hero casting is deliberate: each hero's outfit or prop visually proves the caption. The weak point: shots 3, 4 and 6 use the same blue, so neighbours in the row blur together. Because the set is landscape, only one shot shows in search results, so shot 1 carries everything.
composition_recipe:
Measured on a 1100x619 frame.
HERO: occupies about x 0-45%. The body bleeds off the left edge and is cut off at the knees or thighs by the bottom edge. The top of the head sits 3-10% from the top, and the face centre is around x 25-30%, y 30-40%. Pose is 3/4 with the body turned toward the card. The hero overlaps the card's left edge by 3-8% of frame width (gun, arm or hand).
GAMEPLAY CARD: x 42-96%, y 4-75%. It is rotated about 2.3 degrees counter-clockwise (top edge runs from y 46 on the left to y 22 on the right). Plain rotation, no perspective, no device frame, no border, square corners, no visible shadow. The right margin is about 4%. The HUD is stripped except name tags and health bars. It is cropped to about 5 characters at the peak effect moment.
CAPTION: right-aligned to the card's right edge, filling y ~68-93% and about 55-60% of frame width. It overlaps the bottom 5-8% of the card, which locks the layers together. It never touches the hero: the two sit in separate quadrants.
FLOOR STRIP: a brighter tint of the background hue fills the bottom 3-6%. Its top edge rises from left to right with one small notch step.
BACKGROUND: a radial glow sits behind the hero's head and shoulders and falls off to a flat, darker tone across the right 20%, behind the card and caption. A faint tone-on-tone icon pattern sits at about 5-8% contrast.
DEPTH (back to front): gradient and pattern, floor strip, tilted card, hero, caption.
READING PATH: a Z. Face (top left), then gameplay (top right), then caption (bottom right).
PORTRAIT VERSION FOR COMET GARDEN (1290x2796):
- Caption block at y 5-18%.
- Frameless gameplay card at x 7-93%, y 17-79%, rotated 2-3 degrees and alternating direction each shot. Use large rounded corners (~56px) and a soft coloured drop shadow. The caption's lower line can overlap the card top by ~1-2%.
- Oversized hero creature, 40-50% of canvas width, in a bottom corner (alternating left and right). It overlaps the card's lower corner and is cropped by the bottom edge, with its face centre at about 78-85% height.
- A soft rolling hill or cloud floor band across the bottom 8-10%.
- A second frame break: a comet streak exits the card into the background.
- Portrait reading path: caption, then planet in the card, then creature face, whose gaze points back up at the planet.
type_recipe:
BRAWL STARS: all caps in a heavy, rounded, slightly condensed display face. White fill, a thick black outline (about 6% of cap height) and a hard black extrusion shadow offset straight down, which gives a sticker or toy-logo feel. Two lines, right-aligned, with tight leading (the lines almost touch). The setup line (verb or adjective) is set at about 70-75% of the punch line's size, and the punch line (the payoff noun) is bigger. Punch-line cap height is about 11% of frame height (about 6.4% of width). There is no caption box: legibility comes from the outline plus the dark zone behind the text. The voice is 2-4 words: verb-led imperatives (Rank up, Discover, Create) alternating with adjective + noun, plus one number-driven claim. Numbers work as nouns for depth.
COMET GARDEN VERSION: keep the two-size structure: a small setup line at about 55-60% of the size of a big payoff line, 2-4 words total, one claim per shot. Use the brand face already on the site (Fredoka 600/700). Set it in sentence case, which reads friendlier to all ages than shouting capitals. Size the punch line at about 8-9% of canvas width in cap height, larger than Brawl relative to width, because portrait thumbnails are small. Style: white fill with a soft outline in the background's deepest hue (not black) plus a soft blurred shadow, or deep navy fill with no outline on pastel skies. Our own touch: colour only the payoff noun, e.g. butter yellow or mint, in "grow a *world*". Voice is gentle verbs: Fling, Grow, Welcome, Discover, Collect. Use honest counts from src/core/world.ts, which currently lists 36 creature species and about 16 biomes; check the numbers before printing.
color_light_recipe:
BRAWL STARS:
- One saturated hue per shot: violet, teal, electric blue x3, magenta.
- The hue is picked to complement the hero's main colour: green-skinned Willow on magenta, yellow-hatted Jacky on blue, pink-haired Shelly on teal.
- Light split: a bright radial glow behind the hero (brightest around x 25-40%) falls to a flat, darker, more saturated tone on the right, where the card and the white caption sit. Sampled on shot 3: about RGB 19,179,255 at the glow and 0,60,174 on the right edge.
- The floor strip is the lightest, most saturated tint (cyan on blue or teal, hot magenta on violet).
- Heroes get a warm key light and a thin cool cyan rim light on their back edges, which cuts them out from the background.
- The gameplay cards are bright and busy with effects, so they pop against the darker right side.
COMET GARDEN VERSION: invert the value logic. Our gameplay is a dark navy space scene, so put it on light, warm-to-pastel twilight skies. Give each shot its own sky pair:
- lilac dusk
- mint dawn
- peach sunset
- powder-blue morning
- rose evening
- butter noon
Make the sky deeper at the top, behind a white caption, and warm and glowing at the bottom behind the creature. Pick the sky complementary to the featured creature: orange Glimfish on mint or teal, green Bog Frog on rose, pink Steam Flamingo on mint, purple Canopy Octopus on butter, brown Ridge Bear on powder blue. Swap the cyan rim light for a soft white or pale-gold halo; the rare creatures already carry glow halos in the sticker sheet. The floor band is the lightest tint of the sky. The background pattern is our own motif (tiny 4-point sparkles, dotted comet trails, sprouts) at 5-8% contrast. Make sure no two neighbouring shots share a sky hue (Brawl's shots 3 and 4 do).
character_staging:
BRAWL STARS:
- One hero per shot, a different hero every time. Each is a high-polish 3D render, three times the scale of anything in the card.
- Confident 3/4 pose: body turned toward the card, eyes mostly on the viewer (Mandy glances toward the card).
- Playful attitude (smirk, grin, peace sign) and a signature prop held near the face or chest.
- Cropped by the bottom and left edges, so the hero feels too big for the frame.
- Always overlapping the card's left edge, which puts the hero physically in front of the game.
- Cast to the claim: the tuxedo alternate skin sells the skin count, the hard-hat builder sells map creation, the regal candy queen sells the headline mode.
COMET GARDEN VERSION:
- Scale one vector creature from the existing sticker sheet (src/ui/art/critters.ts) up 6-10x, so it is still crisp. Place it in a bottom corner, cropped by the bottom edge, alternating sides.
- The creature touches the card: leaning its chin on the card corner, peeking over the edge, hugging the planet's rim, or holding a comet or seed like a treasure.
- Big eyes and blush kept, a happy open smile, gaze up toward the planet so it leads the eye back to the gameplay. Shot 1 can look at the viewer.
- Cast to the claim:
  - Astronaut kid holding an Ice Comet for flinging
  - Sprout seed for lands growing
  - Tide Otter or Hopper Bunny for creatures moving in
  - Prism Unicorn or World Tree Spirit for rare discoveries
  - Cloud and Sun for the weather or galaxy voyage
  - A cozy Ridge Bear for "calm, no ads"
- Small companions (2-3 in-game-size creatures) can sit on the card's edge for a sense of community.
- No weapons and no attitude. Props are comets, seeds, flowers and stars.
what_makes_it_work: One strict template repeated in every shot, so the set reads as a family in the scroll row; variety comes only from background hue, hero, map biome and effect moment.
Personality first: the hero's face is the largest, highest-contrast element and the first thing read, which sells the collectible characters before the mechanics.
A clear Z reading path (face, gameplay, caption) that maps directly onto the three layout zones.
Overlapping layers (hero over the card edge, caption over the card's bottom) fuse three separate elements into one image with real depth.
A small, plain ~2.3 degree tilt makes a flat capture feel like a physical card with energy, without perspective distortion or a device frame.
Light does the legibility work: a bright glow behind the hero and a dark flat zone behind the white caption, so no caption box or banner is needed.
Gameplay shows the peak effect moment with the HUD stripped to name tags and health bars, so the card is readable and exciting at thumbnail size.
Hero casting proves each claim visually (tuxedo skin for the skin count, hard-hat builder for map making).
Two-size captions: a small setup line over a big payoff noun that is instantly scannable, with numbers used to signal depth.
Background hue chosen as the complement of the hero's main colour for maximum figure-ground pop, plus a cool rim light on the hero.
A bright, angled floor strip grounds the composition and adds left-to-right momentum toward the caption.
transferable_to_comet_garden: Build ONE master portrait template (1290x2796) and vary only sky hue, hero creature, planet biome and caption across all shots. The first 3 shots must also work as a trio, because portrait search results show three side by side.

Replace the phone-frame look used in the current site shots (site/img/shot-*.jpg) with a frameless gameplay card: rounded ~56px corners, rotated 2-3 degrees and alternating direction each shot, with a soft shadow in the sky's deep hue.
Break the frame twice per shot: an oversized creature overlaps a bottom corner of the card, and a comet trail flies out of the card into the sky.
Put the creature's face in front: 40-50% of canvas width, in a bottom corner cropped by the edge, gaze aimed back up at the planet so the eye loops from caption to planet to face and back.

Cast the creature to the claim: astronaut kid with an Ice Comet for flinging, sprout seed for growing, otter or bunny for moving in, unicorn or World Tree Spirit for rare discoveries, bear for calm and no ads.
Two-size caption in Fredoka: a small verb setup line over a big payoff noun, 2-4 words, one claim per shot, with the payoff noun optionally tinted (butter or mint) as our own signature.
Let light do the legibility work: sky deeper at the top behind a white caption, warm glow at the bottom behind the creature. No caption boxes.
Pick each sky as the complement of the featured creature's main colour, and never repeat a hue on neighbouring shots.

Capture peak gameplay moments (a land bursting into a new biome, a creature arriving, the +life pop, a legendary discovery, confetti). Strip the pause button and dev text, but keep one small authentic cue such as the new-creature toast or the goal chip.
Use honest counts for depth (currently 36 species and about 16 biomes in src/core/world.ts; re-check before printing), e.g. a count of creatures to meet.
Ground the creature on a soft rolling hill or cloud floor band in the lightest tint, our gentle answer to Brawl's slanted stripe.
Add a faint tone-on-tone pattern of our own motifs (tiny sparkles, dotted comet trails, sprouts) at 5-8% contrast for texture.

Adapted story arc: 1) Fling comets, grow a world (core loop plus hero); 2) lands grow into biomes; 3) creatures move in (count); 4) rare and legendary friends; 5) the galaxy voyage and postcards; 6) cozy trust: no ads, purchases for grown-ups only. Brawl leads with progression, but a new genre should lead with the core loop.
do_not_copy: The tiled skull-in-star background pattern (Brawl Stars' logo motif) or any skull iconography.
Their chunky rounded all-caps display type with a thick black outline and hard black drop extrusion, the Supercell sticker-logo caption look.
The exact landscape layout and proportions: hero on the left, gameplay card tilted ~2.3 degrees counter-clockwise on the right, caption right-aligned at bottom right over a dark right-side zone.
The hot magenta and cyan slanted floor stripe with its notch step.
Their specific saturated violet, teal and electric-blue palette paired with a 3D glossy toy-render character style.
Character attitude language: smirks, eyepatches, masks, weapons and aggressive poses.
Combat and competitive vocabulary (battles, royale, rank up, brawl) and the 'N+ X and N+ Y' boast phrasing.
Name tags with health bars floating over characters in the gameplay captures.

name: Clash of Clans
full_sequence:
The set has 7 screenshots, not 5. All are landscape 2208x1242 and full-bleed, with no device frame and no badges. I downloaded shots 6 and 7 at 460x0w into shots/, and all 7 at 1100 wide into shots_hi/ for detail.
1 BATTLE: the hook. A raid frozen at its most intense moment. The Town Hall sits dead centre under fire trails, a lightning spell and healer angels. An in-game reward pop-up (a silver star with the word "Awesome!") floats just right of centre. The real HUD stays in: resource meters top-right, the troop and hero bar along the bottom, a 50% damage meter bottom-right and the Attack button bottom-left. Its job is to prove the core action is spectacular and rewarding.
2 DEFEND: a calm counterpoint. A symmetrical base layout editor with gold-filled storages in the middle, a column of green option buttons on the right and level cards along the bottom. Its job is to show strategy, ownership and depth.
3 TEAM-UP: first palette break. A clan-war map in sepia parchment with four friendly chat bubbles stacked on the left (encouragement plus emoji), an orange Join Clan button bottom-centre, and the villager portrait tucked into the Return Home button. Its job is social proof that friendly people are playing.
4 BUILD: the first composited marketing shot. The villager mascot is cropped at the waist bottom-left, making an open-hand gesture, with a speech bubble that says "Build Your Village". A rough white brush-stroke diagonal splits the frame. The left side is a close-up of a humble starter hut and the right side is real placement gameplay (green grid, X and check buttons, level cards). Its job is a warm, welcoming face and making onboarding feel easy.
5 TRAIN: character appeal. Troops sit around campfires under an in-game "Army Camp" label. Three high-fidelity hero renders crowd into the lower-right corner, cropped by the bottom and right edges and overlapping the gameplay. Its job is to promise collectible characters and personality.
6 CLAN WARS: second palette break (sand and tan). A war map with star ratings over each base, a blue Watch Live button and numbered tabs 1-7 along the bottom. Its job is a long-term goal and competition.
7 COLLECT: the close. A forest reward path with green check diamonds, labelled rewards on stone plinths and a glowing hero on a pedestal with a green Claim button. Its job is to end on generosity and progress.
Corrections to the first-pass notes. The set is 7 shots, not 5. There is no dark vignette behind the captions: top-left luminance was equal to or higher than the frame mean on every shot. Legibility comes from the letter treatment itself. Shots 2 and 3 show older game eras and UI than 5 to 7, so the set has been refreshed shot by shot. The fixed caption system is what makes that swapping seamless.
composition_recipe:
Caption block: the same anchor on every frame, top-left, about 2% of width from the left edge and about 4% from the top. Cap height is about 10% of frame height and the width about 25-40% of the frame. Nothing important in the gameplay sits under that corner. Across 7 shots it reads like chapter tabs.
Hero element: the gameplay subject is placed centre or just right of centre (Town Hall, base core, Join Clan, reward plinths), away from the caption corner.
Gameplay placement: 100% full-bleed real captures at the native camera zoom, with no plate, frame or margin. The real HUD is kept in the bottom ~15% band (troop bar, level cards, tabs, CTA) and top-right (resources), so every shot reads as the actual game.
Depth layers: (1) the gameplay capture; (2) in-game feedback and labels such as the reward star pop, building labels and reward names; (3) marketing-only foreground art, used on only 2 of the 7 shots. That art is a mascot with a bubble or a hero trio. It bleeds off the frame edges and overlaps the HUD, which implies a bigger world beyond the screenshot.
Framing devices: one rough brush-stroke diagonal (about 3% of width thick) joins two scenes in one frame. It runs from top ~20% x to bottom ~50% x, and the mascot sits on the seam side.
Rhythm: green, green, parchment, green (composited), green (composited), sand, forest green. About every 2-3 frames the palette or the composition type changes, so the gallery never feels like a single repeated screen.
Margins: essentially zero outside the caption inset. Characters enter from the corner opposite the caption (bottom-left or bottom-right), which keeps a clear diagonal from caption to action.
type_recipe:
Main caption: a heavy, rounded, chunky display face (the game's own brand typeface), all caps, 1-2 words, tight tracking. The fill is a vertical gradient from pure white at the top to pale cool blue-grey at the bottom. A thin dark-navy keyline sits around each letter (about 3% of cap height). A darker blue-grey extrusion or bevel lip sits under each letter (about 8% of cap height). A small soft drop shadow finishes it. Together these give a hard-candy sticker look that stays legible over any busy scene with no backing plate or vignette. The words are mostly bare imperative verbs naming the core loop (Battle, Defend, Build, Train, Collect), with two noun or compound exceptions (Team-up, Clan Wars). There are no sub-lines and no sentences.
Secondary text is always the game's own UI type: white mixed-case labels with a dark outline hovering over objects (the camp label, reward names), plus in-game button text. The one marketing sentence lives inside the mascot's speech bubble: a white card with ornamental corners, heavy black mixed-case text on 2 lines, and a tail pointing at the speaker. All type is in one family, so captions and UI feel native to each other.
color_light_recipe:
Temperature contrast: a cool white and blue-grey caption over warm, saturated scenes, so the caption pops without a plate. The dominant field is saturated grass green on 5 of 7 shots. It is deliberately broken by sepia parchment (shot 3) and sand/tan (shot 6) so the thumbnails alternate.
Accent logic follows the game's UI grammar: orange for the primary CTA (Attack, Join Clan), green for positive or done (Claim, checkmarks, the placement grid), red for cancel, pink/purple and gold for resources.
Light: the game's even top-light is used as captured, with frames chosen at peak FX (fire trails, a lightning bolt, sparkles, smoke, glowing heal circles). Marketing hero renders get a stronger key light, a warm rim and emissive glows (glowing eyes, a fireball in the hand). That makes them noticeably higher fidelity than the game layer, so they read as special.
Reward emphasis: the claimable character in shot 7 sits inside a soft white-green halo glow, and the pop-up star in shot 1 is a bright neutral silver against warm fire. Rewards are the brightest, least saturated spot on the frame.
character_staging:
Characters are used sparingly. Big marketing renders appear on only 2 of the 7 shots. Everywhere else the characters are tiny in-game units, which makes the 2 big moments feel earned.
Shot 4 (guide): one friendly human mascot in the bottom-left corner, cropped at the waist by the frame edge. She is turned three-quarters toward the gameplay, making an open-palm "look at this" gesture, with a speech bubble to her right that states the instruction. She faces inward and her eyeline leads into the scene.
Shot 5 (cast): a trio of heroes packed into the lower-right corner in a stepped triangle of heights. All are cropped by the bottom and right edges and overlap the gameplay and HUD. Each is in a mid-action pose (spear on shoulder, charged glowing hand, determined look), angled toward the centre of the frame.
Shot 7: the reward character is shown as an in-game object on a pedestal, glowing and paired with a Claim button, so the character itself is the prize.
Shot 3: the mascot even appears inside UI (the Return Home portrait), which keeps one familiar face through the set.
Rule: characters come in from the corner opposite the caption, never cover the gameplay's focal point, and always bleed off at least one edge.
what_makes_it_work: A strict caption system: the same corner, size and treatment on all 7 shots. Scanning the row gives the whole core loop in about 7 words, like a table of contents.
Verb-first one-word labels promise things you will DO, not features you will read about.
Honest full-bleed gameplay with the real HUD kept in. No device frame means the landscape art is big and immersive, and players trust what they see.
Shot 1 is frozen at the most intense moment of the loop, with in-game reward feedback ('Awesome!' star) visible, so the thumbnail sells the feeling as well as the mechanic.
The palette rhythm (green, then parchment, then green, then sand) keeps a long gallery from reading as one repeated screen.
Marketing character art is rationed to 2 frames. Cropping it off the frame edges implies a larger world and gives the set a premium, cinematic lift without hiding the game.
Social proof is shown through friendly in-game chat bubbles instead of claims or review quotes.
One brush-wipe composite puts two scenes in one frame (a humble start next to active building), a compact way to show progress.
The set ends on a reward and Claim moment, so the last impression is generosity and progress.
The modular template lets individual shots be refreshed as the game evolves (older and newer eras sit together) without breaking the set's unity.
transferable_to_comet_garden: Change the caption system from sentences to short verb labels: 1-2 words, all caps or bold title case, in one fixed position on every portrait shot (top-centre or top-left inset). Example loop: FLING, GROW, MEET (creatures move in), MIX (Fusions/Combos), COLLECT (Lifebook), HOME (Homeworld). The current full sentences could move to the App Store subtitle and description.

Drop the device frame and flat colour plate and go full-bleed in portrait. Zoom the capture so the planet fills about 70-85% of the frame width. Today it is small inside a phone mockup, which undersells the cute creatures.

Make the caption a legible 'sticker' without a plate. Use the game's own rounded display font with a light gradient fill, a thin keyline and a small bottom extrusion. Reverse Clash's temperature logic for our dark-space scenes: warm starlight cream-to-peach fill with a deep night-navy keyline, so it glows against cool navy and purple space.

Shot 1 = the peak moment: a comet mid-flight on the curved aim line, the impact burst, a '+life' score pop and a creature hopping into new land, all in one frozen frame. That is our equivalent of the reward star pop.

Keep real HUD elements that tell the story (throw counter, life bar, goals, the 'new creature' card), but hide currency and gem counters on every shot. Clash showing currency is a minor red flag we should not copy for a no-ads family game.

Use one guide shot: a large, clean render of the in-game astronaut kid (or a flagship creature) cropped at the bottom corner opposite the caption, facing inward, with ONE short speech-bubble line in our own bubble style (a rounded cloud or star-shaped bubble, not an ornamental card).

Use one cast shot: 3 hero creatures (e.g. bunny, otter, octopus) rendered large, stepped in height, peeking in from a bottom corner and bleeding off the edges over the Lifebook or Homeworld capture. Limit big renders to 2 of 8 shots so they stay special.

Replace the brush-wipe with a signature seam of our own: a glowing comet trail or orbit arc curving through the frame. It splits a bare rocky planet ('before') from a blooming, crowded planet ('after') in one image, to sell growth.

Replace chat-bubble social proof with safe, non-social life proof: a stack of friendly 'moved in' or Visitor gift cards down one side of the frame. There is no multiplayer chat, which fits an all-ages game.

Build a palette rhythm on purpose: pick planets whose dominant biome differs from shot to shot (ocean blue, then forest green, then volcano warm, then ice). Break the run of dark-space frames with 1-2 lighter frames (daytime Homeworld, Lifebook pages).

Close on generosity and trust: a Lifebook or Star Road 'collect' moment with a soft halo on the newly collected creature (free lane only, no Cosmic Pass lane or prices visible), then the grown-ups and no-ads promise as the final frame.
Template the set (fixed caption anchor, fixed type treatment, fixed character-corner rule) so single shots can be swapped per update or season without redoing the whole gallery.
do_not_copy: Supercell's proprietary chunky display typeface, and its caption look: a white-to-blue-grey gradient with a navy keyline and bevel. Build our sticker treatment from Comet Garden's own font and colours.
The rough white brush-stroke diagonal wipe, a recognizable Supercell/Clash marketing device.
The speech bubble card with gold ornamental corner flourishes (Clash UI framing).
Any look-alike of the Clash characters: the red-haired villager guide, a crowned barbarian king, a hooded wizard with glowing eyes, a red-haired valkyrie.
The exact caption word list and order (Battle, Defend, Team-up, Build, Train, Clan Wars, Collect), and combat vocabulary in general.
The sepia parchment or sand war-map treatment with three-star ratings floating over bases.
Orange and green candy-bevel buttons (Attack, Join Clan, Claim) and the numbered orange war tabs.
The isometric grass-tile village with wall grids, and the gold / pink-elixir / dark-elixir / gem resource meters at the top-right.
The combination of top-left all-caps single-word caption + extruded white type + full-bleed isometric green scene. Borrow the system, not that exact signature pairing.

name: Colorever: Gem Art Puzzle
full_sequence:
The set is 5 portrait shots. apps.json lists only these 5 iPhone URLs (there are also 5 iPad shots, which I did not study). I checked shots 1 and 4 at full 1242x2688 resolution. All five use the same template. Only the pixel-art hero and the fill state of the tray change from shot to shot.

1) "Super Relaxing". A pixel-art Christmas tree, caught partway through solving. You can see flat, pale "empty socket" cells among glossy placed gems. The tray is almost full of greens with a yellow row. Its job is the mood hook: it sells a feeling before any mechanic. At search-result size the half-filled art also shows the core loop without a word.

2) "So Satisfying Every Time". A full-bleed square flower tile (peach field, pink petals, green leaves, dark outline beads). It is the densest and most "finished-looking" picture in the set. The tray holds mixed colors. Its job is to promise the payoff, a whole picture completed.

3) Caption about a sparkling art puzzle. A chunky satchel or purse in orange, yellow and pink. It is the widest hero, at about 83% of canvas width. Its job is to name the genre, echoing the "Gem Art Puzzle" in the title so browsers learn what kind of game it is.

4) Caption about one tap sending gems home. A cupcake that looks fully gemmed. The tray has 2.5 rows filled and the rest are empty peach sockets. The two tool buttons are missing in this shot. Its job is the only how-to line in the set. It is weak, though: nothing in the image shows gems in flight (no trails or arcs), so the caption carries all the explaining.

5) "No Timers No Fails". A ball of yarn with a knitting needle in browns, oranges and yellows, plus a teal accent. The tray is almost full. Its job is to close on reassurance: it removes the fear of pressure or losing.

Story arc: calm, then satisfaction, then category, then how it works, then no stress. The emotional claims come first, the mechanic fourth and objection-handling last. There is no logo, app name, character or social proof anywhere in the set.
composition_recipe:
Canvas is 1242x2688 (6.5-inch). There is no device frame and no status bar. The top game HUD (level, coins) is removed. The vertical zones, measured from the files, are identical in all 5 shots:

- 0-13% of the height is empty sky, a deliberate breathing margin.
- 13-49% is the hero art, centered horizontally at 60-83% of the width. Its bottom edge sits on the same line (about 48.5-49%) in every shot, while its top floats with the object's shape. Swiping feels stable because the ground line never moves.
- 49-59% is an empty gap.
- 59-73% is the tray: a rounded rectangle about 78% wide, 4 rows by 12 sockets.
- 78-84% holds two round tool buttons, deliberately tucked half under the caption band.
- 82.5-100% is the caption band. It has a convex dome top: 82.5% at the center, 84.6% at the edges. It takes about 17.5% of the height.

There are three depth layers: a flat pale field, then the real game UI, then the caption band as a foreground "stage apron" that covers part of the UI. That overlap is the only depth cue in the set. There are no callouts, arrows, badges, hands, particles or frame-breaking elements. Roughly 40% of the canvas is empty space, and that emptiness is what makes "relaxing" believable. The caption sits at the bottom, so the art is the first thing the eye lands on from the top.
type_recipe:
The typeface is a heavy, bubbly, rounded display sans (the Fredoka, Baloo, Lilita family of feel). Captions are in Title Case, 2-5 words, always split into two balanced, centered lines with tight leading (about 1.0). Cap height is about 4.5% of canvas height, and the text block spans 40-65% of the width.

The signature treatment is a candy-sticker double outline:
- a white fill (about #FBFCFF),
- a thick inner stroke in deep royal blue (about #0B4DBB, around 6 px at 1242 wide),
- a second, outer halo stroke in pale aqua (about #B4FAFC, around 6 px) that separates the lettering from the mid-blue band.

There is no heavy drop shadow. The type reads at thumbnail size because of weight and outline, not size.

Copy voice: soft first-person-free benefit claims ("Super Relaxing"), one plain mechanic line, and one pair of negations for reassurance. There are no verbs aimed at the player in 4 of 5 captions, no punctuation and no numbers.
color_light_recipe:
Field: a flat, cool pale sky, about #E3F5FF, with no gradient or texture.

Caption band: a vertical gradient from bright cyan (about #44EAFF) just under the rim to deep azure (about #178EEC) at the bottom. The dome edge has a thin pale rim highlight (about #D5EFFE), like a water or jelly surface. The band carries a tone-on-tone five-point-star pattern at about 10-15% contrast.

Tray: warm cream (about #F8E6D8) with a peach bevel rim. It is the one warm neutral against the cool field, so the art and gems pop between two temperature zones.

Hero art: fully saturated candy colors, each bead faceted with a top-left specular and a darker bottom bevel. Every piece has a thin pale die-cut sticker outline and a very soft shadow, so it lifts off the field.

Lighting is flat and even: no vignette, glow, bloom, spotlight or night mode. Saturation is kept for two things only, the art and the band. Everything else is pastel.
character_staging: There are no characters. Each shot's hero is one cheerful everyday object (tree, flower, satchel, cupcake, yarn ball) drawn in bead or pixel art, and the object's charm stands in for a mascot. The heroes change subject and color family in every shot (green, pink/peach, orange/yellow, red/pink, brown/orange), so the swipe feels varied even though the layout never changes. There is no hand, finger or cursor, so the "tap" mechanic is only implied.
what_makes_it_work: Strict template consistency: the same zones, baseline, tray, band and type in all 5 shots, so the set reads as one designed system. That makes it cheap to produce and localize, and each new hero is the only thing that changes.
Real gameplay, cleaned: the status bar and top HUD are stripped, but the board and tray are the actual game, so the listing feels honest and matches the first minute of play.
Mid-solve states teach the mechanic without text. Flat empty cells next to glossy placed gems, and filled versus empty tray sockets, show 'fill the picture' at thumbnail size.
Emotion before mechanics: the first three captions sell calm, satisfaction and sparkle. The how-to arrives fourth and the reassurance closes the set.
Reassurance copy aimed at casual-player anxiety: a pair of negations ('No Timers', 'No Fails') lowers the barrier for young and stressed players.
The hero is anchored to one baseline, so swiping feels like flipping pages of the same book.
Temperature separation: cool field, warm tray, saturated art. Three clear planes without any heavy shading.
Generous empty space (about 40% of the canvas) makes the 'relaxing' claim visible, not just stated.
The caption band overlaps the UI a little, which gives cheap depth and makes the band feel like a soft stage apron, not a pasted-on label.
Double-outline sticker lettering stays legible over a busy gradient and pattern at search-result size.
transferable_to_comet_garden: Lock one template for all 8 shots: the planet always at the same center point and size, the caption container always in the same zone. Our own twist, which Colorever cannot do: make the set a time-lapse of one planet. Shot 1 is sparse with the first comet landing; the last is lush and full of creatures, so the swipe itself tells 'lands grow, friends move in'.

Show mid-action, not finished states: comet mid-flight with its curved aim line, land blooming where it hits, and the on-planet aim tag showing a friend about to move in. That is our version of the half-filled picture, and it fixes Colorever's weakness of claiming motion ('fly home') without showing any.

Order the captions: feeling, then promise, then category, then mechanics, then reassurance last. The planned 'No ads. Purchases stay with grown-ups.' closer is exactly Colorever's objection-handler slot, aimed at parents.

Reassurance must be true for our game. Comet Garden has fail states, a 60 s Meteor Rush mode and one-minute levels, so do NOT borrow 'no timers / no fails'. True claims we can make: no ads, no lives or energy timers, no loot boxes, Data Not Collected, the store behind a grown-ups gate, and Zen Garden as a pressure-free sandbox.
Strip HUD clutter: no status bar, gem counters, prices or menus. Keep only the one HUD element that explains the shot (aim tag, Combo beads, the moved-in card).

Use warm/cool temperature planes: a cool deep-space field against warm land, magma and creature colors, with at most one warm neutral panel. Keep saturation for the planet and the caption container only.
Keep a stable anchor line: fix the planet's center and diameter across shots so swiping feels like one continuous garden.

Borrow the idea of sticker-style layered lettering (light fill, dark inner stroke, lighter outer halo for separation over a busy background), but build it from our own palette and font. Example: cream-white fill, deep navy stroke, soft glow tinted with each scene's element color.

Use a shaped caption container with an organic edge instead of a flat rectangle. Make the edge ours: the curve of a planet horizon, or a comet-trail swoosh, with a creature peeking over or sitting on it (as the planned 'creature overlapping the frame' already intends).
Add a faint tone-on-tone motif inside the caption zone for texture, using our own shapes (tiny comets, seeds, dotted orbits), not stars.

Give each shot one cute 'star' creature (otter, obsidian turtle and so on) as its friendly face, the way each Colorever shot has one charming object. Rotate color families across the set so every swipe feels new.
Leave real empty space around the planet. Space is our natural negative space and it makes 'cozy' visible.
Tuck the caption container slightly over non-essential UI for cheap foreground depth, never over the planet or the creatures.
do_not_copy: The sky-blue domed caption band at the bottom: a cyan-to-azure gradient with a pale jelly rim and a tone-on-tone five-point-star pattern
The exact lettering combination: white bubbly rounded display type with a royal-blue inner stroke and a pale-aqua outer halo
Their caption phrases and pairings: 'Super Relaxing', 'So Satisfying Every Time', the sparkling-art-puzzle line, the one-tap gems-fly-home line, and 'No Timers No Fails'
The pale sky field (#E3F5FF) paired with a cream and peach socket tray
Faceted gem-bead or pixel-art rendering, the 4x12 gem tray with empty peach sockets, and the lightning-bulb and refresh tool buttons half-hidden under the band
Everyday-object bead-art heroes (cupcake, flower, satchel, yarn ball, Christmas tree) with die-cut sticker outlines
Gem-centric art or 'Gem Art' naming. Our currency is also gems, so avoid gem-heavy visuals that echo their brand
The practice of claiming 'no fails' when our game has fail states. It would be both a copy and an inaccurate claim.

name: Dice Dreams
full_sequence:
The set has 6 portrait shots at 1242x2688. Shot 6 was downloaded and viewed; the high-res header was checked at 1242w. The asset filenames suggest the order was put together from modules: slot 1 is a separate "Summer" campaign asset, and slots 2-6 are an evergreen "NewFresh 2026" set of five whose store order (1,3,4,2,5) differs from the file numbering. That points to a swappable seasonal hero plus reorderable evergreen shots, which is typical for Product Page Optimization testing. This is an inference from the filenames, not a confirmed fact.
1) Seasonal key art (no header band): the wordmark sits in the upper third over a blue sky. The orange mascot lounges in a pink float ring at the waterline in mid-frame, holding a drink, with a tiny pink winged buddy nearby. The frame is split above and below the water: dice and coins sink in a cobalt underwater zone that fills the bottom 40%. Palm leaves and fruit bunting frame the top corners, and bubbles and cropped dice sit at the edges. Job: brand recall, mood and a "fresh this season" signal. It sells the character before any mechanic.
2) ROLL: no characters. Three white icon dice tumble mid-air, each about 35-45% of the width, with swoosh trails. Coins arc off with motion streaks over a red-and-gold board tile. Behind them are a sunset magenta-to-peach sky and a rainbow, with flowers in the foreground and a crown prop cropped at bottom-left. Job: the core action shown as a heroic prop moment.
3) COLLECT: an orange-yellow sunburst background. Collectible cards orbit a single green SEND button pulled from the UI. Below, the mascot and a larger red companion share fans of cards over an open album, as bust shots cropped by the bottom edge. Job: collection plus social gifting.
4) SPIN: a winding board path with tiles and a chest at the top. A huge prize wheel with a GO button is cropped off the left edge and fills about 75% of the width. The mascot waves at it from the bottom-right, and dice and coins are cropped at every edge. Job: board progression and rewards (a red flag).
5) COMPETE: the mascot flexes proudly in front of a castle. The lower 45% is a 5-row numbered goal list: the first row is orange and oversized, and the rows below are stepped blue and teal banners with named friends and chest icons. Confetti is scattered over it. Job: the social and competitive meta (a red flag: attack, steal and raid language).
6) RAISE: a cool teal jungle at night. A tiger naps on a vine, a blue elephant plays with a butterfly and a green dragon carries a stick, arranged as a triangle on three depth planes, with a pile of dice in the foreground. Job: the newest feature (pets). It ends on a caretaking, cute beat and gives the set a cool finish after warm shots.
composition_recipe:
The art is full-bleed with no device frame. Real UI is reduced to one iconic element per shot, such as a button, the wheel or list rows, and is never a full screen.
CAPTION BLOCK: the band is identical in every mechanic shot and fills the top 17-19% of the canvas (lower edge at about y=460-510 of 2688). Its lower edge is an asymmetric arc, lowest just left of center and rising toward the right, finished with a two-tone lip: a light highlight stripe over a dark underside shadow. The word sits centered in the band, between about 5% and 13.5% of the canvas height.
HERO ELEMENT: one mechanic object or group fills 50-90% of the width in the 25-65% height zone. It is often deliberately oversized and cropped off one side (the wheel off the left, cards off the right).
CHARACTER: bottom-anchored as a bust crop, cut by the bottom edge or a side edge, 40-60% of the width, in the lower 40%. The eyes land near 45-60% of the height, the visual center. The character faces the viewer and gestures toward the mechanic.
DEPTH LAYERS, back to front: (1) a painted backdrop: sky, rainbow, sunburst, castle or jungle; (2) the mechanic hero, with a bloom halo behind it; (3) the character; (4) oversized, sometimes soft-focus foreground props cropped in the bottom corners (coins, dice, flowers, leaves, a crown); (5) at least one object that overlaps the band's lower edge, such as a die, card or coin, so the band sits inside the scene rather than on top of it.
FLOW: objects sit on diagonals and arcs (a triangle of dice, a ring of cards, an S-curve path) that lead the eye from the caption down to the character.
MARGINS: the scene has none; everything bleeds and something is cropped at every edge, so each shot reads as a window onto a bigger world. The caption's side margins vary from 3% to 25% because the cap height is fixed.
SHOT-1 EXCEPTION: the logo spans y 13-30% and about 58% of the width. The mascot sits on a horizontal waterline at about 58% height, which splits the frame into two worlds.
type_recipe: Each caption is one word in all caps, 4-7 letters, and all are imperative verbs, so the gallery reads as a chain of actions. The typeface is a chunky, rounded, heavy display face with soft corners. The cap height is fixed at about 8.5% of the canvas height (about 230 px on 2688), and word width varies from 53% to 93% of the canvas; longer words get wider rather than smaller. The word is centered and rotated about 2-4 degrees counter-clockwise, with the baseline rising to the right, which adds energy. The fill is a vertical gradient from lemon (about #FCE920) to amber-orange, with a thin bright inner bevel at the top of each letter. It has a thick violet-indigo outline (about 7-8% of the cap height) plus an extrusion offset down and to the left for a 3D slab, and a soft shadow on the band. The captions use the same materials as the wordmark (gold face, purple outline), so every caption echoes the logo. The shot-1 logo is a two-tier stacked wordmark, with the first line in gold and the second in white or lilac, both carrying the purple outline. There is no body copy and no second line anywhere in the set; only the list shot adds small condensed all-caps rows.
character_staging: A single recurring host mascot, an orange gummy-bean creature with big glossy eyes and heavy brows, appears in 4 of the 6 shots (1, 3, 4, 5). It is absent from the pure-prop "roll" shot and from the pets shot, so each of those has a different hero. It is always three-quarter view, faces the camera, has an open-mouth smile and is DOING the verb: lounging with a drink, sharing cards, waving the viewer toward the wheel, flexing. It is staged as a bottom-anchored bust at 40-60% of the frame width, cropped by the frame edge so it feels in front of the glass, with its eyes near the vertical center. A second character (a red buddy or a tiny winged pal) appears only as a social or scale cue: slightly behind, smaller and warmer. The pets shot introduces a new cast of three species on three depth planes (top vine, mid-left, bottom-right) in a triangle, each with its own gesture (sleeping, playing, carrying). There are no human avatars, and the characters never look at each other at the viewer's expense; eye contact goes to the viewer.
what_makes_it_work: Each caption is a single short verb that is readable even in a search-result thumbnail, and read left to right the captions become the whole game loop
A band that is identical across shots gives the gallery strip a strong rhythm and a brand block, while only the scene below changes
No device frame plus zoomed, re-staged crops: game objects render at 30-90% of the width, so they stay legible at thumbnail scale
Motion cues (swoosh trails, arcing coins, tilted tumbling objects, a tilted caption) make still images feel kinetic
An expressive host character faces the viewer and points at the mechanic, so appeal and instruction come in one gesture
One dominant ambient hue per shot makes the set feel varied but controlled, and warm and cool alternation stops the strip from blurring together
The scene is brighter than the header band, pulling the eye from the word into the action
Objects overlapping the band edge, plus crops at every edge, create depth and suggest a world bigger than the frame
Real UI is reduced to one iconic element (a button, the wheel, list rows) and shown as a prop, never as a busy screen
Slot 1 is swappable seasonal key art, so the storefront looks fresh without redrawing the evergreen set; modular shots allow order testing
transferable_to_comet_garden: Drop the phone bezel from most shots (our current set frames every shot in a device, which shrinks the planet to about 40% of the width). Re-stage each shot as a hero moment instead: the planet at 95-120% of the canvas width, cropped off one side or the bottom, keeping only the aim line and the on-planet aim tag from the UI, the way they keep only the wheel or a SEND button

Turn the captions into a chain of one-word verbs (two words at most), in our own words and our own warmer voice, so the first three thumbnails alone tell the loop: fling, then the land grows, then friends move in. Keep one fixed cap height of about 8% of the canvas height, let word width vary, and never shrink longer words

Keep one caption container that is identical across shots for rhythm, but make it ours: a deep-space navy cap whose lower edge is a planet's curved horizon or an orbit ellipse traced by a comet trail, with a faint tone-on-tone starfield in place of a glyph pattern
Break that edge in every shot: a comet whose trail starts inside the caption zone and swoops into the scene, a critter's ears or a moon poking over the arc. That puts the caption inside our world

Render our projectiles (rock, ice comet, magma, seed pod) as large floating hero props at 20-35% of the width, tilted, with curved glowing trails and sparkles, the way they treat their tumbling dice. Motion makes the stills feel alive

Use a recurring host pair: the astronaut kid plus one signature critter appear in about 4 of 6 shots as bottom-anchored busts cropped by the edge, facing the viewer with eyes near the vertical center and doing the verb (pointing along the aim line, cheering at new land, hugging a newcomer). Give one shot no characters, with the planet and comets as the hero, and one shot a new cast (a family portrait of rare critters)

Give each shot one dominant hue tied to a biome (meadow green, ocean teal, ember orange, ice blue, aurora violet) and alternate warm and cool along the strip. Keep the scene's middle zone brighter than the caption band so the eye falls into the action
Replace flat color fills with a radial focal glow: a soft star halo or sunburst behind the planet, like their sunburst behind the cards

Try a split-horizon hero: the planet's curved surface crosses the lower half as a horizon, with critters living on it in close-up, while a comet arrives from the sky above. This echoes their above-and-below-waterline split and shows the landscape at critter scale

Make slot 1 swappable key art (logo plus a lush planet plus friends) in a seasonal skin (a snowy planet, a spring-blossom planet), separate from an evergreen set of modular shots that can be reordered for Product Page Optimization tests

Adapt their numbered-list shot kindly: at most 3 cozy things to try (for example, grow a forest beside the sea), each row with a creature portrait instead of a chest and the top row highlighted. No friend names, no competitive or attack verbs, no rewards or currency amounts
End warm: put the collection or caretaking beat (the creature family) as the last creative shot, then our trust shot (no ads, purchases stay with grown-ups)
Borrow the complementary-pair principle rather than their colors: our cool navy space frame against warm glowing planets and sunny critters
Crop foreground props in the bottom corners (seed pods, pebbles, flowers, stardust), slightly oversized and soft, to add a near-depth layer
do_not_copy: The violet header band with a curved lower lip (lilac highlight rim over a dark purple underside) and the faint tiled brand-glyph watermark
Gold-to-amber gradient all-caps captions with a thick violet-indigo outline, a down-left 3D extrusion and a slight counter-clockwise tilt (their logo-matching title material)
Their exact one-word caption words and the same all-caps single-verb cadence (ROLL, COLLECT, SPIN, COMPETE, RAISE)
The two-tier crowned wordmark (a crown perched on the first letter, a gold line over a white or lilac line, purple outline)
The orange gummy-bean mascot with heavy dark brows, its red companion and the tiny pink winged buddy; avoid any orange blob host with bold brows
White dice with icon faces, the spiral-emblem gold coins and the red-and-gold board-tile mat
The prize wheel with numeric wedges and a central GO button, and the winding board path with a treasure chest
A numbered list of friend-named social actions (attack, steal, block, raid) with tiered treasure chests
A mascot lounging in a pool float with a drink as the seasonal hero
A violet-frame-plus-orange-mascot-plus-gold-type palette as our primary scheme
Anything that reads as chance or gambling: rolling, spinning for coin values, chest reveals, currency showers

name: Flambé: Merge and Cook
full_sequence:
The set has 5 portrait iPhone shots and nothing more to download (apps.json lists exactly 5). There is no device frame. Four shots use one orange caption band at the bottom. Read in order, the four captions spell out the game loop. The last shot is logo key art with no band.

1. MERGE (the hook, a real game screen caught mid-action). The whole merge board is visible with the real HUD on top (day, energy, coins, gems, shop) and a customer portrait asking for a dish. Two tomato halves are blown up to about 1.6 board cells, each with a warm glow behind it. A thick orange-to-yellow curved arrow sweeps up from them to a giant carrot, about 2.5 cells and 19% of screen height. The carrot bursts out of the board into the HUD area and over the customer panel, with a yellow starburst bloom behind it. Job: show the core action and its reward in a single glance, sized to read at thumbnail scale.

2. COOK (the rule, shown as a diagram). The HUD stays at the top. Behind everything is a restaurant interior blurred with shallow depth of field. Four ingredients sit in an arc, each on a white glowing sticker halo: garlic, meat, butter, greens. Orange arrows point from them into a pan, then a green arrow points down to the finished dish, which has sparkles and bloom around it. The chef stands in the right third, facing three-quarters, hand on hip, and holds the plate out to the viewer. The band crops her at mid-thigh. Job: teach how the game works (inputs turn into an output) with no words, and introduce the mascot.

3. RENOVATE (the payoff, as before and after). A white seam about 2% of the width runs diagonally, falling left to right at about 25 degrees, which matches the isometric floor angle. Above it is a restored, lit dining room with diners. Below it is the same space ruined, dark and dusty. A curved orange arrow rises from the ruin, crosses the seam and lands in the restored room. The HUD and side buttons are still there. Job: show that you make visible progress you can own.

4. UNLOCK (depth and more to come). The screen is split into three stacked panels by two white seams that tilt in opposite directions (about 8 to 9 degrees each). At the top is a bright teal-and-cream bakery. In the middle is a warm pub full of patrons with food wish bubbles over their heads. At the bottom is a dark, desaturated dining hall with a big glossy gold padlock in the center. Job: show there are many more places to reach and tease what comes next.

5. Key art (no band). The chef is larger, facing three-quarters, one finger raised, over a pan throwing up blue and orange flames. The flaming script logo sits above her. Warm light rays come through a window. Blurred produce fills the foreground corners. A loading bar with a playful status line sits at the bottom. Job: brand recall and mascot charm to close. This is also the weakest slot, because it shows a loading screen and not gameplay.
composition_recipe: Canvas: full-bleed game screen, no device frame, measured at 460x996. Caption band: bottom about 16% of the height. The band's top edge is a shallow convex arch: 83.8% of height at the center and 85.3% at the edges, so it rises about 1.5% of height (about 3% of width) in the middle. A 2 to 3px pale-yellow rim highlight runs along the arch. The band is filled with a vertical gradient plus a tiled pattern of themed line icons at roughly 10 to 15% contrast. The band is identical in every shot and only the word changes. Caption: one centered word, optical center at about 91% of height (a little above the band's middle). Cap height is fixed at about 5.5% of screen height, and words are never scaled to fit, so width runs 42 to 73% of screen width depending on the word. Hero element: sits in the upper half, where the eye lands first. It is enlarged 1.6 to 2.5 times its in-game size and allowed to break its container (the board and the HUD). Behind it are a soft radial bloom and a curved motion arrow tying cause to effect. Gameplay: at least 4 of 5 shots keep the real top HUD strip, so composites still read as the actual game. Depth layers, back to front: (a) the game screen, or a heavily blurred interior used as a bokeh backdrop, (b) seams or panels that split the canvas, (c) oversized hero props on white glow halos, (d) arrows and 4-point sparkles, (e) a character anchored to a side third and cropped by the band so she seems to stand on it, (f) the band as the front stage lip. Split layouts: a single diagonal seam follows the art's own perspective lines (the isometric floor angle). A three-panel stack uses opposing tilts about 8 to 9 degrees off horizontal with about 2%-width white strokes. The dimmed or locked panel always goes last, at the bottom. Margins: the HUD sits against the top safe area, and a hero may cross the HUD but never the band. The band's word keeps at least 13% side margins even for the longest word.
type_recipe: One word per shot, all caps, a verb in the imperative. The typeface is a heavy, rounded, slightly soft and hand-made display sans with blobby joins (in the family of Baloo or Fredoka Bold, but chunkier). Fill is a vertical gradient from near-white (#FFFFF6) at the top of the caps to butter yellow (about #FBF599) at the baseline. A thin darker burnt-orange outline (about #B6613C, roughly 1.5% of cap height) sits outside the fill, plus a soft, slightly offset drop shadow in a darker shade of the band color, no hard black. Tracking is normal to slightly tight. Cap height is fixed across shots (about 5.5% of screen height), so the words feel like one typographic system, not separately fitted headlines. There is no secondary line, subtitle, badge or bullet anywhere, and the one sign-off line of text is the in-game loading status on the key art. Because each caption is a single verb, the words work as a table of contents for the game loop when read left to right in the carousel. For Comet Garden: keep the idea of one fixed-size rounded display face, one verb and one line. The fill should run from warm starlight cream to a pale peach or mint tint, not white to butter. The outline and shadow should be a deep version of our own band color (indigo or violet), not burnt orange.
color_light_recipe: Band: a vertical gradient from amber (about #F89402) at the arch to deep orange (about #F55700) at the bottom, with a pale-yellow (about #FFE155) rim light along the top edge. The pattern is lighter orange line art of kitchen objects. Scenes: warm key light from the upper left or a window throughout, honey-wood and golden interiors, and teal or green accents (upholstery, bakery trim, the green result arrow) as the one cool contrast color. Glow: every hero prop has a soft white sticker halo, and the reward moments add a large yellow radial bloom and starburst. Color-coded arrows: the input or process arrows are an orange-to-gold gradient, and the arrow that points at the finished result is green (the success color). State contrast: ruined or locked areas are darkened to roughly 40 to 50% brightness and desaturated toward grey-brown but not fully grey, so they read as the same place, not yet alive. Unlocked areas are fully saturated and lit. Depth: the backdrop is defocused with a strong blur on shot 2 so the stickers pop, and the key art uses blurred foreground produce in the corners plus light rays for atmosphere. Contrast rule: the caption is always the lightest value on the screen and the band is the most saturated block, so the word reads first even at search-result size.
character_staging: The mascot (the chef) appears in 2 of 5 shots and bookends the second half: the explainer and the closer. In shot 2 she stands in the right third, three-quarter view, head at about 40% of height, making eye contact with the viewer and smiling. One hand is on her hip and the other presents the finished dish toward the center of the diagram, so she acts as the diagram's endpoint and host. The band crops her at mid-thigh, which makes the band read as a stage floor and pushes her toward the viewer. In shot 5 she is bigger and waist-up, in a dynamic pose (finger raised, hip cocked). The logo floats above her head and the effect (flames) comes from what she is doing, so the character is doing the core fantasy, not just posing. Secondary characters give the reason and the life of the game. Shot 1 has a customer portrait in the order panel (someone wants something). In shots 3 and 4, small in-world NPC diners fill the restored spaces, and some have wish bubbles showing the dish they want. Characters never cover the hero prop. They frame it from the side or sit inside UI panels. Nobody appears in the locked or ruined zones: emptiness is part of the before state.
what_makes_it_work: Read in carousel order, the one-word captions state the whole loop (merge, cook, renovate, unlock), so a browser learns the game from four words without reading a sentence.
The first shot is the core action at its peak (mid-merge with the reward bursting out), not a menu, logo or idle board. The hook is the verb happening.
The hero objects are enlarged 1.6 to 2.5 times and allowed to break out of their container into the HUD, so they read at thumbnail size and feel like they are popping out of the screen.
Curved arrows link cause to effect in every explanatory shot, so the eye travels a planned path from input to reward, ending in the top half.
The same band (color, arch, pattern, type size) on every shot makes the set read as one designed system and gives strong brand recall in a crowded search results page.
The before-and-after split follows the art's own perspective (isometric angle), so it looks native to the game, not like a clumsy collage.
Dim, desaturated, empty areas against lit, populated ones make progress visible and aspirational without any text explaining it.
The input-to-output diagram (ingredients to pan to dish) teaches the rule with icons alone. Orange process arrows and a green result arrow add one more layer of meaning.
The real HUD stays on the composite shots, so even staged scenes feel like the actual game and not concept art.
A strict value hierarchy: the caption is always the lightest value and the band the most saturated block, the hero gets the warmest bloom, and the backgrounds are blurred or dimmed so they step back.
It uses only 5 shots, so every slot has one clear job and there is no filler.
transferable_to_comet_garden: Replace the current 8 multi-word captions with one verb per shot in loop order, for example FLING, GROW, MATCH, MEET, COLLECT, and optionally a calm closing line on the last shot. The carousel then reads as the game loop. Localize the verbs, not phrases (German, Japanese and others stay short).

Drop the device frames and go full-bleed so the planet can be about 70 to 80% of the screen width instead of about 45% inside a phone mockup. The current contact sheet shows a small planet lost in a dark frame.

Shot 1 hook: catch a real fling mid-flight with the comet (and its trail) enlarged about 2 times and breaking past the planet rim into the top HUD area. Put a soft radial bloom at the impact point and a curved arrow from the slingshot to the land that is sprouting. Keep the aim tag visible so the reward shows.

Before-and-after planet: split the planet with a seam that follows its own curve or radius (our version of following the isometric angle). One side is a bare grey rock planet and the other is lush with forest, ocean and creatures, with a curved arrow crossing from barren to alive. Dim the barren half to about 45% brightness and desaturate it, but not fully grey.

Recipe diagram for the neighbor rule: Forest and Ocean tiles on white glow halos, warm process arrows converging onto a piece of the planet, then a green result arrow down to the otter that moves in. Put a blurred starfield or nebula bokeh behind it. This is the exact Comet Garden version of the ingredients-to-dish diagram.

Creature wish bubbles: small in-world bubbles over creatures showing the biome they want (a volcano icon over the obsidian turtle). They borrow the diner food bubbles to hint at the matching mechanic with no text.

Stage our astronaut kid mascot like the chef: in a side third, three-quarter view, eye contact, holding out or cuddling a newly arrived creature toward the diagram, cropped by the caption band so they stand on it. Bring the kid back in the last shot, larger, with the logo.

Make one Comet Garden caption band our signature. Keep the same mechanics (bottom 16%, shallow arch, rim light, faint themed pattern, fixed cap height about 5.5%), but make the arch a planet horizon: a twilight indigo-to-violet gradient, an aurora-mint rim light, and a faint pattern of comets, seeds, ice crystals, tiny planets and paw prints. Optionally let a creature's ears or a grass tuft peek over the rim, which is our own twist and something Flambé never does.

Tease depth with a dimmed Star Map stack in three slanted panels (a lit chapter, a lively chapter, a dim silhouetted chapter). Use creature silhouettes plus a twinkle or a question mark, not a gold padlock, so progression never reads as a paywall to parents.

Keep a slim real HUD (planet name, throw count, goal chip) on the composite shots for authenticity, but crop or hide the gem and stardust counters and any shop entry. The current Homeworld and Lifebook shots show 2,710 and 69 currency counters.

The value rule for every shot: the caption is lightest, the band is the most saturated block, the hero gets the warmest bloom, and the background (the dark space) gets bokeh or a gentle vignette so the planet pops at thumbnail size.

Close with key art that is still honest: mascot, planet and logo, plus our family promise (no ads, purchases only for grown-ups) as a small secondary line. Never use a loading screen or a progress bar.
Tighten the set toward 5 or 6 strong shots with one job each, and move secondary features (Troubles, sky obstacles) to later slots or cut them.
do_not_copy: The orange (amber to deep orange) caption band with its tiled kitchen and food line-icon pattern: this is Flambé's signature frame.
The chunky white-to-butter-yellow all-caps word treatment with a burnt-orange outline on orange, which is their exact caption look.
The exact verb sequence and wording (MERGE, COOK, RENOVATE, UNLOCK), including reusing any of those four words as a caption.
The flaming script Flambé logo, the frying-pan logotype and the blue-and-orange flambé flame effects.

The chef character design: a brunette in a white double-breasted chef coat with a red neckerchief, a red headscarf and a striped brown apron, plus her hand-on-hip plate-presenting pose repeated one-to-one.
The elderly customer portrait in a green cardigan inside an order panel.
The glossy gold cartoon padlock centered on a dimmed area as the unlock icon.
The HUD style: a calendar-page day badge, an energy bolt with a timer, coin and gem pills with plus buttons, and a storefront shop icon.
The key-art-on-a-loading-screen closer with a cute cooking status line and a green progress bar.
The restaurant and renovation subject matter (ruined dining room turned plush green-velvet booths), which only makes sense for their game anyway.

name: Foodstars: Merge & Cook
full_sequence:
7 portrait shots (1290x2796, full-bleed, no device frame). Shots 1-6 share the same bookends: the real top HUD strip (avatar/level, energy, coins, gems, shop icon) across the top ~6%, and an identical teal caption band across the bottom ~15-17%. Only the middle changes. The HUD numbers and level badge change on every shot (lvl 44, 30, 8, 40, 19, 5), which quietly signals that these come from different points in a long game.
1 "Choose": a large painted hero chef, rim-lit with a yellow sticker-glow outline, smiles at the viewer and holds a steaming ramen bowl near the center of the canvas. The background is a blurred warm cafe interior. The bottom third is a row of 4 character-select cards: the first is selected with a glow, and a pointer cursor sits on it. Job: lead with a face and personality, show the cast's diversity, and offer the player agency right away.
2 "Merge": the real merge board fills the frame (pink checker grid of items), with two customer-order cards above it. In the center, one merge is enlarged about 2x: two small popcorn cones joined by an orange plus sign, with curved arrows sweeping up into a big popcorn bucket, all on a white-yellow radial burst with sparkles. Job: explain the core mechanic in one glance.
3 "Cook": a hero chef grilling skewers with real flames in the lower half. The upper half is a recipe diagram running diagonally from top-left to lower-right: ingredients with plus signs, then an arrow into a grill appliance, then an arrow to the finished dish. Every node has a yellow glow outline. Job: show the second layer of the loop (production chain) and connect it to a character.
4 "Renovate": a diagonal before/after split with a glowing light-beam divider. The left side is warm, saturated and covered in flowers, with a cafe full of happy customers. The right side is dim, grey-brown, cobwebbed and in ruins, with a tired worker sweeping. A curved teal arrow points from the ruin side to the restored side. Job: the transformation payoff (the meta goal).
5 "Unlock": a vertical list of restaurant cards (No.3 locked, No.2 at a 76% progress bar, No.1 marked completed with a Continue button). Chef characters break out past the left edges of the cards, and a finger cursor on a right-side progress rail implies scrolling. Job: breadth of content and long-term progression.
6 "Help Them": story hook. A cold, frost-covered ruined room, with a shivering mother and a crying child (snow on their heads, shiver lines) in the foreground. Speech-bubble icons for the tools needed (hammer, extinguisher, planks) are pinned to glowing, highlighted repair spots. Job: emotional motive and narrative, 'you fix their lives'. It works by eliciting pity.
7 (no caption band; file named 'en', so localized): full-bleed key art. The logo lockup sits top-center over an autumn park food market, with the whole 4-chef cast running toward the camera flipping pancakes. Job: brand close, an ensemble group shot and a memory anchor. The logo comes last, not first.
Search-result preview (first 3) = face, then mechanic, then face plus recipe.
composition_recipe: Canvas zones: top ~6% is the real HUD strip, which grounds the shot as gameplay and repeats on every shot as a series rhythm. The middle ~77% is one hero idea. The bottom ~15-17% is the caption band, whose top edge is a gentle wave (white ribbon plus thin gold pinstripe) that rises slightly left to right. Hero rules: one dominant subject per shot, 50-65% of canvas height, with its visual center at about 40-50% of the height. Supporting explainer graphics (plus signs, curved arrows, enlarged items) sit in the space the hero leaves open, usually the upper half, and read top-to-bottom or diagonally, ending near the hero's hands or the board center. Depth stack, back to front: (1) scene background blurred like a shallow depth of field, or real gameplay UI dimmed slightly around the focus; (2) mid-layer real UI (board, cards, list); (3) oversized overlay object or character with a glow outline, allowed to overlap UI and break card edges; (4) caption band on top. Before/after uses a diagonal from lower-left to upper-right so the 'after' state sits upper-left, where the eye lands first, with a curved arrow bridging the two halves. Margins: captions about 70% of the width, centered, with no side text. Characters may bleed off the left or right edge, but faces never do. The final shot drops every frame element for pure key art with the logo in the top 20%.
type_recipe: One word (at most two), title case, centered in the bottom band. Cap height about 6% of canvas height, so it reads at search-thumbnail size. Face: a heavy, rounded, chunky display sans with soft terminals. Fill: a vertical gradient from near-white at the top to pale butter-yellow at the bottom. A thin outline in a darker shade of the band color, a soft dark drop shadow offset straight down, and a slight bevel or highlight, so the word looks like a pressed candy or plastic toy rather than flat text. The captions form a verb loop where each is an imperative naming the step shown, so the 6 captions read in order as the game's core loop and meta. No sublines, no body copy, no badges. The only other type is the logo in shot 7.
color_light_recipe: Warm subject, cool anchor. Every scene is warm and saturated (food reds, oranges, yellows, wood browns, pink board), and the constant caption band is a saturated teal with a vertical gradient (lighter aqua at the top to deep teal at the bottom) and a tone-on-tone repeating star pattern at low opacity. The complementary contrast makes each shot's warmth pop and makes the row recognizable in the store. Lighting shows focus: a yellow outer glow or sticker-stroke around whatever the viewer should look at (hero character, recipe nodes, repair spots, the selected card), and white-yellow radial bursts with sparkles behind the result of a mechanic. The background is pushed back with blur and warm bokeh. Emotional states use grading: restored or happy means warm, saturated and sunlit; broken or sad means desaturated grey-brown, and cold uses a blue-grey haze with snow. The before/after divider is a bright light beam, so the transition itself glows. The final key art uses an open daylight sky, autumn oranges, green grass and a pastel skyline for an airy, outdoor release after the interior shots.
character_staging: Characters are high-fidelity painted illustrations, noticeably more detailed than the in-game sprites, composited over real UI. The hero pose is three-quarter or frontal, with eye contact, a big open smile and hands presenting the product (the bowl, the grill), so the character literally hands the game to the viewer. Heroes are cropped at the waist or knees and very large (the shot 1 head is about 25% of canvas width). A glow outline separates them from blurred backgrounds. Supporting characters appear small inside the scene (customers at cafe tables, the worker sweeping) to make the world feel lived-in. In list or card UI, characters overlap and break out of their card frames for depth. The cast lineup in the select cards and the final group shot shows diversity and invites the viewer to pick a favorite. The group shot is an action pose, everyone mid-motion toward the camera doing the game's activity. Shot 6 uses distressed characters (tears, shivering, a pregnant mother in the cold) as a pity hook. That is effective for adults but unsuitable for an all-ages cozy game.
what_makes_it_work: The captions are the game loop: each shot is one verb, and reading the row left to right teaches the whole game in about 3 seconds with no body copy.
Fixed bookends (the same top HUD strip and the same bottom caption band) make the 6 very different middles read as one designed set and give strong brand recall in a crowded search row.
Mechanics are explained with a shared visual grammar (plus signs, curved arrows, enlarged inputs merging into a bigger glowing output) rather than words, so it works in any language.
Each shot has exactly one focal point, marked with a yellow glow and a radial burst, and everything else is blurred, dimmed or smaller.
The first shot is a face, not UI: a big, warm, eye-contact character creates an emotional hook before any mechanic is shown.
The diagonal before/after with a glowing divider and a bridging arrow sells transformation (the meta payoff) in a single frame.
Oversized painted characters composited over real UI get the charm of key art and the honesty of real gameplay in the same shot.
Varied level and currency numbers across shots imply a long, deep game without saying so.
Warm scenes against a cool constant band create complementary contrast that pops at thumbnail size.
The logo and ensemble key art close the set as a memorable brand moment instead of spending the valuable first slot on a logo.
transferable_to_comet_garden: Rewrite the caption set as a short verb loop that tells the game in order, e.g. Fling, Grow, Welcome (friends move in), Fuse, Collect, Build. Apple now reads caption text for search, so pair each big verb with a small 3-5 word subline to keep the keyword value that one-word captions lose (e.g. big 'Grow' + small 'lands bloom on tiny planets').

Drop the device frame and go full-bleed. Keep a thin, real top HUD strip (planet name, throws, life bar), but never show currency or gem counters, and never '+' buy buttons. Our current Homeworld and Lifebook shots show the sparkle and gem counters, so crop or hide them.

Build a consistent bookend for the whole set in our own shape: a caption area whose top edge is the convex curve of a planet horizon, or a comet-trail swoosh, in a deep night-navy that complements warm planet colors, with tiny constellation dots instead of a repeating pattern.

Hero-scale the creatures. Shot 1 should be a large, rim-lit Hopper Bunny or the astronaut kid, about 50% of canvas height, cradling a glowing comet and looking at the viewer, with the real planet and aim line behind it at 50-60% brightness. Our creatures are tiny in-game, so enlarging them 5-10x as hero art fixes the 'can't see the cute' problem.

Fusion explainer in the arrow-and-plus grammar: Ice Comet icon + Ember land tile, then a curved arrow into an oversized STEAM! or Rain Garden result on a radial sparkle burst, placed over the real Fusion moment on the planet.

Before/after for 'lands grow': one planet split diagonally, with a bare grey rock on one side and a lush, creature-filled world on the other. Use a comet streak as the divider, with the comet itself as the bridging 'arrow'. Put the lush side upper-left.

Replace the pity hook with a gentle 'someone needs a home' moment: a curious creature on a bare patch with a thought bubble showing what it wants (a water drop, a tree, warmth), and the matching land tile glowing. The feeling is hopeful, never tears or shivering.

Lifebook or Homeworld as the progression shot: planet or creature cards where the creatures pop out past the card edges, with one card complete, one mid-progress with a bar, and one softly 'coming up' rather than a hard lock.
Use a yellow-gold glow outline on the single thing each shot is about (the aim tag, the new creature, the fused tile), and dim or blur the rest of the UI.

Close the set with an ensemble key-art shot: logo at the top, and all creature friends celebrating on a flourishing planet under a comet shower. Keep our 'No ads. Purchases stay with grown-ups.' trust shot as a differentiator; Foodstars has nothing like it.
Vary the planet number, name and life total across shots (Planet 3, 24, 46...) so the set implies a long journey without saying it.
do_not_copy: The teal bottom caption band with a white wave ribbon, a thin gold pinstripe and a tone-on-tone repeating star pattern
The combined type treatment: a white-to-butter-yellow gradient chunky word with a teal outline and a downward drop shadow sitting on a teal band
Their exact caption words and order ('Choose', 'Merge', 'Cook', 'Renovate', 'Unlock', 'Help Them')
The chef cast and its specific designs (red-bow ramen chef, long-haired blond grill chef, parrot-on-shoulder chef), and the four-chef pancake-flipping group key art
