The Foodstars wordmark style: cream letters in a rounded green frame topped by a chef hat with three stars
The 'No.1 / No.2 / No.3' plaque badges, the 'Completed!' ribbon and the restaurant-card list layout with a right-side progress rail
The pink checkered merge board and the popcorn cone-to-bucket merge vignette
Their exact before/after composition: a diagonal light-beam split with a curved teal arrow and a flower-covered cafe versus a cobwebbed ruin
The pity hook of crying, freezing or pregnant characters under frost; wrong for an all-ages cozy game
Top HUD currency bars with '+' purchase buttons (energy, coins, gems) and the shop-awning icon; a red flag for a no-pressure, family game

name: Hay Day
full_sequence:
The live set has 7 landscape shots (2688x1242 source), not 5. Source filenames say "YellowVersionRoundedCornerTextboxes", which suggests they tested caption box colors and corner styles. Slot 4 comes from a separate 2026 "BoatDestinations" file that was dropped into the evergreen template. First-pass correction: the caption plaque is a level rounded rectangle, not slanted.

1. KEY ART, brand promise. Full-bleed painted farm with a dirt path that leads the eye to the farmhouse at the vanishing point. Logo with a wheat sprig sits top-left. The plaque sits top-right and bleeds off the right edge, with a headline about a pocket-sized country escape and no subline. A cow in extreme close-up (sleepy half-lidded eyes) fills the left third. A chicken peeks out below it, and a wide-eyed sheep is cropped off the bottom-right corner. There is no UI. Job: in landscape only one shot shows in search, so this one carries the brand, the mood and the promise alone.
2. CORE LOOP ("Embrace Farm Life", subline about tending crops and raising animals). The card shows real farm gameplay: animal pens, crop rows, the delivery truck and the HUD. A chicken hero leans in from the bottom-left over the card edge. As a gag, a second chicken hangs upside down from behind the card's top-right corner. Job: prove the game looks like the key art, and show the everyday loop.
3. SOCIAL ECONOMY ("Share The Bounty", subline about trading with neighbors). The card shows the roadside shop screen: crates of goods with coin prices under a striped awning, so a UI panel reads as a market stall. A grinning pig with big teeth sits bottom-left. Job: show trading and that other people are in the game.
4. BREADTH / LIVE-OPS SLOT ("More Than A Farm", subline about new places to explore). The card holds a collage of three tilted painted snapshots (beach, harbor town, night swamp), each with a handwritten place name on a paper strip. A purple-green fish leaps out of a water splash at bottom-left and breaks the frame. Job: novelty and "there is more". This is the swappable seasonal slot, placed 4th so the evergreen opener stays.
5. EXPANSION ("Find New Pastures", subline about growing the farm and exploring). The card shows a lakeside expansion area with a fishing dock. A dog with its tongue out sits bottom-left. Job: progression and new land.
6. SELF-EXPRESSION ("Express Yourself", subline about decorations). The card shows the decoration catalog panel next to a decorated farm path. A calico kitten with its mouth open sits bottom-left. Job: customization and ownership.
7. COMMUNITY / ASPIRATION ("Farm With Friends", subline about starting a neighborhood). The card shows a lush late-game friend's farm with a welcome sign, gazebo and pets. A bug-eyed sheep sits bottom-left. Job: aspirational end state plus social close. The sheep also bookends shot 1.
composition_recipe:
Shots 2-7 use one fixed template (measured at 1200x554):
- BACKDROP PLATE: one identical painted landscape on every shot: sky with a cloud at top-left, tree clump at right, dirt path and picket fence at bottom-left, wheat field at right. It is slightly softer and less detailed than the card.
- GAMEPLAY CARD (mid layer): a full screenshot scaled to about 70%, keeping the device aspect ratio (about 2.1:1). It spans x 14-85% and y 5-77%, is roughly centered and pushed up, with about 5% top margin and 23% bottom margin. It has a thin white rim (about 0.8% of frame width) and large rounded corners (about 3% of width). There is no device frame. The real HUD stays in and gets partly cropped or covered.
- CAPTION PLAQUE (front layer): about 52% of frame width and 27% of height. It is anchored bottom-right with a margin of about 2% of frame width. It overlaps the bottom of the card by about 10% of frame height and runs past the card's right edge onto the backdrop.
- HERO CHARACTER (front layer): anchored bottom-left, about 25-30% of frame width and 55-65% of frame height. It is cropped by the left and bottom frame edges and overlaps the card's lower-left edge. It never overlaps the plaque.
- The result is a triangle of card (top-center, "look"), plaque (bottom-right, "read") and character (bottom-left, "feel"). Positions never change, so the eye learns where to read after one shot.
- KEY ART (shot 1) breaks the template on purpose: full-bleed scene, logo top-left, plaque top-right bleeding off the edge. Characters frame the vista like theater curtains at three depths (huge foreground cow, mid-ground chicken, sheep on the right). A path leads to the vanishing point.
- The collage variant (shot 4) keeps the same card frame but fills it with three tilted snapshots, so even the special slot stays on template.
PORTRAIT TRANSLATION for Comet Garden (1290x2796):
- Plaque fixed at the top (about 4-22% of height), overlapping the card's top edge. The first three portrait tiles show together in search, where the top band is read first.
- Card at y 18-80% and about 80% of width, cropped tight on the planet and aim line rather than the full screen.
- Hero creature at the bottom (about 40-45% of width), breaking the card's bottom edge and bleeding off the frame. Alternate the left and right corner shot to shot so a three-tile row zig-zags.
- One constant backdrop plate behind everything.
type_recipe:
Hay Day:
- Face: a custom chunky, condensed, hand-cut display face with quirky letterforms (for example a dotted lowercase i inside title-case words).
- Treatment: white fill, thick black outline and a hard black shadow offset down-right, so it reads at thumbnail size on any background.
- Two tiers:
  - Headline: 2-4 words, title case, benefit or feeling ("Share The Bounty", "Express Yourself"). Cap height about 9% of frame height, one line on shots 2-7.
  - Subline: same face at about 55% size, 4-6 plain words that start with a verb and say the actual activity (trade, decorate, explore).
- The key art uses a 2-line headline with no subline.
- Text is centered inside a plaque of fixed width, so every locale must fit the same box.
- The voice is warm and inviting, and never lists features.

For Comet Garden:
- Keep the two-tier idea but use our own face: Fredoka 700 for the headline, Fredoka 600 for the subline, both in sentence case (the case we already use).
- Headline: 2-4 words about a feeling or benefit ("Cute friends move in" already fits).
- Subline: one plain-language sentence a parent could read aloud, e.g. flinging a comet to grow new land, or a friend moving in when the land is right.
- Avoid the black stroke plus hard offset shadow. Use deep navy text on a light plaque, or white text with a soft colored glow in the shot's accent color.
- Budget the plaque for German and Japanese length. Hay Day's fixed box shows this has to be designed in up front.
color_light_recipe:
Hay Day:
- Saturated cyan-blue sky with a fluffy white cloud, yellow-green meadows and warm dirt paths.
- The golden plaque is the complement of the sky, so it is the strongest contrast in every frame. Samples: top highlight about #FFDE6F, body about #FFB00E, bottom lip about #BC6B1A. The lip reads as a glossy, pressable 3D button.
- The white card rim separates busy gameplay from the busy backdrop.
- Warm sunlight from the upper-left falls on every character. The heroes are high-fidelity furry 3D renders with glossy eyes and soft ambient occlusion, a step above in-game fidelity.
- The backdrop is lower in contrast and detail than the card and the characters, which gives depth without blur.
- Palette logic: one cool field (sky), one natural field (grass), one warm accent (plaque).

For Comet Garden:
- Keep our identity: deep indigo/navy space, the orange sun core and pastel creature colors.
- Replace the per-shot solid color blocks with one painted "garden sky" plate on every shot: indigo-to-violet gradient, soft nebula, a couple of distant pastel moons, twinkles.
- For progression, drift the plate's hue slowly across the set (dusk, then night, then dawn) instead of hard color changes.
- Our warm complement to indigo is sunrise peach/coral, so the plaque and the key glows should use it, not golden-yellow-with-amber-lip.
- Replace the white rim with a thin cream "starlight" rim that has a soft outer glow.
- Light flat vector creatures with a warm orange rim light (from the planet's core) plus a cool lilac fill and a soft contact shadow on the card. That adds dimension without faking 3D.
character_staging:
- One different animal per shot, and none repeats inside shots 2-6. The sheep bookends 1 and 7.
- Each gets a distinct, exaggerated expression: sleepy lids, toothy grin, tongue out, mouth-open meow, bug eyes. The row reads as a cast of personalities.
- Heroes are huge (more than half the frame height), cropped by the frame edge, and lean in from the bottom-left toward the viewer or the card. They feel as if they are right in front of the glass.
- They overlap the card edge, which breaks the frame and tells you these characters live in that world.
- Motion is added when it fits: the fish bursts out of a water splash.
- A second small character gives a surprise gag: a chicken hanging upside down, peeking from behind the card's top-right corner.
- In the key art, three animals at three depths frame the vista like curtains. The mascots own the edges and the world owns the center.
- The characters are marketing-grade renders of in-game designs, so the promise stays honest.

For Comet Garden:
- Use the 36 creatures as a rotating cast and match each hero to its shot's topic. Examples: octopus for friends moving in, otter or fish for water Fusions, penguin or seal for the frost sky, owl for Lifebook collecting, bunny for Homeworld.
- Use the existing happy and wave poses at about 40-45% of frame width, cropped by the bottom corner and overlapping the card edge.
- Our gag: the astronaut Keeper floating upside down on a tether from the top of the card, or waving from behind the plaque.
- Our motion break: a comet shooting out of the card with the dotted aim line continuing onto the backdrop, optionally running from one tile into the next.
- Key art: two or three creatures at different depths around a small grown planet, with the Keeper mid-ground.
what_makes_it_work: A rigid template (fixed backdrop, card, plaque and hero positions) makes the set feel like one designed campaign and lets the eye find the caption without searching
The key-art opener sells the feeling and the brand before any UI. It stands alone because landscape search shows only one tile
Real gameplay in a clean rounded card over painted art: honest about the game, yet the whole frame looks illustrated rather than like a raw screenshot
A huge, expressive mascot per shot brings personality and emotion that small in-game sprites cannot deliver at thumbnail size
Breaking the frame (characters over the card edge, fish splash, upside-down peek) adds depth and playfulness and says the world spills out of the screen
Two-tier captions: an emotional headline for the scroll-by viewer and a literal verb-led subline for the parent or player who wants to know what you actually do
The warm plaque on the cool sky gives the strongest contrast in the frame and pulls the eye to the words first
The sequence climbs a ladder of motivations: escape, then daily loop, trade, novelty, growth, self-expression, community
A modular swap slot (shot 4) lets live-ops content rotate in without disturbing the evergreen opener or the template
The same backdrop and the same box make localizing and A/B testing cheap: only the card, the hero and the text change
transferable_to_comet_garden: Add a true key-art shot 1 with no UI: our logo, a small lush planet mid-bloom, 2-3 big creatures at different depths framing it, the Keeper, and a one-line cozy promise. Today shot 1 opens straight on a device frame

Replace the device-frame mockups and per-shot solid colors with one shared painted night-garden sky plate, plus a gameplay card with rounded corners and a cream glowing rim, cropped tight on the planet and aim line

Lock a portrait template in store/tools/shots.mjs: plaque top 4-22%, card 18-80% at about 80% width, hero creature at the bottom (40-45% width) overlapping the card edge, alternating left and right corners so the first three search tiles zig-zag

Give every shot a different creature hero matched to its topic, taken from the existing happy and wave poses. Rim-light it warm from the sun core and add a soft contact shadow so the flat vectors pop at thumbnail size

Switch to two-tier captions in Fredoka: a 2-4 word feeling headline plus a 4-7 word plain-language subline a parent can read aloud (e.g. headline about friends moving in, subline explaining that the right land invites them)

Make our own frame-break motifs: a comet streaking out of the card with the dotted aim line continuing onto the backdrop, and the Keeper tethered upside down peeking over the card as the recurring gag

Build a 'planet postcards' shot in our own style: three tilted snapshots of different biomes (Mossy World, Ember Haven, Frost Haven) shown as Sticker Album stickers with a peeling corner, names in Fredoka on a colored sticker tab. It sells variety and our sticker feature at once

Order the set as a motivation ladder: key art promise, fling and grow, friends move in, planet variety, Fusions and combos, Homeworld (make it yours), Lifebook collecting, then close on family trust (no ads, purchases with grown-ups). Hay Day closes on community; our closer is trust
Reserve one mid-set slot (for example position 4) as the swappable seasonal or new-planets slot, so updates never touch the opener
Use a warm sunrise-peach/coral plaque against the indigo sky as the one hot accent. Keep the sky constant and drift its hue dusk to night to dawn across the set to suggest a journey
Keep the HUD in the card only where it helps (throws, life bar). Crop gem counters out of kid-facing shots so the set reads cozy and never pushy
Size the plaque for the longest locale (de, pt) up front, since a fixed-box template needs copy written to fit
do_not_copy: The Hay Day logo and its lettering with the wheat sprig, or any similar grain or farm ornament on our logo
Supercell-style chunky condensed display type with white fill, heavy black outline and hard black offset shadow (their house caption look)
The golden-yellow rounded rectangle plaque with a glossy highlight and dark amber bottom lip, anchored bottom-right
The exact template geometry: white-rimmed card at x 14-85% and y 5-77%, plaque bottom-right overlapping it, hero bottom-left
The farm backdrop plate: blue sky with a cloud top-left, dirt path with white picket fence, wheat field and tree clump
Their animal cast and furry 3D render style: sleepy cow, toothy pig, tongue-out dog, calico kitten, bug-eyed sheep, purple-green leaping fish
The upside-down chicken peek gag (our peek must be our Keeper or a creature in our flat style, in a different pose and place)
Postcard collage with beige paper strips, dashed stitched borders and cursive handwritten place names
Their caption phrasing and farm vocabulary: the pocket-sized escape line, 'Share The Bounty', 'More Than A Farm', 'Find New Pastures', 'Farm With Friends', and bounty/pastures/neighborhood wording
A striped shop awning used to frame a UI panel as a market stall
Sunny-daylight farm palette of sky blue, meadow green and golden yellow as our overall look (ours stays indigo space with sunrise-peach accents)

name: Hotel Legacy: Merge Game
full_sequence:
6 portrait shots (460x995 thumbs; source 1284x2778), all full-bleed, no device frame. Shots 1-5 carry the same bottom caption band with one Title Case verb. Shot 6 is key art with no band.
1. "Unlock": a 3D toon top-down hotel corridor in idle-arcade style. The host walks a red carpet carrying a stack of cash while broom "clean me" icons and red no-entry icons float over rooms, and a level-star and cash counter sit at the top. Job: the first thumbnail shows an avatar in the middle of doing something, so a scroller sees a clear action right away. The source file is named "minigame", and it is drawn in a different style from shots 2-6. It most likely matches the UA ad creative more than the core game.
2. "Merge": the merge board fills the width under the HUD, with the painted lobby showing in the top ~12%. Two matching door-hangers are scaled to about 3x cell size and backed by yellow sunburst halos, so you can see "two of the same" even as a thumbnail. The host's head and shoulders sit bottom-left at about 45% of the width, overlap the board edge, make eye contact and hold up a gold key as a reward. Job: explain the core mechanic in one look.
3. "Serve": a painted lobby with no HUD at all. Four guests of different ages and styles (grandma, businessman, young traveller, goth teen) each have a white rounded speech bubble holding one wanted item. Those items (salad, tea, etc.) are the same ones on the merge board, which closes the loop. The host is behind the desk top-left, and a red carpet runs diagonally bottom-right to top-left. Job: explain why you merge, and add warmth and people.
4. "Renovate": a diagonal before/after wipe. A glowing white-yellow light beam runs from the upper-left edge down to the lower-right. Below it is a desaturated, rain-streaked, cracked ruin; above it is a saturated, sparkling restored castle district. A big curved gold arrow sits on the seam and points from ruin to castle, which is the hero at centre. HUD kept. Job: the payoff and the sense of progress, as a transformation you can read in one second.
5. "Travel": an isometric Mediterranean island map. Floating tags show a padlock with a level number, a green key "Upgrade" tag, and character portrait pins with % progress (60%, 80%). The top and bottom edges fade into soft white haze. Job: breadth and long-term goals ("there is more after this").
6. Key art or loading screen, last: the logo is centred high, the host and an animal bellhop mascot rush a trolley of stacked pastel suitcases, warm window light comes from the left and there is a swirled carpet floor. No caption band, no HUD. Job: brand recall and personality at the end of the swipe, instead of spending the first slot on it.
Taken together, the verbs walk through the whole loop in order (unlock, merge, serve, renovate, travel), so the captions work as a 5-word game summary.
composition_recipe: Full-bleed scene, no device frame, no solid backdrop. Vertical bands at 1284x2778: top ~7-8% is the HUD strip (dropped on the scene shots 3 and 6); the hero sits in the middle band, about 20-75% of height; the bottom ~9-11% is the caption band. The band's top edge is a gentle convex wave, highest around 25% of the width (~89% of height) and lowest at the right edge (~96% of height). It has a thin darker rim and a solid fill. The caption is left-aligned at a ~5% margin, cap height ~5% of image height, and even the longest word ("Renovate") uses only ~60% of the width. That leaves the right side of the band calm and makes the wave feel like it is pushing the word along. Hero rules: (a) scale key objects 2-3x their real in-game size and put a radial glow behind them; (b) run a diagonal leading line (carpet, wipe seam, path) from one lower corner up through the hero; (c) let one character break the gameplay layer by overlapping the board edge in the lower-left quadrant, just above the band, so the face is near the caption and reads together with it. Depth layers: soft, hazy or faded environment at the edges (white atmospheric fade on the map, blurred lobby above the board) → sharp gameplay mid-ground → oversized glowing props, speech bubbles, arrows and tags in the foreground. Framing: nothing important in the outer ~4%, and HUD pills kept small so the scene dominates. Before/after uses a single diagonal seam, not a side-by-side split, so the two states flow into each other and the hero straddles the seam, leaning toward the "after" side.
type_recipe: One word per shot, Title Case, an imperative verb that names a step of the loop. Very heavy, slightly rounded sans in forward italic (~10-12° slant). Fill is pure white with a thick burnt-orange outline (~#D85817), a thin lighter peach inner edge, and a slight offset that makes the letters look like a raised sticker. Set on a saturated golden-yellow band (~#FDBD04) with an orange rim (~#F08A00) along its wavy top edge, so the same hue family runs from band to outline and the white fill carries all the contrast. Cap height ~5% of the image height, which keeps it legible at search-result size. Left-aligned, sitting low in the band, never centred. The caption's colours and style are identical on every shot, so the set reads as one unit. No subcaptions, no body copy, no badges. The logo appears only on the last shot, as a separate script-plus-caps lockup.
color_light_recipe: Warm-dominant palette: golden yellow and orange UI chrome, red carpets and vests, gold trim. Cool accents (teal board tiles, blue dome roofs, blue-grey water) sit in the mid-ground so the warm foreground pops. Saturation is used as meaning: the "before" half of the wipe is desaturated grey-green with diagonal rain streaks and dark cracks, and the "after" half is fully saturated with sparkle stars. Light is used to aim attention: sunburst halos behind the merge items; the wipe seam is a glowing white-to-yellow light beam rather than a hard line; four-point sparkle glints sit on the hero building; the key art has warm window backlight from the left with a soft bloom on the chandelier. Map edges fade to near-white haze (atmospheric perspective), which also keeps the busy map from fighting the caption band. Floating UI tags are cream or white with soft drop shadows, so they read as a layer above the world. Scene art is mostly mid-to-high value, with no true blacks except hair, shoes and outlines.
character_staging: A recurring host face ties the set together. She appears as a big head-and-shoulders portrait in shot 2, small and in context behind the desk in shot 3, and full body in action in shot 6. She shows up about every other shot, so the brand has a person without her crowding the gameplay. In the portrait she makes direct eye contact with a big open smile and holds up a reward (a key) near her face, which makes the reward object and the face one focal point. Guests in shot 3 are posed in a loose zigzag at different depths. Their bodies angle toward the desk while their bubbles float up and outward into clear space, so every want is legible. Casting is deliberately wide: a senior, a Black businessman, a young woman, an alt teen. It signals "for everyone" without a word. A cute animal sidekick (otter bellhop) shows up small as a map portrait pin in shot 5 and then co-stars in the key art, so the mascot is set up before the payoff. The key art is all motion: both characters lean into a diagonal push with open-mouth laughs, and the stacked luggage makes a strong vertical that balances the logo. Characters never sit in the caption band; they sit just above it or overlap the gameplay layer.
what_makes_it_work: The captions double as the game's instruction manual: five one-word verbs, in loop order, explain the whole game even if a viewer reads nothing else
An identical caption band and type treatment on every shot make six images read as one designed set, and the band stays recognisable at thumbnail size
Key objects are scaled far past their real in-game size and haloed with light, so the mechanic ('two of the same') reads at 1/10 scale
The before/after uses a diagonal glowing seam plus a big directional arrow, and a saturation swap (grey rain vs sparkling colour) gives a one-second transformation story
Speech bubbles holding the exact items from the merge board connect two screens into cause and effect
One recurring character face with direct eye contact adds warmth and a brand persona without a logo on every shot
Deliberately varied cast (ages, ethnicities, styles) quietly widens who feels invited
Scene-only shots with no HUD alternate with gameplay shots with HUD, which keeps the set from feeling like a UI dump
Soft atmospheric fades at busy edges keep dense maps from fighting the caption and pull the eye to the centre
The key art is saved for the last slot, so the first three search-visible slots all sell play and progress
transferable_to_comet_garden: Switch from the current framed-device-on-flat-orange layout to full-bleed gameplay: let the dark sky and the planet fill the whole canvas and put captions on an overlay band, so the planet can be 2-3x larger in the thumbnail
Loop-in-verbs caption set, in our own words and our own type: e.g. Fling -> Grow -> Welcome -> Decorate/Explore -> Rest, one step per shot, in play order, so the captions alone explain the game

Give our caption band a shape from our own world instead of a swoosh: the curved horizon of a tiny planet (a slice of mossy or grassy planet surface along the bottom edge) with the caption sitting on it. Same unifying job, clearly our motif

Before/after with our own seam: split a bare grey rock planet from a lush, creature-filled one along the glowing trail of a comet, with the comet itself as the directional 'arrow'. Desaturate the 'before' half and scatter soft star-glints on the 'after' half
Hero-scale and halo: enlarge the comet in flight and the newest land tile or creature to 2-3x in-game size, each with a soft radial glow in our palette, so a single throw reads at thumbnail size

Thought bubbles over creatures showing what they want (a pond, a flower, a tree) link 'fling' to 'move in' the way their guest bubbles link merge to serve. Use our rounded bubble style and our creatures' own icons

Creature head-and-shoulders peeking over the caption band in the lower-left of the gameplay shot, looking at the viewer and holding or pointing at the comet. This is a warm face near the caption without adding a human host
Alternate HUD-visible gameplay shots with clean scene or close-up shots (a creature village on the planet surface, no UI) so the set breathes
Use saturation and light as meaning: a dim, cool, unlit planet vs a warm, glowing, alive planet. This matches our cozy, all-ages tone better than drama
Show breadth with a gentle galaxy or planet-map shot of many small planets, soft-faded edges, and progress shown as creature portraits or garden icons rather than level-lock padlocks
Put the brand or key-art card last, after the gameplay slots, as a family portrait of creatures around the planet with our wordmark
Keep one recurring character (a single signature creature or the little astronaut) across 3 of the shots as the persona thread
Show a varied, gentle cast of creatures to signal 'for everyone', since that is our all-ages equivalent of their diverse guests

Strip every currency counter from the HUD in the shots. Their HUD shows coins, gems and cash in most shots, and we should show only throws, planet name and progress, or no HUD at all, which fits our no-ads, purchases-only-for-grown-ups promise and App Review guidance
do_not_copy: The golden-yellow curved swoosh caption band with the orange rim, which is their signature frame on every shot
The caption lettering: white heavy italic with a thick burnt-orange outline and sticker bevel
Their exact verb set and order (Unlock / Merge / Serve / Renovate / Travel); write our own verbs from our loop
The host character: blonde updo, black glasses, red vest, name badge
The otter bellhop mascot in a red pillbox cap and blue jacket, or any animal-in-a-uniform mascot
The 'Hotel Legacy' logo lockup: gold script over a maroon ribbon with a keyhole in the lettering
The star-badge level icon plus the pill row for energy, coins and gems in the HUD
The H-monogram door hangers and coins, and stacked-pastel-suitcase-trolley key art
The exact renovate treatment of a white-yellow light-beam seam plus a gold curved swoosh arrow over a rainy ruin (use a comet-trail seam in our palette instead)
The whitewashed-dome Mediterranean island map with padlock 'Level N' tags, green 'Upgrade' key tags and %-progress portrait pins
Opening the set with a mini-game in a different art style from the core game (their shot 1). Every shot of ours must be the real game, as our store package already does

name: Jelly Busters: Puzzle Game
full_sequence:
8 portrait shots, all built on one template: a real gameplay capture fills the frame, a curved colour band sits at the bottom with a 2-word caption, and a 3D mascot stands bottom-right. Measured at 460x996; the source is 1242x2688.

1. Level 31. A pixel-block copy of a famous expressionist painting of a screaming figure, about 70% busted, with the edges crumbling. Jellies in the tray fire white streaks up into it. Orange band, caption 'ASMR visuals'. A yellow mascot laughs with its mouth wide open. JOB: the hook. It pairs a recognisable image you can read in half a second with a promise of a satisfying feel.
2. Level 36. A bespoke zoomed composition (the file name contains 'ZoomLibertyShocked'): the Statue of Liberty face redrawn with a shocked open mouth, with the conveyor track wrapped around it. One jelly rides the track and another shoots with a trail. Sky-blue band, caption 'Epic win'. A blue mascot throws its arms wide with a huge toothy grin. JOB: shows the second mechanic (the track) and the payoff feeling.
3. Level 15. A grumpy magenta radish/strawberry monster face (file name 'AngryStrawberry'). Two jellies are on the belt. Magenta band, caption 'Chill out'. A pink mascot sits cross-legged, meditating with its eyes closed. JOB: comic contrast between an angry picture and a zen mascot. It sells relaxation.
4. Level 77. A pharaoh bust on a magenta ground, with three jellies on the belt and the counter at 1/5. Emerald band, caption 'Level up'. A green mascot belly-laughs. JOB: progression and depth; the high level number implies a lot of content.
5. Level 85. A rainbow chameleon that is sparse and busy. All 5 slots are empty. Cobalt band, caption 'Unique levels'. A blue mascot smiles smugly. JOB: variety.
6. Level 130. A panda on pink/green stripes, almost untouched. Violet band, caption 'Fun puzzles'. A purple mascot smiles softly. JOB: variety and a cute subject. This is the highest level number shown.
7. Level 125. A smiling pizza slice with a pink drip outline. Hot-pink band, caption 'Solve puzzles'. A pink mascot grins mischievously. JOB: variety with food, plus a plain genre label.
8. Level 7, 0 coins. A red horned face with jellies on the right side of the track. Teal band, caption 'Think fast'. A teal mascot winks and points back toward the caption. JOB: the closer, a skill/challenge promise with a wink as a sign-off.

Craft notes:
- The first 3 are bespoke hero compositions (each has its own file name), and 4-8 come from a batch template. The investment goes where search results show 3 thumbnails.
- Shots 5-7 were visibly rendered in a different pipeline: warmer, over-sharpened wood, the HUD shifted and scaled up, and an identical 5,000 coin count with a green '+' button. Next to the others they look inconsistent.
- The captions for 5-7 are generic filler compared with 1-3.
- File names suggest a tested 'colorful CTA' band variant.
composition_recipe:
Layered stack, back to front:

1. **Gameplay.** A full-bleed, unframed, 1:1 real capture from 0-100% of the height. There is no device frame. The HUD stays intact in the top 3-7% (coin pill left, level pill centre, pause button right).
2. **Hero subject.** The busted picture sits centred at about 10-58% of the height and fills 80-90% of the width. The belt/track frames it like a picture frame.
3. **Caption band.** The top edge is curved and sweeps upward to the right: about 87% of the height at the left edge, about 86% at centre and about 83% at the right. That makes the band 13-17% of the height. A thin white keyline (about 0.6% of the width) runs along the top edge. The fill has a subtle top-to-bottom gradient from lighter to darker. The band only covers the least important UI, the lower queue of pieces, which fades under it.
4. **Caption.** Left-aligned with about a 7% left margin, taking up about 5-55% of the width. It is two stacked words, vertically centred in the band, and rotated about -3 to -5 degrees so it follows the swoop.
5. **Mascot.** Front-most, on the right, about 35-40% of the width with a 2-4% right margin. It spans from about 79% of the height down to the bottom edge. Its head breaks about 6-8% above the band into the gameplay, but it never touches the hero picture. Its feet stand on the band floor. Some gestures (an outstretched arm or a pointing finger) reach left toward the caption.

The result: the top 80% reads as authentic gameplay, and the bottom 20% reads as a branded sticker layer. No extra badges or callouts.
type_recipe:
**Face and treatment**
- Heavy rounded geometric display sans at near-black weight, in the Lilita/Fredoka-Black family feel. ALL CAPS, tight tracking.
- White fill with a thick tone-on-tone darker outline, about 8-10% of cap height. The outline colour follows the band: burnt orange on orange, plum on magenta, forest on emerald, deep teal on teal.
- A soft, darker drop shadow falls straight down, so the letters look embossed or sticker-like.

**Size and layout**
- Two stacked lines of one word each; one line when both words are short ('Level up').
- Cap height is about 4.5% of the screen height (about 45px at 996, about 120px at 2688), so it stays legible at search-thumbnail size.
- The baseline is tilted about -3 to -5 degrees to match the band curve. The lines are left-aligned, with a slight optical offset.

**Voice**
- 2-word feeling or benefit labels with no punctuation and no sentences, e.g. 'Chill out', 'Epic win'.
- The mascot pantomimes each word, so the image repeats the caption.
color_light_recipe:
**Stage**
- A deliberately dull warm mauve-grey board, about rgb(130,118,122), with a lighter floor strip of about rgb(172,157,160) under the tray.
- Desaturated to about 10% chroma, so every saturated element pops.

**Content**
- Fully saturated pixel art: glossy cubes with soft top lighting and small contact shadows.

**Band and mascot colour**
- One fully saturated hue per shot. Measured: orange #E76801, sky #1BA1F8, magenta #DD27CA, emerald #00B46D, cobalt #1355C5, violet #9200C5, hot pink #F6116E, teal #02B9B7.
- Neighbouring shots jump across the hue wheel (warm, cool, warm, cool), so the store row reads as a rainbow and each tile is distinct.
- The band gradient runs about 10% lighter at the top to darker at the bottom, with a thin white rim.
- The mascot body is the same hue as its band. It is a studio 3D render with a soft top-left key light, broad glossy specular highlights and a subsurface/vinyl sheen, plus a thick white die-cut outline (about 2% of the width) that separates it from both the band and the grey board.
- No cast shadow from the mascot onto the band. It reads as a sticker placed on top.

**Motion**
- White motion streaks from the projectiles add energy without adding colour.
character_staging:
**One species, one mascot per shot**
- The mascot is the in-game piece hero-ised: the numbered jellies in the tray are the same cube species, upgraded to a premium 3D render.
- The marketing character is therefore literally the thing you play with, not a bait-and-switch.

**Expression and gesture act out the caption**
- Mouth-wide laugh for the sensory hook.
- Arms flung wide with a toothy grin for the win.
- Eyes closed and cross-legged meditation for 'Chill out'.
- Belly laugh for levelling up.
- Smug closed-mouth smile for uniqueness.
- Gentle smile for fun.
- Mischievous grin for solving.
- Wink with a finger pointing at the caption for 'Think fast'.

**Placement and pose**
- Bottom-right, 3/4 front-facing, feet planted on the band, head poking into the gameplay.
- Arms and fingers are used as leading lines back toward the caption.

**Two faces in every frame**
- The puzzle picture is almost always a face with a strong emotion (screaming, shocked, angry, smiling), and the mascot face reacts next to it.
- The eye travels from the big picture face, down to the mascot face, then left to the caption.
what_makes_it_work: Gameplay is left almost untouched and takes up about 85% of the frame. The overlay only covers the least important UI (the lower piece queue), so every shot is honest and instantly shows what you do.
The mascot is an upscaled, premium render of the actual game piece. Ad art and gameplay share one character, and that builds attachment and trust.
The mascot's expression acts out the 2-word caption, so the message lands even if the words are not read.
The band colour matches the mascot, and the hue changes every shot. That gives the scrolling row a candy rainbow rhythm, and each tile is easy to tell apart in search results.
A desaturated neutral stage (the grey board) makes the saturated content and the band pop without the frame feeling noisy.
Each frame is a freeze of the transformation in progress: half-busted pictures with motion trails show cause and effect in one still.
Faces everywhere: an emotional picture face plus the reacting mascot face give a clear two-point eye path, then the caption.
Recognisable subjects (a famous painting, a landmark, an animal, food) read at thumbnail size in under a second.
The first three shots are bespoke hero compositions, including a zoomed crop of the board, and the rest are templated. Effort goes where search results show three tiles.
Widely spread level numbers (7 to 130) quietly signal lots of content.
transferable_to_comet_garden: Drop the device frame used in the current set and go full-bleed. Let the real planet scene fill 0-83% of the height and put a short curved caption band in the bottom 13-17%, so the band only covers the lower launcher/HUD strip, never the planet.

Hero-ise a real in-game creature as the per-shot mascot: Hopper Bunny, Canopy Octopus, Moss Deer, Tuxling or the little astronaut kid, rendered large (35-40% of the width) with a thick white die-cut sticker outline. It stands on the band bottom-right (or bottom-left for variety) and its head breaks up into the space scene. Because it is the same creature players collect, it stays honest.

Make the mascot act out the caption. For example: the astronaut mid-fling with a comet for the throwing shot, the bunny hugging a new sprout for the 'friends move in' shot, the octopus with its eyes closed and a soft smile for the cozy shot, the owl or seal gasping at a Combo, and the parrot winking at the grown-ups shot.

Colour-match band to mascot, one hue per shot. Reuse our own existing palette from store/captions.json (#ff9a3d, #3fbf7f, #ffc93d, #5aa8ff, #ff6f6f, #7ad7c7, #b58cff, #2d3a8c), ordered so neighbours alternate warm and cool. Our softer pastels read cozier than their candy neon.
Treat our deep-navy space as the neutral stage, the way they use the grey board. Keep the planet as the only saturated centre and let the band and mascot carry the rest of the colour.

Compress the current 3-6-word captions to 2-3-word feeling labels in two stacked lines, big enough for search thumbnails (cap height about 4.5% of the screen height), e.g. 'Grow a world', 'New friends', 'Cozy combos'. Keep one plain-language trust shot for grown-ups ('No ads').

Freeze mid-transformation: a half-bare, half-green planet, the dotted aim line and a comet trail, a splash of land just landing, and a creature mid-hop. It shows cause and effect in one still, like their half-busted pictures.

Build zoomed hero variants for shots 1-3. Render the planet about 1.3-1.5x larger than the live UI shows so creatures and their faces are legible at thumbnail size. Our creatures are currently tiny in the shots.
Put at least one readable creature face near the planet focal point in every shot, plus the mascot face: two faces per frame.
Keep one capture and render pipeline for all 8 shots, so the lighting, HUD scale and sharpening do not drift the way their shots 5-7 do.
Signal depth with varied planet numbers, including one late planet (e.g. Planet 80+). Hide currency, gem counts and any '+'/buy affordances in captures, so all-ages parents never see a purchase cue.
do_not_copy: The cube-bodied, cat-ear-horned glossy vinyl jelly mascot design, or any square-bodied horned blob. Use our own creatures, and our own round and soft silhouettes.

The exact band signature: a swoosh that rises bottom-right with a thin white keyline and the mascot standing on it bottom-right in every shot. Give ours a different shape, e.g. a convex planet-horizon arc, a soft nebula or cloud edge, or a sparkle-dotted orbit ribbon. Also vary which corner the mascot uses.

The white all-caps lettering with a tone-on-tone dark outline, tilted a few degrees. Use our own rounded game font, e.g. white with a deep-navy outline, or our dark-on-pastel style, and tilt it only if it follows our own arc.
Their caption words and phrasings ('ASMR visuals', 'Epic win', 'Chill out', 'Level up', 'Think fast', 'Unique levels').
Pixel-block mosaics of famous paintings, landmarks or pop icons, and the half-busted-picture reveal look.
The warm grey board with the wooden conveyor-track frame, the numbered jelly pieces and the 5-slot tray.
Their exact 8-hue neon sequence (orange, sky, magenta, emerald, cobalt, violet, hot pink, teal) in that order.
The gold-star coin pill with a green '+' and the blue level pill HUD styling. Do not stage any currency or buy button at all.

name: Merge Cooking®
full_sequence:
There are 8 portrait shots at 460x997 (iPhone 6.9"). None use a device frame. Shots 1-6 share the same top block: a caption band, then the real HUD pills right under it. Shots 7 and 8 drop the caption.

1. MERGE (orange band). This shot explains the core mechanic. It shows the real merge board with the order bar above: three big customer portraits, with order bubbles, coin and star rewards, and a green tick. On the board, two strawberry cake slices glow at the bottom with a green plus between them. Two curved green arrows rise from them into a whole cake that is about 3x a grid cell (about 40% of canvas width) and ringed with sparkles. A stream of coins arcs from the cake up to a grandma customer, who pumps her fist. The shot does two jobs: it says what you do (combine two items) and what you get (a happy customer and coins).

2. COOK (sky-blue band). This is the production step. A pastel kitchen: the top half is a glossy dessert spread on a table (layer cake, sundae, donuts, macarons, a tulip vase). A diagonal streak of golden light cuts the frame. An oven item is picked out with green corner brackets and a tutorial hand tapping it. The lower kitchen and the raw ingredients (eggs, flour, butter, rolling pin) are dimmed and cooler, so they read as the "before" for the dishes above. The job is to show the tap interaction and the raw-to-finished promise.

3. RENOVATE (red band). This is the emotional payoff. The frame is split on a torn diagonal. On top, a cold, navy-grey wrecked kitchen with snow and a broken window, where a mother in a red bandana hugs a shivering, crying toddler. A big teal curved arrow leads down into a warm, amber, renovated kitchen where the same two characters are beaming. The job is transformation plus empathy, pairing a sad state with a happy one.

4. UNLOCK (green band). This is the meta map. An isometric street: in the middle is a tarp-covered, locked stall with a gold padlock and a yellow outline glow. Around it are three finished seating areas, each with a big green check tile and a small customer relaxing there. Lush trees crop the corners, and a red vintage car adds charm. The job is to show a world that grows as you play, with visible progress (checks) and a pull toward the next goal (the lock).

5. COLLECT (magenta band). This is the collection hook. The background is a dimmed grid of postcards. At the bottom, a golden foil pack with the logo and five stars bursts open with light rays. A fan of postcards floats up, with a landmark centred and enlarged and the others (aurora, flamingo, a beach sign) tilted behind it. The job is completionism, but it reads as a loot-pack reveal.

6. HELP OR IGNORE? (violet band). This is a story or ad-creative hook, not gameplay. Three taped photo panels, each tilted, sit on a wooden backdrop in a more cinematic, near-photoreal 3D render: a sad child crouched in a snowy street, a hand reaching for a fallen baguette, and the child feeding bread to a collapsed woman. The job is to create a moral-choice cliffhanger that pulls you into the narrative.

7. No caption: key art. The logo sits top-centre. A mother and daughter at a zoo café, with a giraffe leaning in to eat a leaf the child is holding out. Giraffe-themed desserts fill the foreground table, and autumn leaves frame the top corners. The job is brand, warmth and a themed-event flavour; it is the only shot built like a poster.

8. No caption: raw gameplay. The whole unedited board, 7 columns by about 12 rows: fruit, drinks, desserts, pets, coins, gems, energy, chests and generators, with the full HUD and orders above. The job is to prove there is a lot of content for anyone who scrolls to the end, as an honest "this is the real game" close.

Arc: the five verbs in shots 1-5 walk the loop in order (combine, produce, restore, expand, collect). Shots 6-7 then switch to story and brand, and shot 8 ends on the raw game. The first three, the ones visible in search results, cover mechanic, action and emotional payoff.
composition_recipe:
- **Canvas.** Full-bleed and frameless. The game scene is the background, and no phone bezel is ever shown.

- **Caption block** (measured on the 997-px-tall shots):
  - The band is solid colour from 0 to about 5% of the height, then a vertical gradient dissolves it into the scene by about 13-15%, so there is never a hard edge.
  - The caption's cap height is fixed at about 45 px (4.5% of height) and runs from about 4% to 8.5% down.
  - It is centred horizontally. Short verbs span about 35-65% of the width; the 3-word shot runs nearly edge to edge (about 5% margins).
  - Size stays constant across the set; only the width changes.

- **Authenticity strip.** The real HUD pills (level badge, energy, coins, gems, shop) sit at about 13-17%, directly under the caption on every gameplay shot. The caption plus HUD form one constant top block that ties the set together while the scene below changes.

- **Hero element.**
  - One focal object per shot, scaled 2.5-3x above true game scale (the cake is about 40% of canvas width against a grid cell of about 13.5%).
  - It sits in the middle band, about 40-70% of height, slightly off-centre.
  - It is backed by a radial glow, sparkle stars and a bloom ring, and it overlaps the grid lines to break the UI plane.

- **Callout grammar** (all diagrammatic, all in the game's UI style):
  - item + item with curved arrows up to the result
  - a tutorial hand plus corner brackets on the thing to tap
  - one big curved arrow from the before state to the after state
  - padlock and green-check tiles on the map
  - light rays from a reveal

- **Depth layers.**
  - Back: the scene, dimmed, desaturated or blurred. Examples are the lower kitchen in shot 2 and the postcard wall in shot 5.
  - Middle: the real gameplay plane (board, table, isometric street).
  - Front: the enlarged, glowing hero, plus a reward trail (a coin stream) that links the hero to a character reacting to it.

- **Diagonals.** Two shots split the frame on a diagonal: a light streak in shot 2 and a torn edge in shot 3. This adds motion and lets one frame hold two states.

- **Framing.** Foliage or leaves crop into the corners (shots 4 and 7). Grid rows and the street run off every edge, so the world feels bigger than the frame.

- **Margins.** Nothing important sits in the bottom 5%. The hero never touches the caption; the HUD strip is the buffer.

- **Band hue.** The band colour is picked to match what is directly beneath it (green over treetops, blue over blue kitchen walls, orange over the sunset), so the fade is almost invisible.
type_recipe:
- **One idea per caption.** One imperative verb per shot (a 3-word question once), ALL CAPS. There is no subline, logo or feature list on gameplay shots.

- **Face.** A heavy, rounded display sans with a slight forward slant, soft corners and slightly flared stroke ends. It reads as friendly and bouncy rather than geometric.

- **Colour.** Pure white fill with no outline stroke.

- **Shadow.** A soft drop shadow in a darker shade of the band hue (dark orange on orange, dark red on red), offset straight down about 3-4 px at 460 wide (roughly 1% of width), with light blur. This gives a slightly raised, sticker-like lift without a hard outline.

- **Tracking and size.** Tracking is tight to normal. Cap height is identical across the set; width follows word length.

- **Placement.** Always top-centre, in the same spot.

- **Readability.** A 5-8 letter word at this size is readable in search thumbnails, and the five verbs read as one sentence when the shots are seen side by side.

- **Key-art shot.** The only other type is the logo on the key-art shot: a chunky yellow-to-orange bevelled wordmark with a dark brown outline and a small subtitle.
color_light_recipe:
- **Header bands.** One saturated, flat hue per shot, stepping around the colour wheel. Sampled: orange #FF8500, sky blue #0093D8, red #C92323, green #16C082, magenta #DA318E, violet #B231FF. Each fades through a gradient into the scene's own top colour.

- **Scene palette.** Warm pastels (cream, blush pink, butter yellow, mint, teal) with glossy, high-spec food renders: white speculars, a subtle rim light and soft contact shadows.

- **Hero lighting.**
  - A radial yellow-white glow directly behind the hero.
  - Crisp 4-point white or gold sparkle stars scattered around its silhouette.
  - A golden light streak or rays when something is produced or revealed.
  - A yellow outline glow on objects that can be interacted with (the locked stall).

- **Pushing the hero forward.** The background layer is dimmed and cooled (the lower kitchen, the postcard wall), so the lit hero pops without needing a vignette.

- **Emotional temperature.** "Before" states are cold, low-saturation navy and grey with snow particles. "After" states are warm amber and golden with pendant lamps and sunlight. The arrow between them is a bright cool teal, so it reads above both halves.

- **Reward colours.** These stay the same across all shots, as a small colour language: gold coins, green for success (ticks, arrows, plus signs), a gold padlock for what is next, and pink hearts for delight.
character_staging:
- **Characters as reaction.** Characters mostly receive the action rather than perform it. In shot 1, three customers sit in a row above the board as large 3/4 portraits. Coins fly from the merged cake to the centre grandma, who pumps her fist, so the mechanic ends on a face.

- **Readable at thumbnail size.** Faces are big, with oversized eyes, glasses and clear silhouettes, and expressions are pushed hard (joy, tears, shivering shown by little motion ticks).

- **Continuity.** The same mother and daughter appear across shots 3, 6 and 7, first in need, then happy, then at leisure. Repeating the same pair turns separate shots into a relationship story.

- **Before/after as expression.** The characters sit in the same spot on each side of the split. Only their pose changes (a huddled hug becomes arms up), so the change reads instantly.

- **The world coming alive.** Small secondary characters relax in finished areas of the map (shot 4). They quietly show that people come to the places you build.

- **Animal moment.** In the key art (shot 7), a giraffe leans into the frame from the right, eye-line to the child. Adult, child and animal form a triangle, with a themed dessert table in front.

- **Never covering the gameplay.** Characters fill the top third (above the board) or take a split half. The tutorial hand in shot 2 is the only human body part over gameplay, and it is a UI device.
what_makes_it_work: One-word verb captions turn the whole set into a readable sentence of the game loop, so a browser gets the pitch in about 2 seconds without reading any copy.
Constant cap height and a fixed top position, plus the real HUD under every caption, give a strong family look even though every scene is different.
The rainbow band hue per shot makes each thumbnail distinct in the scroll; matching the band to the scene's top colour makes the fade feel native, not pasted on.
The mechanic is drawn as an equation (item + item, arrows, bigger result) at 2.5-3x game scale, so the core verb is understood before a word is read.
Every action ends in a reaction: a coin trail links the hero object to a delighted face, which ties the mechanic to the emotional reward.
Before/after on a diagonal split with warm/cool light contrast is the strongest single-frame way to sell transformation.
Dimming or cooling the background layer and blooming the hero creates depth and focus without heavy vignettes or frames.
Frameless, full-bleed art uses the whole 9:19.5 canvas, so the game is shown much larger than a device mockup would allow at thumbnail size.
Progress markers (green checks on finished areas, a glowing padlock on the next) make the meta game readable at a glance: done, and what comes next.
Ending on an untouched, dense gameplay board is an honesty and depth signal for anyone who scrolls to the end.

Flaw to avoid: shots 5 and 6 lean on loot-pack imagery and distressed children rendered in a different, cinematic style. This works as a hook but conflicts with a wholesome, no-dark-patterns, real-gameplay promise.
transferable_to_comet_garden: Go frameless and full-bleed. Our current set puts the planet at about 40% of canvas width inside a phone bezel; instead, let the cosmic scene fill the canvas and scale the planet to about 80-95% of width, so the lands, critters and aim arc read in search thumbnails.

Keep our rainbow-per-shot idea but make it a top band that fades into the scene. Use a solid band for about 5% of the height, then a gradient into our deep-space navy by about 14%. Pick each band hue to echo that shot's hero: ice blue for an ice comet, lava orange for magma, leaf green for seeds and forest, violet for the Lifebook.

Write one verb per shot that spells our loop across the first 5 shots, in the spirit of Fling, Grow, Welcome, Fuse, Collect, each paired with a small sentence-case subline in our current rounded font (for example 'Gravity bends every shot'). The big verb is our version of their scannability; the warm subline is our own voice.

Keep our own type: our rounded display face in sentence case, with a soft darker-hue drop shadow instead of an outline, at the same cap height on every shot (about 4.5% of canvas height). Do not switch to their slanted all-caps treatment.

Recipe equation hero: draw our adjacency rule literally, with a Forest tile and an Ocean tile, a plus, curved arrows, and an enlarged otter popping out with sparkles, or Ice comet + Magma making a STEAM Fusion. Scale the hero 2.5-3x over real game size, with a radial glow and 4-point sparkles.
Action-to-reaction trail: after a comet impact, send a ribbon of stardust from the crater to a cheering critter or our astronaut kid, so every mechanic shot ends on a happy face.

Gentle before/after on a diagonal: a cold, grey, bare rock planet (cool navy light, no creatures) with a big curved arrow to the same planet lush, warm-lit and crowded with critters. The before state is empty and sleepy, never suffering characters. This is the strongest candidate for shot 2 or 3.

Drag-to-fling tutorial callout: a friendly hand pointer (or our astronaut's glove) pulling back the slingshot, the dotted gravity arc bending around the planet, and corner brackets on the landing-spot tag (the '+life, new land' aim tag). This makes the gesture obvious in one frame.

Progress-map shot: the Star Map or Homeworld with green checks (or star stamps) on finished planets or plots, a softly glowing lock on the next one, and critters relaxing on finished ones. This shows the world growing and gives a sense of what comes next.

Collection shot made earned, not random: the Lifebook opens with light rays and a fan of creature cards (Canopy Octopus, Moss Deer and so on), each lifting out with its habitat icon. No packs, foil or stars.
Depth trick: dim and blur the starfield and orbit rings behind the planet, and bloom the planet rim and the impact flash, so the hero pops without a phone frame.
Warm/cool emotional lighting: frosty blue for empty or icy states, golden sunrise for blooming states. It matches our ice-and-magma palette naturally.

Keep a minimal real HUD strip (planet name, throws, life bar) under the caption on gameplay shots as the authenticity layer. Since we have no energy timers, a HUD without an energy pill is itself a quiet selling point. Keep gem counts out of the first 3 shots.

Close the set with a dense, honest shot, such as the full 36-creature Lifebook grid, untouched. Keep our 'No ads, purchases stay with grown-ups' trust card as the final shot. It is a differentiator Merge Cooking cannot claim.

If we add a poster-style key-art shot, place it late (6th or 7th), built from real in-game renders: the Comet Garden logo over the planet with the astronaut kid and a critter reaching toward each other, like their child-and-animal eye-line moment but ours.
do_not_copy: Their exact header treatment as a unit: white, slanted, heavy all-caps single word on a saturated gradient band with a same-hue drop shadow. Use our own rounded sentence-case face and subline.
Their verb sequence word for word ('MERGE', 'COOK', 'RENOVATE', 'UNLOCK', 'COLLECT'). Write verbs that belong to our loop (fling, grow, welcome and so on).
The 'Merge Cooking' bevelled yellow-orange wordmark, the 'Theme Restaurant' subtitle, and the golden foil card pack with the logo and five stars.
Their recurring characters: the red-bandana mother with round glasses and her pigtailed toddler daughter, the fist-pumping grandma, and the portrait-row customers with order bubbles.

The green curved double-arrow plus green-plus merge equation styling (bright green arrows from two items into one). If we use an equation, draw it in our own cosmic style (a stardust ribbon, our colours).
The torn-diagonal before/after with the big teal curved arrow and the snowy wrecked-kitchen motif.
The 'HELP OR IGNORE?' moral-dilemma device and the taped tilted-photo collage on a wooden backdrop, including the near-photoreal cinematic render style that differs from the game.
The landmark postcard collection (a famous statue, an aurora, a flamingo, a beach sign) and the card-fan-from-a-pack reveal.
Their HUD look: the blue flower-shaped level badge, the lightning/coin/gem pills with green plus buttons, and the pink storefront shop button.
The giraffe zoo-café key art with giraffe-shaped desserts and autumn-leaf corner framing.
The overall merge-board grid look (square tiles with bevelled item icons on a wooden tray).
Their emotional-distress hooks (crying child, shivering mother, a collapsed woman). This is off-brand for an all-ages cozy game, and the reveal-pack imagery conflicts with our no-loot-box promise.

name: Merge Mansion: Puzzles & Story
full_sequence:
There are 9 listing shots at 1290x2796 portrait. Shots 6 and 8 are pixel-identical, so there are really 8 unique images. The set splits in two: shots 1-4 are a designed story set (tilted caption band, art direction) and shots 5-9 are raw, uncaptioned captures of the game's screens from an older batch.

1) HERO / HOOK. Waist-up 3D grandma in a lavender sweater, 3/4 pose, looking straight at the viewer with a knowing half-smile. She holds a wicker basket with a checkered cloth and two antique keys. Behind her are the mansion's front doors and stone steps in golden-hour light. White lilies (bottom-left) and sunflowers (bottom-right) frame her in the foreground and overlap the band. A custom black-and-cream serif logo sits top center. The caption is a two-line, all-caps, staggered tease about family secrets, ending in an ellipsis. Job: brand, a face to care about and a mystery. The key prop quietly sets up the mechanic.

2) CORE MECHANIC AS CAUSE -> EFFECT. The top shows the resource HUD. Upper half: an isometric glass greenhouse with a padlock in a speech-bubble tag above it (the goal). Lower half: a cream, rounded card showing a zoomed-in crop of about 4x4 board cells. At its center is one golden key, blown up about 3x on a radial glow. The red-haired heroine peeks out from behind the card's left edge with her hands on her cheeks, delighted. Caption: a huge verb, "MERGE", over a smaller object line. Job: in one glance, lock above plus key made on the board below equals how the game works.

3) STAKES / STORY BEAT. A comic panel split on a diagonal with a white gutter. Top: the heroine frowns, hand on chin, against blue sky and a house. Bottom: grandma, smug, behind bars in an orange jumpsuit. Caption: a big verb over "GRANDMA". Job: motivation plus a comic twist. The HUD still sits on top.

4) TRANSFORMATION PAYOFF. An isometric estate split by a glittering S-curve trail. Upper-left is sepia and broken (smashed umbrellas, a muddy empty pool). Lower-right is full colour and restored (blue pool with an inflatable croc, tennis court, hedges). A big glossy green curved arrow crosses from ruin to restored. A tiny heroine jumps for joy on the ruined side. The game's own buttons are visible. Caption: "REBUILD" over the object line. Job: show the payoff of long-term progress.

5) RAW WORLD VIEW. A barn and vegetable garden with full UI: event portraits with day/hour countdowns, task bubbles with checkmarks, mail and quest badges. No caption. Job: proof of the world, but noisy.

6) RAW INTERIOR. A lounge/casino room (blackjack table, roulette, slot machine, wine glasses) with full UI. No caption. Job: room variety. It is a family red flag.

7) RAW MERGE BOARD, FULL SCREEN. Gardening tools, energy generators, coins and cardboard-box blockers. Order cards along the top, a shop cart icon, and a gem-priced skip at the bottom. No caption. Job: show the full mechanic honestly.

8) EXACT DUPLICATE OF 6: a wasted slot.

9) RAW MERGE BOARD #2. Renovation tools, gems and coins on the board, butler and worker order portraits, and an "info here" bar with a typo. No caption.

Arc of the designed half: mystery hook -> how you play -> why it matters -> the payoff. The emotional arc runs through the heroine's face: surprise -> suspicion -> joy.
composition_recipe:
Canvas 1290x2796 (the 6.7/6.9-inch portrait slot). Layers, back to front: (1) warm painted scene art filling the whole frame; (2) optional gameplay 'card' (a rounded cream panel holding a cropped, zoomed slice of the board); (3) a character overlapping the card or panel edge; (4) foreground props (flowers) in the bottom corners, reaching into the band; (5) the caption band as the top layer, cropping everything beneath it.

CAPTION BAND: full-bleed, bottom ~16-18% of height. Its top edge tilts about 3.5 deg (82% of height at left, 84% at right), which adds energy and still reads as a steady frame across the set. Fill is a vertical cream -> blush gradient with a thin rose stroke on the top edge. The text block is centered and spans ~70-75% of width, leaving 12-16% side margins.

HERO ZONE: 8-80% of height. Shot 1: logo in the top ~15%, torso from ~25% down into the band, slightly left of center, eyes at ~35-40% of height. Shot 2: goal icon in a speech-bubble tag at ~15-25%. The board card runs ~42-80%, inset ~8-10% at the sides, with cells shown at ~2x in-game size and one reward item at ~3x on a radial burst at the card's center. The reaction character overlaps the card's left edge. Shot 3: diagonal split near mid-height with a slanted white gutter. Shot 4: an S-curve wipe from top-right to bottom-left, with a directional arrow near the center.

GAMEPLAY PLACEMENT: never a device frame. Gameplay is either a zoomed crop set into scene art (2) or a staged, art-directed game view (4). The HUD strip stays at the very top to say 'this is the real game'.

Rule of thumb: one idea per frame, one hero object per frame, and the eye path runs top (goal/context) -> middle (hero/action) -> bottom (caption).
type_recipe:
All caps. A heavy grotesque/humanist sans with slightly softened corners. Solid deep oxblood (~#A80000) on the cream-blush band, with no outline, drop shadow or gradient: legibility comes from contrast and size alone, so it reads cleanly at search-result thumbnail size.

TWO-TIER STACK (shots 2-4): a one-word imperative verb on top at cap height ~14% of canvas width (~180px at 1290w). Below it, a 1-2 word object line at ~60% of that size (~105px). Line gap ~0.35x the verb's cap height. Both centered. Pattern: verb / object. The verb carries the idea, and the object line supplies the context.

OPENER VARIANT (shot 1): two equal-size lines (~90px caps), the first flush left and the second pushed right (a stagger), ending in an ellipsis. It reads like a whispered line of dialogue, not a feature claim.

Typical length is 2-3 words, never more than 4. Voice: story tease first, then plain verbs in the imperative.

The logo appears only on shot 1: a custom chunky serif in black with a cream inline and an offset shadow, kept visually separate from the caption font.

For Comet Garden: keep the two-tier verb-over-object hierarchy and the no-effects, size-plus-contrast legibility, but use our own voice. Set it in Fredoka 700 (our site font) in our --ink #1b1040 on a light band, or --text/--dust on a night band. Title case or a softer, rounded all-caps. Nothing condensed or red.
color_light_recipe:
Golden-hour key light from upper-left, soft warm bounce, gentle painterly render (Pixar-adjacent 3D characters over painted isometric environments). The palette is warm midtones (lavender, sunflower yellow, terracotta, peach stone, leaf green) plus one cool accent per frame (a blue sky or a pool) so the hero pops. The caption band is warm cream (~#FEEAC9) fading to blush (~#FCCDBD) with oxblood type (~#A80000). It is the same in every designed frame, which makes the gallery read as one strip.

Colour does the storytelling: in the before/after, 'before' is desaturated sepia and 'after' is fully saturated. Reward items get a radial light burst and a warm gold rim. Magic is shown with white-gold sparkle particles.

For Comet Garden: keep our night-space base (--space #0b0a24 / --panel #19164a) with the warm sun-core glow as the key light on the planet. Use the desaturate-vs-saturate trick for a barren grey rock vs. a living planet. Put a radial --dust #ffd76a glow behind the comet or a new creature, and use --life #5ef2b0 and --gem #4de1ff as the cool pop. Keep one consistent band colour across all shots.
character_staging:
Big-eyed, stylized 3D characters, shown waist-up in 3/4 view and cropped by the caption band so they feel close and life-size.

The hero shot uses direct eye contact and a knowing expression to build an instant relationship. A second character (the heroine) acts as the audience's stand-in: her face tells the viewer how to feel in each frame. She is delighted and surprised at the reward (2), skeptical and thinking at the plot twist (3), and leaping with joy in the restored world (4).

Characters overlap UI panels and card edges, peeking from behind the board. That joins the 'story' layer to the 'game' layer and adds depth.

Props in hand set up the mechanic: the basket of keys in shot 1 pays off as the merged key in shot 2.

Scale shifts across the sequence: huge portrait (1) -> medium reaction (2, 3) -> tiny figure in a huge world (4), which sells the world's size.

For Comet Garden: we already have creature idle, happy, surprised and wave poses, the Keeper avatar, and peeking creatures. Stage a creature at close range as the hero with eye contact. Have a creature peek over the planet's rim or the card edge in surprise at a new land. Show a tiny Keeper or creature cheering on a big, lush planet for the payoff.
what_makes_it_work: It opens on a face, not a UI: an expressive character with eye contact plus a teasing line makes the thumbnail feel like a story, and it stands out among search results full of gameplay.
Each designed frame has one idea and one hero object (grandma, the key, the jail twist, the restored pool), so each reads in under a second at thumbnail size.
It explains cause and effect inside one frame: the goal icon above (a padlock on the greenhouse) and the result on the board below (the key) teach the core loop without text.
Cropped, zoomed gameplay: showing ~4x4 cells at about 2x, with one item at 3x on a glow, makes the mechanic legible where a full-screen board would be mush.
Two-tier verb-first captions: one huge action word plus a small object line gives instant hierarchy and a confident, directive voice.
A consistent tilted band across the designed set: the same colour, position and type make the gallery read as one strip, and the slight tilt adds motion.
Before/after told through colour (sepia vs. saturated) with a magical trail as the divider shows progress without any numbers.
An emotional arc on a recurring character (surprise -> suspicion -> joy) turns the screenshots into a mini storyboard.
Depth layering (scene -> card -> character overlapping the card -> foreground flowers -> band) makes flat marketing frames feel like a diorama.
Weakness to avoid: after shot 4 the set falls apart into noisy raw captures with timers, currency and a pixel-identical duplicate, which wastes slots and weakens the finish.
transferable_to_comet_garden: Shot 1 = creature hero, not UI. A big close-up of one of our cutest creatures (happy or wave pose) with eye contact, cradling a small glowing comet the way grandma holds the keys, so the prop previews the mechanic. The tiny planet sits behind or below with the sun-core glow as back light. Logo on top, and a short, warm, curious line at the bottom (our own wording, in our voice, not a mystery-secret tease).

Shot 2 = one-frame cause -> effect. The aim arc and a flung comet in the upper half, and in the lower half a zoomed crop of the planet rim where a new land blooms with a radial dust-gold glow, plus a creature peeking over the rim in surprise. Caption as verb over object (e.g. 'Fling' big, 'a comet' small), in our own words.
Drop the device frame we use today and crop or zoom the gameplay instead: show about a quarter of the planet's rim at 2-3x so lands and creatures read at thumbnail size.

Before/after on the planet itself: the left half a desaturated grey barren rock, the right half lush with lands and creatures. The divider is our comet's own sparkling tail curving around the planet (our signature), not an arrow.
Welcome frame instead of a stakes frame: a creature's silhouette reveal or a 'moved in' moment with a tiny Keeper waving. Keep an emotional beat but make it gentle and all-ages (no peril, no jail).
One recurring guide character (a mascot creature or the Keeper) whose expression changes across shots (curious -> amazed -> proud) to give the set a storyboard arc.
Two-tier captions in Fredoka 700: one big verb (Fling / Grow / Welcome / Collect) over a small line, 2-4 words total, flat colour, no stroke, legible from size and contrast alone.

A consistent caption band across every designed shot, in our own shape. Suggestion: a gently curved night-sky or horizon arc (the planet's curvature) at the top or bottom in --panel with --text/--dust type. It does the same job as their tilted band without looking like it.
Depth layering: starfield/nebula backdrop -> planet -> creature overlapping the planet or card edge -> foreground sparkles or comet tail -> caption band on top.
Payoff shot at a small figure-to-world scale: a tiny Keeper cheering on a big, fully grown planet, to sell how much the world can grow.

Put the four strongest designed frames first. Never pad with raw captures, never repeat a shot, and keep currency, timers, the shop and badges out of every frame. That also honours our no-ads, grown-ups-only-purchases promise.
Colour as narrative: desaturated for 'before' or 'empty', full saturation for 'alive'. Warm sun-core key light on the planet against cool space, with one cool mint/cyan accent per frame.
do_not_copy: The cream-to-blush caption band with a ~3.5 deg tilted top edge and rose stroke, paired with deep oxblood-red, heavy all-caps type: that exact band-plus-colour combination is their signature.
The chunky black serif logo with a cream inline and an offset drop shadow.
Grandma/family-secrets mystery framing and the staggered two-line ellipsis tease on the opening shot.
Key and padlock iconography, a padlock in a speech-bubble tag, and a golden key on a radial burst as the reward.

The glossy green curved arrow in before/after shots, and a before/after wipe that is literally an S-curve glitter trail across an isometric estate (we use our comet tail wrapped around a round planet).
Their caption wording and the 'verb THE noun' formula word-for-word (e.g. 'MERGE THE CLUES', 'REBUILD THE MANSION').
The red-haired heroine in a yellow sweater as the reaction character, and the grandma look (grey bob, black glasses, lavender sweater).
Isometric mansion/estate rendering with a painted golden-hour environment: our look is a round planet in night space, and it should stay that way.
The comic diagonal split panel with a jail scene or orange jumpsuit (also off-brand for all-ages).
A top resource HUD (level star, lightning energy, coins, pink gems with + buttons), event countdown timers, gem-priced skips, shop cart icons and notification badges.
Casino, gambling or alcohol props (blackjack table, roulette, slot machine, wine glasses).

name: Pokemon TCG Pocket
full_sequence:
7 portrait shots, all with the same pastel caption band across the top. Shots 6 and 7 were downloaded and checked.
1) PACK-OPENING HOOK. Caption: open two free packs every day. Three booster packs are fanned out; the centre one is larger, sits in front and reflects on the floor. Above it, a rounded speech bubble shows a carousel of cards you could pull. Real UI is visible (rates button, points counter, bottom nav bar). The background is split on a diagonal, blue and white, continuing the band's slant. Job: the core loop plus a daily reason to come back (a red flag for us).
2) SIGNATURE TECH plus SOCIAL. Caption: share cards with friends. One large hero card on a plain mint background. The 3D character's head pushes out of the card's art window. Real share UI (count stepper, big pill button). Job: shows the thing only this game has, framed as a social benefit.
3) LIVE-OPS NEWS BEAT. Caption: more cards can now be traded. No UI. Two foil cards float at about a 30-degree tilt on a mint glow with white sparkles. The front card is larger and cropped by the bottom-left edge. Job: 'there's something new', plus a spectacle break between two UI shots.
4) BREADTH. Caption: show off your collection. Real binder grid with a count of about 1,025. The rows naturally make a rainbow of card-type colours. Job: proves there's a lot of content, so it will last.
5) EMOTIONAL CLOSER-STYLE ILLUSTRATION. Caption: show favourite cards to players worldwide. One soft pastel hero card sits in a lilac hand-drawn scene. Chibi characters crowd the four corners, cropped by the canvas edges and facing inward. Job: warmth and character love; the most 'cute' frame.
6) GAMEPLAY PROOF. Caption: casual battles in your free time, low-pressure wording. Real battle board with HP numbers; the active card has a cyan glow outline. Job: shows the actual play; the 'casual' wording reassures lighter players.
7) DEPTH / ASPIRATION. Caption: test your skills in ranked matches. A slanted purple 'Ranked up!' banner echoes the caption band's angle. Rank emblem with orange up-arrows on near-white. Job: tells competitive players there's a long tail.
Arc: hook -> unique tech -> news -> breadth -> emotion -> play -> mastery. They alternate real-UI frames (1, 2, 4, 6) with pure art frames (3, 5, 7), so the carousel never shows two dense UI screens in a row.
composition_recipe:
CAPTION BLOCK: a full-width band at the top, about 12% of canvas height on the right and about 17% on the left. Its bottom edge is a straight slant of about 5 degrees, lower on the left, with a thin white stroke and a soft shadow underneath, so it reads as a ribbon laid over the scene. The band is identical on all 7 shots. The caption is 2 centred lines with generous side margins (about 8% each side), sitting in the band's upper two-thirds.
HERO: one hero object per frame, centred horizontally, its visual centre at about 45-55% of canvas height, filling 60-75% of the width. When there are several objects (shot 1 packs, shot 3 cards), the frontmost is about 15-25% larger and overlaps the others, so there's always one clear focal point.
GAMEPLAY PLACEMENT: real UI runs full-bleed with no device frame, starting right under the band. Bottom navigation is kept in some shots (1, 4) for authenticity. UI panels are soft frosted-white, so the saturated hero carries the colour.
DEPTH LAYERS (back to front): (a) a flat pastel field or diagonal colour split, (b) a soft bloom or halo behind the hero, (c) the hero, tilted off the UI plane where it's a pure art frame, (d) a floor reflection or sparkle particles, (e) foreground chips or buttons.
FRAMING: art frames push objects past the canvas edge (shot 3 front card, shot 5 corner characters) to suggest a bigger world. The only element allowed to cross the band's edge is the band itself. Ranking and news beats reuse the band's slant angle inside the scene (shot 7 banner), so the geometry repeats.
RHYTHM: background hue changes per shot (blue-white, mint, mint, grey-white, lilac, pale blue, near-white) while the band stays fixed. That gives the set variety and identity at the same time.
type_recipe: Two weights in one caption. Connecting words are set in a thin-to-regular humanist rounded sans, white, with a soft grey drop shadow for legibility on the pastel band. One or two keywords per caption (a number, the verb, or the payoff noun) are set in an ultra-heavy rounded display face. They're about 1.2-1.4x taller, filled with a vertical yellow-to-amber gradient, and carry the same drop shadow. The keyword usually starts line 1 (the verb) or finishes line 2 (the payoff), so the eye reads 'bold, light, bold'. Sentence case, and nearly every caption ends in an exclamation mark. Typically 6-8 words, verb first, second person, benefit before feature, never the name of a system. The ranked shot adds a second, in-scene type layer: a huge heavy italic-ish word on a slanted colour banner. That shows you can use one scene-level shout per set, kept apart from the caption. For Comet Garden: keep the two-weight idea but use our own face (Fredoka 400 for connecting words, Fredoka 700 for keywords). Don't use a gold gradient; colour each keyword with the accent of that shot's story (life mint for creatures, sun orange for flings, gem cyan for sky shots).
