color_light_recipe: Every frame is bright and pastel. Most background pixels are 80-100% brightness and low saturation (pale mint, sky, lilac, grey-white). Nearly all the saturation goes into the hero (foil cards, pack art), so the hero pops from colour contrast rather than dark/light contrast. The caption band is a horizontal pastel rainbow (blush pink -> lavender -> sky -> mint) and never changes. Light is soft and even, with no hard shadows. UI uses soft neumorphic frosted panels with faint drop shadows. Heroes get a white bloom behind them (shot 3), a coloured glow outline when active (shot 6, cyan), or a floor reflection (shot 1). Negative space has scattered white four-point sparkle stars. Foil and iridescent highlights on the hero connect back to the rainbow band, so the band feels like it came from the product. The closer changes key (lilac with hand-drawn swooshes) but stays pastel. For Comet Garden: our game is a dark space scene (deep indigo ground, warm sun, mint life, cyan gem), so flip their recipe. Use a dark, low-saturation indigo field with the saturated, glowing planet and creatures as the only bright objects. Use a warm rim light on the planet from a sun source, stardust sparkles in the empty space, and change the sky hue per shot (dawn peach, day teal, dusk violet, night indigo) instead of a pastel rainbow.
character_staging: Characters almost never appear as free-standing mascots. They live inside the product object (the card) and are made special by breaking its boundary. In shot 2 the character's 3D head pushes out of the card's art window, which adds depth and a moment of delight. Only on the emotional frame (shot 5) do characters leave the product. There they are chibi, hand-drawn versions that ring the four corners, cropped by the canvas edge and looking or leaning toward the centred hero. They frame the hero like an audience instead of competing with it. Characters are shown mid-action or expressive (sleeping, cheering, a winking face), never in a neutral stance. Scale rule: the framing characters are big (each about 30-40% of the width) but partly off-canvas, so they feel huge and close without covering the centre. For Comet Garden: the creatures should live on the planet (our 'product object') and break its silhouette, peeking over the horizon or hanging off the planet's edge. On one closer shot, circle big, cropped creatures around the planet and have them look at it.
what_makes_it_work: One fixed header band on all 7 shots makes the carousel read as one designed set and makes it recognisable at thumbnail size
The slanted band edge brings energy to an otherwise calm, pastel set; the slant comes back inside a scene (the rank banner), so the geometry feels deliberate
The two-weight caption lets a quick scroller get the message from the bold keyword alone
Colour contrast: saturated heroes on pale grounds, so the product is always the brightest thing on screen
Real UI shown without a device frame and softened, so it looks authentic but not cluttered
Real-UI frames alternate with pure art frames, so the scroll never feels like a manual
Each frame has one hero, with a clear front-to-back size hierarchy when there are several objects
The signature tech (character popping out of the card) appears early and is framed as a social benefit, not a feature list
The collection-grid shot proves how much content there is without explaining it
A warm illustrated character frame brings emotion late in the set, after the functional proof
Low-pressure words (casual, free time) widen the appeal beyond core competitive players
Objects cropped at the canvas edge suggest a world bigger than the phone
transferable_to_comet_garden: Make one fixed caption header of our own for all 8 scenes. Instead of a straight slant, give the band's bottom edge a gentle convex arc, like the horizon of a tiny planet, with a thin stardust stroke. The fixed band builds set identity; the arc is ours.

Change the sky colour under the band per shot (dawn peach -> day teal -> dusk violet -> night indigo) so the carousel reads as one day in the garden. This echoes their rotating background hue under a fixed header.

Use two type weights: Fredoka 400 white for connecting words and Fredoka 700 at about 1.3x for 1-2 keywords, each keyword coloured with that shot's accent token (life #5ef2b0 for creatures, sun #ffb13d for flings, gem #4de1ff for sky shots). Our current captions already suit this, e.g. with the verb or payoff noun bolded.
Pick one hero per frame. Scale the planet up 10-20% beyond its in-game crop, centre it at about 50% height, give it a warm rim light and soft bloom, and keep the UI soft and frameless around it.

Our version of 'breaking the frame': a comet's glowing trail starts inside the caption band and arcs down to the planet. That connects headline to gameplay, and the first shot shows the verb (fling). A creature can also peek over the planet's silhouette or hang off its edge.

Colour-contrast rule: dark, low-saturation indigo space field; only the planet, creatures and comet trail are saturated and bright. Add stardust sparkles in the empty space instead of their white four-point glints.

Alternate real-UI frames (fling aim line, Fusion/Combo, Ember Vent forecast) with pure art frames (hero planet with creatures, creatures ringing the planet) so no two dense UI screens sit next to each other.
Show breadth with a collection grid: the Lifebook page full of creatures, arranged so the rows make a colour gradient, with our real count (36) in the caption instead of a scroll counter.
Emotional closer: circle big, cropped, hand-drawn-style versions of our creatures around the planet, facing it and cropped by the canvas edges. This should come after the gameplay proof, not before.
Spectacle-break frame: a tilted, floating, glowing planet on sparkles with no UI. Good for a new-content or update beat when we add planets or creatures in future versions.
Borrow the low-pressure wording (play whenever, gentle, no rush) and use it in the Grown-ups/No ads trust frame. Keep captions verb-led and in second person, 5-7 words.
Set up a one-per-set scene shout: one in-scene display word (e.g., a COMBO or STEAM! burst from the game's own VFX) on the Fusion shot, echoing the band's arc, kept apart from the caption.

Avoid their red flags: no loot or daily-pack lead, no 'every day' habit hook, no rates/points/currency UI, no ranked or competitive frame. Our last frame should be the trust promise (no ads, purchases stay with grown-ups).
do_not_copy: The horizontal pastel rainbow caption band (blush pink -> lavender -> sky -> mint) with a straight slanted bottom edge and thin white stroke; it's their signature on every shot
The exact type pairing: thin white rounded sans with an ultra-heavy yellow-to-amber gradient keyword and grey drop shadow
Trading-card shapes, foil/holo card borders, card backs, binder grids of cards, and booster-pack packaging as hero objects
The 3D character bursting out of a card's art window (their 'immersive card' feature)
Poke Ball / Master Ball iconography, rank emblems, and the slanted purple rank-up banner with orange up-arrows
The lilac hand-drawn border scene with pink/purple swooshes and white dotted lines around a centred card
Their neumorphic frosted-white UI panels and the speech-bubble card carousel over a pack fan
White four-point sparkle glints on mint glow as a signature texture (use our own stardust and comet-trail particles)
Their caption phrasings about sharing cards with friends, showing off a collection, or showing favourites to the world; write our own verb-led lines
Any gacha framing: pack opening, offering rates, points counters, 'every day' pull hooks

name: Pokémon GO
full_sequence:
7 portrait shots at 1242x2208, all viewed; shots 3, 4, 2 and 7 were also checked at full resolution. Shots 2 to 7 share one template: a two-tier caption on top, a glowing rounded screen card in the middle, a blurred themed scene behind, and one creature standing outside the card at bottom right.
1) Seasonal key art with no gameplay. The logo and a 10th-anniversary badge sit at top center, then a thin white divider, then an ornate event plaque. The top 40% is dark starry sky that holds the logos. The bottom 60% is a painted dusk farm scene: a dirt path leads the eye to an orange sunset horizon, and about 7 creatures are spread along the path at different depths. Job: brand hook, plus proof that the game is updated right now.
2) Magenta field with a stormy city and lightning. A pink verb meaning "win" sits over a battle mode name. In the card, a giant flaming boss fills most of the screen, with HP bars and a meter kept in. A fire-type fighter stands in front, bottom right, about 46% of canvas height, bleeding off the bottom edge. Job: spectacle and power.
3) Icy cyan field with snowy forest and sparkles. An orange verb meaning "raid" sits over a line about playing with other people. The card shows the co-op raid screen: two name/CP panels, a big countdown timer, hit flashes. An ice creature stands at bottom right on a snow drift. Job: social co-op.
4) Blue-green park with diagonal light rays from the left. A pink-red "CATCH" over the franchise name. The card shows the catch screen: a creature on grass and the ball at the bottom. The flagship mascot, with a thick white sticker outline, waves at bottom right on a grass strip that covers the card's bottom edge. Job: the core loop. It comes 4th only because the brand is already famous.
5) Crimson field with red rocky mountains. A green verb meaning "mega evolve" sits over a possessive line. The card shows the evolved form powering up on a dark stage with a rainbow energy streak. Outside the card stands the same creature's cute baby form, with a white outline, sitting on rocks. Job: progression. Tiny baby outside, powered-up form inside, so the payoff is shown as a before and after.
6) Purple dark forest. A cyan verb meaning "defeat" over the villain team's name. The card is split into two stacked panels (villain on top, player below) with a round VS badge on the seam. A small creature wrapped in purple shadow smoke stands at bottom right. Job: villain and variety.
7) Blue field with light streaks and sparkles. A lavender verb meaning "collect" over a huge number plus the creature word. The card shows the collection grid. Two cells are lifted out, scaled up about 1.2x with drop shadows, and one overlaps the card's rim. A creature stands at bottom right on a rock ledge. Job: breadth, with a number as proof.
Hue order: dusk amber/navy, magenta, cyan, green-blue, crimson, purple, blue. No two neighbors share a hue, so the row of shots reads as a rainbow strip.
composition_recipe:
Measured on the 1242x2208 canvas.
- Caption block: the top ~20% of the canvas. Tier 1 (the verb) is centered at ~8% of the height, with a cap height ~9% of canvas height and a width of 65 to 75% of canvas width. Tier 2 is centered at ~17%, with a cap height ~5%. It is often wider than tier 1 (up to ~95% of the width). Its lower edge overlaps the card's top rim by a few percent, which locks the caption and the card into one unit.
- Hero card: a bezel-less rounded rectangle, not a realistic phone. It is inset ~15 to 16% on each side (~68 to 70% of canvas width), runs from ~19% down to ~95% of the height, and has a corner radius of ~5% of canvas width. The rim is a thin light line (~1.2% of the width) in a light tint of the shot's hue, with a soft outer glow ~7% of the width. The gameplay fills the card edge to edge. The status bar is cropped, but real HUD (HP bars, timers, counts) is kept.
- Foreground stage: a strip of ground that matches the theme (grass, snow drift, rocks, stone) runs across the bottom ~8 to 12% and covers the card's lower edge, so the card looks planted in the world.
- Character: always bottom right. It covers 30 to 46% of canvas height and 33 to 50% of the width. Roughly half its body overlaps the card's right edge and the rest sits over the background margin. Its feet stand on the foreground strip or bleed off the bottom edge.
- Depth, back to front: 1) blurred, color-washed themed environment with a vignette and sometimes light rays, 2) glow halo, 3) screen card, 4) foreground ground strip, 5) character, 6) caption (on top of everything, overlapping the card's top). A few 4-point sparkle glints sit only in the side margins, never over the card.
- Variants on the template: a split card with a round badge on the seam (shot 6), UI elements lifted out of the card and past its rim (shot 7), and a full-bleed key art shot with a logo stack and a path as a leading line into the horizon (shot 1).
type_recipe:
- Two-tier stack in all caps, heavy geometric sans, centered, with tight but normal tracking.
- Tier 1 is a single power verb, occasionally two words, and is about 1.8x the cap height of tier 2.
  - Fill is a vertical gradient in a hue picked per shot: light glossy highlight at the top, saturated middle, a slightly deeper base. A white specular sheen sits on the upper left of the letters.
  - A thick dark navy outline (~1.5 to 1.8% of canvas width), a darker extruded bevel under each letter, a soft drop shadow, and a faint outer glow in the verb's hue.
- Tier 2 is 1 to 3 words: the object or context. White fill with the same navy outline (a bit thinner) and a small drop shadow, no gradient.
- The outline color stays the same across every shot. Only the tier-1 fill changes color, which holds the set together.
- Voice: imperative verb plus object. Captions run about 2 to 4 words in total, and one uses a big number as proof (e.g. "COLLECT 1000+").
- Line breaks are fixed: the verb always sits alone on line 1.
color_light_recipe:
- Each shot owns one saturated field hue. The tier-1 verb is filled in a contrasting, often near-complementary hue so it pops:
  - orange verb on icy blue
  - green on crimson
  - cyan on purple
  - pink-red on green-blue
  - lavender-pink on blue
  - pink on magenta is the one low-contrast case, rescued by the navy outline.
- Backgrounds are real 3D/photo environments, blurred and washed toward the field hue. Edges are darker (vignette) and brightest behind the card, like a backlight.
- The card rim glow uses a lighter tint of the field hue (for example a near-white cyan rim on a cyan field). This makes the card look lit from behind and pulls the eye to the center.
- Light rays: diagonal god-rays or light streaks from the upper left in daylight shots, lightning in the battle shot, and sparkle and snow particles in the icy shot.
- Contrast between the card and the background:
  - the gameplay inside is crisp and fully saturated
  - the environment outside is soft and lower in contrast
  - the character is crisp, with rim light.
- Shot 1 uses warm-cool contrast: an amber sunset horizon under a deep navy starry sky. Purple glow on one creature adds a secondary accent.
character_staging:
- One creature per shot, staged outside the screen card at bottom right, and never the same creature twice.
- Each creature is chosen to theme with its shot:
  - fire type on the fiery boss shot
  - ice type on the snowy raid
  - the flagship mascot on the core catch shot
  - the baby form of the creature evolving inside the card
  - a creature wrapped in shadow smoke on the villain shot.
- Scale contrast is the key move. The card holds something huge and dramatic (a boss, an evolved form), while the creature outside is small, cute and close to the viewer. The cute one is still the biggest thing on the canvas, because perspective makes it read as standing in front of the screen.
- Poses face the viewer or three-quarter, with eye contact and open, reactive expressions: waving, cheering, surprised, bracing. Several have a thick white die-cut sticker outline (the flagship mascot, the baby form) that separates them from a busy background. Others rely on rim light.
- Feet are grounded on the foreground strip, or the body is cropped by the bottom edge, which adds depth.
- In the key art shot, about 7 creatures are spread along a path at near, mid and far depths, all small. That builds a world, with no single hero.
what_makes_it_work: One strict template repeated across 6 shots, varied only by hue, verb color, environment and creature. The row reads as one confident set, and each tile is still distinct.
Verb-first two-tier caption: the eye takes in one huge colored action word in under half a second, and the smaller white line then adds context.
The glowing bezel-less card reads as a screenshot without the dated, cramped look of a phone mockup. The rim glow in the shot's hue makes it look lit from inside.
The creature outside the card breaks the frame, which adds depth, personality and eye contact. Changing the creature every shot works as a mini collection teaser.
Scale contrast: the huge thing inside the card and the small cute thing outside tell 'epic' and 'adorable' in one image.
The foreground ground strip covering the card's bottom edge plants the screenshot inside a world instead of floating on a flat backdrop.
Themed environments (snow for raids, storm for battles, park for catching) add setting and mood that a flat color can't.
Hue rotation with complementary verb fills makes the strip vivid, and every caption stays legible thanks to one constant dark outline.
Real in-game HUD is kept inside the card, so the art feels honest even though it is heavily staged.
Lifting 2 cells out of a dense grid turns a boring inventory screen into a showcase, and pairs a big number with proof.
Sparkles stay out of the card and in the margins, so the gameplay area stays clean.
transferable_to_comet_garden: Swap our dark phone mockup for a bezel-less rounded screen card (~70% of canvas width, corner radius ~5% of width, running from ~19% to ~95% of the height) with a thin rim and soft outer glow in each shot's hue. Our dark-space gameplay will glow like a window into the cosmos.

Replace the flat color fields with soft themed scenes built from our own art. The existing bg hues from captions.json become atmospheres: dusk-orange nebula with comet trails (fling), meadow-green bokeh with drifting leaves (friends move in), gold sparkle haze (Fusions), sky-blue with bubble moons (sky), warm ember glow (Troubles), mint garden (Homeworld), lavender starfield (Lifebook). Blur them, add a vignette, and brighten the area behind the card.

Critter outside the card, our own way: render one of our 36 vector critters large (30 to 40% of canvas height) with a thick white sticker outline, on a foreground ground strip at the bottom that covers the card's lower edge and matches the planet's biome (grass lip, sand, ice shelf). Pick the critter to theme with the shot: the otter on the forest-beside-ocean shot, the obsidian turtle on the volcano shot, Floe Seal on the ice shot. Make it cozy instead of heroic: peeking over the rim, hugging the card's corner, or pointing at the planet.

Inverted scale story: the card shows the tiny planet where critters are specks, and the same critter stands huge outside. That is a 'zoom-in on a resident', where Pokémon GO uses a baby form next to its powered-up form.

Two-tier caption in Fredoka 700 (our rounded face, not their geometric sans). Tier 1 is one gentle verb (FLING, GROW, MEET, MIX, COLLECT, BUILD) in a candy gradient with a soft deep-plum or indigo outline and a small soft shadow instead of a hard extruded bevel. Tier 2 is short, in white, and may be sentence case. Keep the verb alone on line 1. Size tier 1 at ~1.8x tier 2 and let tier 2 slightly overlap the card's top rim.

Pick each verb's fill to contrast with its field (for example a peach-orange verb on the sky-blue shot, a mint verb on the coral Troubles shot). Keep one outline color on every shot so the set feels unified.
Lifebook shot: lift 2 or 3 critter cards out of the grid at ~1.2x with drop shadows, letting one cross the card's rim. Pair it with a number caption (our '36 creatures').

Use the split-card-with-round-badge variant as a before/after instead of versus: a bare rock planet on top, a lush planet full of critters below, and a small comet or arrow badge on the seam. Growth replaces combat.
Keep our real HUD in the card (aim line, aim tag, combo text, creature reveal). It proves the art is real gameplay.
Order the hues so no two neighboring shots match, and scatter a few 4-point sparkles only in the side margins.

Because Comet Garden is unknown, lead with the fling-and-grow core loop in shot 1 (Pokémon GO can hold it until shot 4). Borrow the key-art look instead: a comet trail as the leading line that curves into the planet, used as the shot 1 background behind the card.
Keep the grown-ups shot calm: same template but a quieter hue, and either no critter or one sleeping or reading critter, so it doesn't compete.
do_not_copy: Any Pokémon IP: creature designs or lookalikes, especially a round-cheeked yellow mouse mascot. The red-and-white ball with a center band: our comets and pods must never read as a capture ball.
The Pokémon GO logo, the 10th-anniversary badge style, and the ornate purple-gold event plaque with filigree.

Their exact caption look as a package: a hard navy outline, a glossy extruded all-caps gradient verb, and a white outlined second line in a geometric heavy sans. Use our rounded Fredoka, a softer plum or indigo outline, and no hard bevel.
Their exact verbs and phrasing formula around catching, raiding, mega-evolving, defeating villains, and 'collect 1000+ [creatures]'. Also words like Trainers, Pokédex, CP.
Combat framing: a VS badge, villain-versus-player split screens, lightning storm cities, battle HP bars and meters, aggressive fighter poses.
Their collection grid look (CP numbers over little green bars in pale cells).
A real-world AR photo of grass or a park inside the screen, and photoreal 3D environment backgrounds. Ours should be illustrated and space-cozy.
A seasonal event key art shot as the first shot, or anniversary or limited-time badges. That creates FOMO and doesn't suit a new game with no live events.
Cloning their exact geometry pixel for pixel (card inset, bottom-right creature at the same size on every shot). Vary our critter placement and pose so the set reads as ours.

name: Rotate Rings
full_sequence:
8 portrait shots, all using one template: the real game screen full-bleed (Level/score/gear HUD kept at top), a golden caption band over the bottom ~18%, and a costumed squirrel mascot standing on the band at the right. All 8 files viewed (6-8 downloaded at 460x999).
1) Teach the verb (Lv 65): a chain of open C-rings with acorns inside. A cartoon tap hand presses the green ring, which gets a yellow selection glow, and a blue praise word ('Great!') floats beside it. Painter squirrel. The caption is three verbs that spell out the loop. Job: show how to play at a glance.
2) Payoff (Lv 85): a flower/pinwheel-shaped level. Three acorns fly along glowing gold streaks with ghost echoes into an acorn-counter pill that glows and appears only in this shot. Ballerina squirrel. The caption says rotating = winning. Job: the reward moment.
3) Power (Lv 36): a dense tangle with an oversized glowing booster hammer in a white radial burst with sparkles. Gardener squirrel. The caption pairs 'brain' with 'relaxing'. Job: power-up, plus the double promise of smart and calm.
4) Hazard and wellness (Lv 75): concentric target rings with lit bombs sitting on them, pipes below. Scholar squirrel holding a puzzle book with a lightbulb over its head. The caption is a daily-calm habit claim. Job: add stakes and a reason to come back every day.
5) Depth (Lv 42): a symmetrical pipe-and-ring layout. A winking detective squirrel with a magnifier. The caption is about mastery. Job: 'there's more to this than it looks'.
6) Safety net (Lv 89): a mandala layout with the tap hand on the glowing center ring and a purple 'Excellent!'. A girl squirrel in a bow and gingham, winking. The caption names the hint system. Job: reassure players who worry about getting stuck.
7) Variety (Lv 46): the level itself forms a robot face (ring eyes holding acorns, a bomb on its head) with a green 'Good!'. Barista squirrel. The caption is about ring types. Job: novelty, 'every level is different'.
8) Finale (Lv 98, the highest number shown): the level forms a rocket with an acorn in the porthole and two stacked praise words. Astronaut squirrel planting a planet flag. The caption is about a perfect match. Job: an aspirational close. The picture-level and outer-space theme send you off on an upbeat 'look how far you get' note.
Arc: how-to, reward, booster, hazard, mastery, hint, variety, picture-puzzle climax. Weakness: from shot 3 onward the tangles look alike, so the story flattens. The level numbers jump around (36-98) instead of climbing.
composition_recipe:
Canvas 1290x2796 equivalent (measured on 460x999). Three stacked zones, the same in every shot:
(a) HUD strip, top ~10%: the real game HUD, kept for authenticity.
(b) Gameplay stage, y ~15-80%: the whole puzzle is visible and centered, never cropped, with ~5% side margins. Almost no text sits on the gameplay except one in-game praise word placed at the right edge of the action, sometimes slightly past the puzzle.
(c) Caption band, bottom ~18% (top edge at ~y 81.5%): a gentle S-wave top edge with a thin cream highlight rim above the fill, like a glossy lip. The fill has a faint tone-on-tone doodle pattern at ~10% contrast.
The caption block sits bottom-left: left margin ~3% of width, baseline ~3.5% above the bottom, taking ~60-65% of the band width and ~9% of the canvas height.
The hero character sits bottom-right, ~33% of width and ~20% of canvas height. Its feet sit on the band floor near the bottom edge, and its head and props rise ~5-6% above the band's top edge into the stage. This break is what joins the marketing layer to the game layer. The character's gaze or props often point up-left toward the puzzle.
Depth layers, back to front: flat canvas color, then the flat gameplay pieces, then the tap hand, praise word and flying collectibles, then the band, then the caption, then the character (topmost, overlapping the band edge).
Only the rewards shot adds a second focal element: a collectible arc from mid-puzzle to a top-left counter. The booster shot scales one object to ~35% of width inside a light burst.
type_recipe:
Two-line stacked caption, left-aligned, all caps.
- Line 1 is the lead-in, cap height ~8% of canvas width.
- Line 2 is the key word or phrase, set ~1.3-1.5x larger (~11-12% of width), and often only one word.
- 2-3 words in total, never more than 4.
- Face: a very heavy, rounded, slightly condensed display sans (Lilita-One-like). White fill, thick deep amber-brown outline (~#8A5008 to #B0601F, roughly 12-15% of cap height), plus a darker extrusion/drop offset down and to the right for a chunky 3D sticker look.
- The whole block tilts about 2-4 degrees upward to the right for energy. Tight leading: the lines nearly touch, and line 2 tucks under line 1.
Voice: mostly verb-led imperatives (verbs chained as the loop, 'rotate to win'), mixed with benefit claims (calm, daily, brain) and a few flat feature labels (hints, ring types). The feature labels are the weakest.
In-game praise words ('Great!', 'Excellent!', 'Good!') use a different face: a bold geometric sans in saturated blue, purple or green with a white outline and a soft shadow. They sit on the gameplay, so the two type systems never compete.
character_staging:
One mascot per shot, always the same species (an orange squirrel) and always in the same spot: bottom-right, standing on the band and rising above its edge. What changes each shot is the costume and prop, which act as a visual pun on that shot's message. Painter's palette for the colorful opener; tutu and tiara for 'win'; straw hat and trowel for 'relaxing'; scholar with a book and a lightbulb over its head for 'brain/calm'; detective with a magnifier for 'master'; bow and gingham for the friendly hint shot; barista mug for variety; astronaut with a planet flag for the rocket finale.
Poses are friendly and give eye contact: a wink appears in 2 of 8, a grin in the others. Props usually reach toward the gameplay or break the band edge. The character never appears inside the gameplay. It is a marketing-only host, so the costume changes add novelty to every swipe while the frame stays fixed.
The in-game 'characters' are the collectibles (acorns), and they act as the reward thread through the set.
what_makes_it_work: A rigid, repeated template (same canvas, band, caption position and mascot spot) turns 8 screenshots into a recognizable series. In a scrolling store row it reads as one brand at thumbnail size.
Gameplay is shown whole and uncluttered in every shot. The caption lives on its own band, so the puzzle is never covered and the player sees exactly what they will play.
The host character stands on the band and breaks into the gameplay area. That single overlap joins the marketing layer and the game into one image and adds depth.
The costume-per-shot gimmick gives every swipe a small surprise while the layout stays constant. The prop reinforces the caption: a lightbulb for brain, a magnifier for mastery.
Shot 1 teaches the gesture with a tap hand, a glowing selected piece and a praise word, so it's clear how to play in under a second.
The reward moment is staged as motion: collectibles fly along glowing arcs with ghost echoes into a counter that glows. The still image implies a satisfying animation.
Hero-object treatment for the one special feature: the booster is scaled up about 3x and wrapped in a radial light burst.
Levels shaped like pictures (flower, robot face, rocket) make abstract puzzles readable as illustrations and show off variety.
Two-size caption stacking puts the key word at the largest size, so the 1-2 word takeaway reads even at thumbnail size.
A limited palette: one soft neutral ground and one warm band color, so saturated game pieces and the mascot own all the contrast.
Real HUD elements (level number, score) with high level numbers quietly signal authenticity and lots of content.
transferable_to_comet_garden: Adopt a fixed series template. Keep one canvas treatment for all 8 shots, one caption zone and one fixed spot for the host character, and vary only the gameplay and the character's pose. Our captions.json currently gives each scene its own bg color. Consider a constant sky canvas with a constant band, or at least a shared band shape, so the set reads as one series.

Make the caption band OUR shape. Instead of a wavy strip, curve its top edge as the convex arc of a planet horizon. That echoes the tiny planet and gives the host 'ground' to stand on. Use a faint tone-on-tone pattern of our own motifs (tiny stars, seeds, comet dots) at ~10% contrast.

Rotate a different creature from our real 36-creature roster (idle/happy/wave poses) as each shot's host, standing on the horizon band and peeking up into the play area. The costume-change gimmick becomes a 'meet a different resident' gimmick, and it's more honest because the host actually lives in the game. Match the host to the scene: a whale or fish for a water/Rain Garden fusion, a dragon for the Ember Vent troubles shot, the Keeper for the Homeworld shot.

Use the Keeper as the host for bookend shots (shot 1 and the grown-ups/finale shot), posed with a caption-linked prop. For example, cheering next to a fling on shot 1, or leaning on the band for the calm grown-ups shot.
Stage the character so it breaks the band's top edge by ~5-6% of canvas height, with its gaze or a waving paw pointing up-left toward the planet.

Two-line stacked caption: a small lead-in line and a key word ~1.4x larger, tilted slightly upward, left-aligned, 2-4 words. Paraphrase our existing captions into verb-first lead-ins with one big payoff word, e.g. small 'Fling comets' over a large word about growing.

Build our own chunky caption lockup: a rounded heavy display face, cream or white fill, outline and extrusion in a darker cousin of OUR band color (e.g. deep indigo or plum), so it looks printed on the band.

Shot 1 teaches the gesture: a drag-back finger on the comet, the curved aim line glowing, the aim tag on the planet, and one in-game exclamation beside the action. Use our real feedback text (a Combo or Fusion callout), not generic praise.
Stage the reward as motion. The comet's arc trail with 2-3 fading ghost copies landing on the planet, with sparkles of 'life' flying to the relevant counter, implies the animation in a still.

Give ONE special moment per shot the hero-object treatment: scale it up and add a soft radial bloom and 4-point sparkles. Candidates are a Fusion burst (STEAM!) or a new creature's reveal. Keep this treatment off anything purchasable.
Show the gameplay whole and uncluttered: the full planet, never cropped by text. All text goes on the band except the game's own on-screen callouts.

Treat the planet as a 'picture level': make each shot's planet visibly different at thumbnail size (lush garden, ice, ember, water world) so shots 3-8 don't blur together the way Rotate Rings' tangles do.
Keep a real HUD sliver for authenticity and let the progress numbers climb across the sequence so the set tells a growth story. Rotate Rings' jumbled level numbers are a missed chance.

Sequence: teach, reward, variety, stakes and helpers, collection, calm close. End on an aspirational, emotional image (a fully grown, crowded planet) and our trust message about no ads and grown-up-only purchases.
do_not_copy: The orange squirrel mascot, and especially the costume-per-shot squirrel (painter beret, ballerina tutu, gardener straw hat, scholar with lightbulb, detective deerstalker, bow and gingham, barista, astronaut planting a flag). Also avoid any astronaut-with-planet-flag pose for our host.
The golden-yellow bottom band with a wavy top edge, a cream highlight rim and a faint donut/star doodle pattern.
The peach canvas (~#FAE7D9) paired with the golden band: that color pairing is their store identity.
Their caption lockup: white chunky rounded all-caps with an amber-brown outline, brown extrusion and a slight upward tilt, bottom-left on the band.
Acorns as collectibles and the glowing acorn-counter pill, and the gold streak arc of acorns flying to it.
The white cartoon glove tap hand with a yellow cuff.
Multicolor outlined praise words 'Great!', 'Excellent!', 'Good!' floating beside the action.
The purple star-emblazoned booster hammer in a glowing orb, and the lit cartoon bomb hazards.
Levels shaped like pictures from colored tubes and rings (flower, robot face, rocket).
Their HUD layout: 'Level N' stacked at top-left, a centered tan score pill and a gear button.
Their caption phrases: 'Twist align unlock', 'Rotate to win', 'Calm mind daily', 'Master the puzzle', 'Smart hint system', 'Unique ring types', 'Perfect gap match', 'Brain and relaxing'.
The 3D-rendered, Pixar-style mascot look layered over flat gameplay. Keep our host in our own flat vector in-game style.

name: Royal Smash! - Physics Puzzle
full_sequence:
The set has 5 portrait screenshots at 1242x2208 (apps.json lists only 5, so none needed downloading). Every shot is full-bleed, with no device frame, HUD, logo, badges or characters. All five use the same camera: a symmetric one-point view from just behind the launcher, with a curved caption ribbon at the top.

1) The setup (meadow). A calm, untouched pyramid of silver-blue cans stands on a purple tray on a lollipop pedestal, with a dirt patch below. Behind it are a castle, mountains and banners. The cannon sits at the bottom center. The caption is a verb triplet ("Aim, fire, destroy"). Job: teach the whole game in one glance. Target, weapon and goal are all readable at thumbnail size.

2) The payoff (tropical sea). This shot catches the exact moment of impact. The ball sits at the center of a starburst flare, a white-gold vapor trail runs straight up from the muzzle, and striped-lid jars burst outward with jam splashes. Some jars fall into the water. The caption promises one shot and big damage. Job: sell the satisfaction and the power fantasy. It is also the first change of biome.

3) The charm and challenge beat (meadow). The background plate is shot 1's, slightly reframed. A wall of gold crown blocks holds a pixel-art heart made of red jars. The caption is a taunt ("Too hard for you?"). Job: show that levels are designed puzzles, plus a cute, shareable image. Pairing the loving heart with the taunt creates tension.

4) The second payoff (desert ruins). Blue and purple blocks, wooden crates and cone-topped towers fly apart mid-explosion, with the same ball, flare and vapor trail as shot 2. The cannon's base changes to a desert-toned platform. The caption sells stress relief. Job: an emotional benefit (catharsis) plus a third biome.

5) The hook (meadow). The background plate is pixel-identical to shot 1 (measured diff 0.0). A two-pedestal colonnade of purple fleur-de-lis blocks, cream pillars and orange jars stands intact. The caption is an easy-to-learn, hard-to-put-down promise. Job: close on low effort and replay value, showing a structure that invites the next shot.

Rhythm: calm, boom, calm, boom, calm. The three calm shots reuse one meadow plate. The two explosion shots carry all the biome variety (sea, desert). The cannon and its framing never move.
composition_recipe:
Measurements are taken on the 460x818 thumbnail and given as fractions of the canvas.

CAPTION BLOCK: a full-width ribbon at the top. Its bottom edge bulges downward, sitting at about 9% of height at the sides and about 14% at the center. A thin gold piping line (about 1%) runs along that edge, with a darker orange hairline under it. The two headline lines are centered in the band, and the text block spans only 35–55% of the width. The rest of the band is plain patterned color, which keeps it calm.

HERO ELEMENT: the target structure, dead center horizontally. Its vertical center sits at 38–46% of height and it spans 65–77% of the width. A pedestal lifts it to the optical center, and the pedestal base (a dirt patch or water ring) sits at about 73–78%.

GAMEPLAY PLACEMENT: the launcher is always bottom-center and cropped by the bottom edge. The muzzle top is at about 82% of height, and a concentric-ring platform spans the full width. This gives the viewer a "you are the shooter" first-person anchor. In the payoff shots, a vertical trail from muzzle to target forms a strong central leading line.

DEPTH LAYERS (5): (1) the caption ribbon overlay; (2) far background: sky, mountains or sea, and a castle, with the horizon at about 28–32% so the ground plane fills most of the frame like a play table; (3) midground props framing the left and right edges: trees, boulders, banners, palms; (4) the hero on its pedestal; (5) the foreground launcher on its platform. The background is only lightly softened, with no heavy depth of field.

FRAMING: strict bilateral symmetry. The downward arc of the top ribbon and the arc of the launcher platform bracket the hero between two curves, like a lens. Explosion debris spreads outward to the edges but stops just below the ribbon. There are no margins in the usual sense. Everything is full-bleed and only the caption band is reserved.
type_recipe:
The headline is two centered lines in all caps, 1–2 words per line and 2–4 words total. Both lines use a heavy, rounded, geometric display face with tight tracking (in the Lilita-style family).

Line 1 is cream-white with a subtle white-to-blush vertical gradient. Line 2 is equal or slightly larger (cap height about 3.4% of canvas height against about 3.0% for line 1) and filled with a yellow-to-orange gradient. Both lines have a dark maroon 3D extrusion (offset downward about 8–10% of cap height) plus a soft contact shadow, so the letters look like chunky toy plastic.

Hierarchy comes from color and value, not size: the second, gold line is always the punchline word or payoff. The point size stays fixed across the set, so the text width varies with word count, which keeps the set feeling consistent. No body copy, sublines, logos or badges appear anywhere.

Voice: imperatives and benefit claims ranging from 2 to 5 words. There is one verb triplet, one power promise, one taunt question ("Too hard for you?"), one emotional benefit, and one effort/replay hook.
color_light_recipe:
VALUE STRUCTURE: the only large dark mass is the deep maroon caption band at the top (about #950334, with tone-on-tone pattern). Directly below it is the brightest, most saturated zone of the image, so the caption gets maximum contrast exactly where thumbnails are read. The foreground launcher returns to mid-dark saturated colors (red, royal blue), which weights the bottom and closes the frame.

LIGHT: high-key midday light from the upper left. Soft ambient light with strong glossy specular highlights on every prop (cans, jars and blocks look like candy or toy plastic), plus gentle rim light. No shot is dim, dusk or night.

PALETTE LOGIC: (a) Every scene carries the brand pair of purple and gold on the pedestal, trays and launcher platform, whatever the biome, which threads the set together. (b) The hero target is always colored against its biome: silver-blue on green, red, yellow and purple on turquoise water, cool blue and purple on warm sand. The target never blends into the background. (c) The payoff shots add a warm white-gold flare at the impact point, the brightest pixel cluster in the frame, placed at the geometric center. (d) Sky blue (about #3598F6) and grass green dominate the calm shots, so the saturated juice colors in the payoff shots feel like an event.
character_staging:
There are no characters. Personality is carried by a mascot-like object instead: the chunky, rounded, crown-emblazoned toy cannon. It is shown from behind at the same scale and position in all five shots, so it works as a stand-in for the player. The props themselves (glossy striped-lid jars, the pixel heart) carry the charm.

The consequence for us is that the set feels cohesive but impersonal. There is nobody to love, only a toy to use. That is the biggest gap Comet Garden can exploit. Our astronaut kid, the fox companion and the planet's creatures can take the emotional role Royal Smash leaves empty, and they can sit in the same foreground-anchor slot that the cannon owns.
what_makes_it_work: A fixed first-person anchor. Measured, the cannon crop is effectively identical in shots 1, 3 and 5 (diff 0.1–4.6), and only its base changes in 2 and 4. The five shots read as one continuous system, and the viewer is always 'the one who fires'.
One-glance mechanic: launcher at the bottom, target in the middle, trail between them. Someone who has never played understands the whole game from a single thumbnail with no UI.
Calm and action alternate (setup, boom, setup, boom, setup). Each explosion reads as an event because it follows a still, readable 'before' state.

Cheap variety. The three calm shots reuse one meadow background plate (shots 1 and 5 measure pixel-identical), and all the biome variety (sea, desert) goes into the payoff shots, where novelty has the most impact.
The value contrast is engineered: a dark caption band sits on top of the brightest part of the scene, and in 2 and 4 the brightest spot (the impact flare) sits at dead center.
The hero is colored against each biome (complementary pairs), so the silhouette always reads at thumbnail size.
The two-tone headline puts the payoff word on the gold second line. Hierarchy comes from color rather than size, which keeps the band short.
Strict symmetry and the two arcs (ribbon edge on top, launcher platform below) frame the hero like a lens and focus the eye on the center.
A level shaped like a recognizable icon (the pixel heart) turns a puzzle into a cute, shareable image and shows that levels are designed.
Removing all HUD gives clean poster moments. This is also a red flag: the polished, render-like finish may exceed real in-game fidelity (unverified).
transferable_to_comet_garden: Go full-bleed and drop the device frames in the current store/captions.json set. With a full-bleed shot, zoom the in-game camera so the planet spans about 70–78% of the width with its center at about 42–46% of height, instead of the roughly 40%-wide planet inside a phone mockup. The creatures on the ring grow from about 3% to about 5–6% of the width and become readable.

Promote our existing bottom-center launcher ring (the comet in its gold ring) to the fixed anchor: identical position and scale in every shot, cropped slightly by the bottom edge so it feels like the viewer's own hand. Let only its surroundings change per shot, the way Royal Smash swaps the cannon's base.

Use the curved dotted aim line and comet trail as the leading line from launcher to planet. In calm shots show the dotted aim arc. In payoff shots show a glowing trail ending in a soft bloom at the impact point, placed as the brightest spot in the frame.

Alternate calm and payoff, but make our payoff growth instead of destruction. Calm: a lush planet with creatures lounging. Payoff: the frame where a comet lands and land sprouts, flowers or steam burst out, or a creature pops in. Example order: 1 aim at a half-grown planet, 2 impact bloom with a friend moving in, 3 a charm beat, 4 a Fusion burst, 5 a fully grown planet.

Spend variety where it counts. Keep one signature deep-space backdrop for the calm shots and vary planet biome plus nebula tint for the payoff shots (Mossy, Frost, Ember, Comet Haven). Pair each planet with a complementary sky, for example a mint or green planet on violet space, a frost planet on a warm peach nebula, an ember planet on cool teal.

Thread two brand colors through every shot on the launcher ring and the planet's aura. Use our own tokens: sun #ffb13d plus life mint #5ef2b0, set against space #0b0a24 and violet #b3a3ff. Avoid the purple-and-gold pairing, and don't lean on --dust #ffd76a as the headline color, because it sits close to Royal Smash's gold.

Engineer the value contrast for our dark scenes, which invert Royal Smash's bright ones. Put the caption on a lighter band that fades into the scene: a soft sunrise or nebula gradient with a gentle cloud-scallop or orbit-arc lower edge that echoes the planet's curve, not a piped ribbon. Alternatively, set glowing type directly on space with a vignette behind it.

Two-line headline where the second line carries the payoff. Use Fredoka (our site face) Bold, with line 1 small in soft white #f4f2ff and line 2 larger in sun orange or life mint, and a soft navy #1b1040 drop shadow instead of a hard 3D bevel. Keep the point size fixed across the set, 2–4 words total. Sentence case keeps it friendlier than all caps. Example voice: 'Fling a comet / watch it bloom', 'Tiny world / big welcome'.

Charm beat in the style of the pixel heart: a real in-game Homeworld painted or planted in a heart or smile pattern (the Paint feature exists), or creatures arranged around the ring. Pair it with a warm invitation, not a taunt.

Fill the empty foreground Royal Smash leaves unused. Put the astronaut kid and fox beside the launcher bottom-left as spectators facing the planet, and one more creature bottom-right for symmetry. Once in the set, let a creature peek over the caption band edge as a signature beat that Royal Smash does not have.

Hide HUD (pause button, planet name, throws, life bar, goals) with a capture or marketing flag, but use real engine frames only, freezing time at the true impact frame instead of painting renders. Keep 1–2 later shots with the actual UI visible (Lifebook, Grown-ups) so the listing stays honest under guideline 2.3.

Close on reassurance instead of a compulsion hook. Our final beat is the existing 'No ads. Purchases stay with grown-ups.' shot. Avoid the 'hard to stop' framing entirely; it clashes with a cozy, all-ages, no-ads brand.
do_not_copy: The curved maroon ribbon header with a tone-on-tone crown-and-star pattern, gold piping and a dark orange underline
The two-line cream-over-gold chunky all-caps headline with a maroon 3D extrusion (their exact type treatment)
The crowned red, royal-blue and gold toy cannon, its crown-emblem cannonball, and the purple-and-gold concentric-ring launcher platform
Royal motifs: crowns, fleur-de-lis blocks, castles with pennants and banners, and the royal purple plus gold brand pairing
Stacked cans and red-white striped-lid jam jars on a purple tray and lollipop pedestal over a dirt patch
Juice and jam splash destruction bursts and the flying-debris explosion look
A pixel-grid heart built from blocks inside a wall of crown tiles (a heart motif is fine, but not this block-wall construction)

Their caption lines and structures: the 'Aim, fire, destroy' verb triplet, the one-shot/max-damage promise, the 'Too hard for you?' taunt, the stress-relief claim, and the easy-to-play/hard-to-stop couplet. Avoid 'one shot' as a caption phrase even though our repo is named oneshotgame.
The taunting or provocative challenge voice, which is off-brand for a cozy all-ages game

name: Screwdom
full_sequence:
8 portrait shots at 1290x2796, all built on one locked template: the same sky gradient, the same minimal HUD (four colored screw bins plus five slot dots) and the same wooden caption sign at the bottom. Only the hero object and the caption change from shot to shot. Shots 1-5 were already on disk; I downloaded 6-8 to shots/6740043080_6..8.jpg and viewed them.
1. Hook and mechanic. An orange voxel cat covered in multicolor screws faces the viewer. A cartoon tutorial hand (green cuff) plucks a blue screw with a sparkle burst, and a curved motion trail runs from the screw up into the blue bin, which already shows screws landing. The caption is a verb-led instruction to tap and unscrew. Job: teach the one gesture and show what it causes in a single frame.
2. Goal. A white and mauve blocky poodle in 3/4 profile facing right. The bins are partly filled (a red bin holding two screws, a blue screw dropping in). The caption states the win condition (empty the box). Job: tell the player what winning looks like.
3. Depth. A green-headed duck with a yellow block beak, facing right. The caption says to remove screws with strategy. Job: signal that there is thinking behind the ASMR.
4. Challenge and breadth. A cake slice with cream and a cherry on a segmented plate. The caption is an IQ-test claim. Job: challenge hook, and the first non-animal object shows content variety.
5. Sensory payoff. A daisy in a terracotta pot. The caption names the ASMR click. Job: promise tactile, audio satisfaction.
6. Rewards. A grey robot with a screw-studded face plate. The caption is about claiming rewards, and all bins are empty. Job: hint at a reward loop (weak proof).
7. Filler. A wooden drum or chattering-teeth contraption. It repeats shot 6's caption word for word, a wasted slot.
8. Close. A pink and mint retro camera. The caption is a brain-training claim, echoing shot 4. Job: breadth plus a benefit, but repetitive.
In search results only the first three portrait shots show, and all three are cute animals (cat, poodle, duck), so the cuteness is front-loaded where it earns taps. Food, plant and gadget come later to show breadth. The set runs out of distinct messages after shot 5: shots 6-8 repeat claims and stop showing play progress (empty bins).
composition_recipe:
Measured on the 460x997 downsample; all values are % of canvas height or width.
- 0-6% H: empty sky, the status-bar safe zone.
- 6-14% H: HUD row of four chunky bins spanning about 8-92% W.
- 17-20% H: a row of five hollow progress dots.
- 20-30% H: breathing sky.
- 30-78% H: the hero, a single 3D object, centered (visual center about 52-55% H), 70-90% W wide. The camera sits roughly 20-30 degrees above and about 30 degrees around, so three faces show and the object reads as a solid toy. The object floats: no ground plane, no cast shadow.
- 78-83% H: a breathing gap.
- 83-97% H: the caption sign, nearly full-bleed (about 3% gutters, x 3-96% W). It is two stacked wooden boards rotated about 3 degrees counter-clockwise (right side higher), with four corner screws, and the text sits inside it.
No device frame, no panorama across shots, no frame-breaking elements, no badges or laurels.
Depth layers, back to front: (1) the smooth vertical sky gradient; (2) the flat-ish 3D HUD; (3) the hero object; (4) the caption sign as the foreground anchor.
The only per-shot variables are the hero and the caption. Everything else stays pixel-identical, so the eye goes straight to what changed. Shot 1 adds one overlay: the pointer hand plus an arc trail that joins the action point to the HUD goal.
type_recipe:
Captions are all caps, set in a heavy rounded display face with soft, bulbous terminals.
- Size and layout: always two centered lines of 1-2 words each (2-3 words total, one outlier with a long second word). Cap height is about 4-4.5% of canvas height, the block spans about 75-85% of width, leading is tight (about 1.0-1.05) and tracking normal.
- Fill: a cream-to-gold vertical gradient (about #FFE9A8 at top to #FDD27A at bottom).
- Outline and depth: a thick very dark brown outline (about #2A0800), then a deeper brown offset extrusion or drop shadow below. The letters look embossed or stickered onto the wood.
- Voice: verb-led imperative instructions (tap / clear / remove) alternate with benefit hooks (a sensory click, rewards, brain claims).
No body copy, no secondary line, and no type anywhere else on the canvas. The HUD carries zero text, so the caption is the only reading task.
color_light_recipe:
Field: one cool vertical gradient on every shot. Sky blue at the top (about #9EDDFF) moves to aqua mid-frame (about #96E8FE) and lightens to pale ice at the bottom (about #C1F3FE). The lightest band sits behind the caption sign, so the dark-outlined warm wood pops hardest there.
Warm and cool split: the whole field is cool, and the only large warm mass is the brown-orange wooden sign. That warm anchor at the bottom is the strongest contrast on the canvas.
Hero objects use mid-saturation base colors (orange, lilac-white, jade, chocolate, pastel pink and mint) scattered with fully saturated candy screws in 8 colors (red, yellow, blue, cyan, pink, green, brown, white). The result is a confetti texture that reads as colorful even at thumbnail size, and it quietly explains the color-sorting mechanic.
Light: a soft key light from the upper front-left, broad and even fill, gentle bevel highlights on every block edge, light ambient occlusion in the seams, glossy specular dots on the screws, and no hard shadows. The render reads as clean toy plastic, bright and friendly, with no dramatic lighting.
The HUD bins repeat the saturated screw colors with a white face, so the top band and the hero are tied together by color. The only effects are the sparkle stars and one glowing arc in shot 1; there is no bloom, vignette or particles elsewhere.
character_staging:
There is no mascot and no recurring character. The puzzle objects are the characters.
- Animals first. A voxel cat faces the viewer head-on with big eyes and whiskers. A poodle and a duck stand in 3/4 profile facing right, with the eyes always visible. The proportions are chunky and big-headed, like a toy block kit.
- Presentation. Each creature is shown whole, never cropped, floating dead center at a size that fills the frame width, so the face and silhouette read at thumbnail size.
- Player proxy. Shot 1's cartoon hand is the only human element. It enters from the right edge, mid-gesture, with a sparkle burst on contact, and it is used once only.
- Breadth. After three animals the set switches to food, a plant, a robot and gadgets. That tells the viewer the object library is wide, but it also drops the emotional pull of faces in the later slots.
- No emotion acting. Creatures do not react, emote, or interact with each other. The cuteness comes purely from form and color.
what_makes_it_work: Locked template: the background, HUD and caption position are identical across all 8 shots, and only the hero and caption change. The set looks designed as a family, and the eye goes straight to the one thing that changed.
One huge hero per frame (70-90% of width) on an empty field. Each thumbnail reads in a fraction of a second at search-result size.
The first three slots, the ones visible in search, are all cute animals. The emotional pull is spent where it earns the tap.

Shot 1 teaches the whole game in one frame. A pointer hand does the gesture, and an arc trail links the action to its result (screw flying into the matching bin), so cause and effect are both visible.
The caption holder is a themed physical object (a wooden workshop sign with screws) that reinforces the fantasy instead of sitting as a generic text box.
Warm-on-cool contrast: a warm wooden sign on the lightest part of a cool sky gradient, with dark-outlined cream-gold caps, reads at any size.
Captions are 2-3 words, verb-led, in two lines, with no competing text anywhere else in the frame.
The confetti of saturated screw colors over calmer base colors adds visual richness and silently explains the color-sort mechanic.
The HUD is stripped to a textless minimum (bins plus dots), which proves real gameplay without adding clutter.
The soft, even toy-plastic lighting with bevel highlights feels tactile and safe, and it matches the ASMR promise.
Weaknesses to avoid: shots 6-8 repeat captions (one is used twice), show empty bins (no progress proof), and lean on unverifiable IQ and brain-training claims. The back half of the set is filler.
transferable_to_comet_garden: Drop the device frame and render the game full-bleed. Make the planet the hero at about 75-85% of canvas width, centered around 50-55% height. In our current set the planet is only about 40% of width inside a phone bezel, and that single change would roughly double its thumbnail impact.

Lock one template for all 8 shots: one background gradient, one caption holder in one position, one minimal HUD. Vary only the planet's biome and creatures plus the caption. Our current set changes background color every shot, which reads as 8 separate ads rather than one family.

Keep our own signature field instead of a sky blue. For example, a cozy twilight gradient running from deep indigo at the top to a warm peach or rose glow at the bottom, with the lightest, warmest band behind the caption. It keeps the warm-cool contrast principle, uses our night-sky identity, and does not look like Screwdom.

Shot 1 is a cause-and-effect frame. Show a finger or glowing touch point pulling the comet back, a dotted aim arc curving to the planet, and a sparkle bloom where it lands, with a patch of new land and a creature popping in. The action and its payoff should both appear in one image. Use our own pointer style (a soft glowing fingertip, a starry trail or a mitten), never a copy of their hand.

Put the three cutest creature moments in slots 1-3, since those show in search. Each one gets a close, uncropped creature with a visible face, large enough to read at 1/10 scale. Move the menu-style screens (Lifebook, Homeworld UI, Grown-ups) later.
Show breadth the way they swap objects: same framing, different planet biome per shot (ocean, forest, frost, desert, ember). The viewer sees content variety without extra explanation.
Cut the HUD down to one or two textless proof elements, such as the progress ring and the comet queue. Remove small text: planet names, the life counter, goals chips, and the bottom tooltip line.

Design a themed caption holder that belongs to our world, for example text riding on a comet-tail ribbon, a little garden-stake or seed-packet tag, or a puffy cloud. Keep it the same across every shot and give it the warmest color on the canvas.

Captions: two short lines, 2-4 words per line, verb-led for mechanics (fling, grow, meet) and benefit-led for feelings. Include one sensory shot that is honest for us (soft pops, cozy hums) as the counterpart to their ASMR slot.
Give every slot a distinct job with no repeated captions, and keep the proof of progress visible in every shot. End on the trust message (no ads, purchases only for grown-ups) instead of filler.
Never use IQ, brain-training or other unverifiable skill claims. They conflict with our all-ages, calm positioning and invite review scrutiny.

Lighting for the planet hero: a soft key light from the upper left, a gentle rim light to separate it from the sky, bevel-like highlights on land tiles and creatures, and no hard shadows, so the whole scene reads as a soft toy.
Run a thumbnail check on every shot. Downscale to about 129x280 and confirm the planet silhouette, one creature face and the caption all still read.
do_not_copy: Carved wooden plank caption sign (two stacked boards, about 3 degree tilt, four yellow corner screws). This is their signature device.
Cream-to-gold all-caps lettering with a thick dark-brown outline and brown extrusion set on wood.
Sky-blue to pale-aqua gradient field as the constant backdrop.
HUD of four colored screw bins with three holes each plus a row of five hollow progress dots.
Voxel or blocky animals and objects studded with multicolor Phillips-head screws, and any screw, bolt or toolbox motif.
Cartoon tutorial hand with a green sleeve cuff and sparkle burst on a screw.
Their caption wording and structure: the tap-to-unscrew instruction, the clear-the-box goal, the strategic-removal line, the ASMR click, the claim-rewards line and the IQ and brain-training claims.
Their specific hero lineup (orange cat, poodle, duck, cake slice, potted daisy, robot, pink retro camera) and the head-on 3/4 floating-toy presentation of those exact subjects.

name: Search It - Hidden Objects
full_sequence:
Only 5 portrait shots exist (apps.json lists 5; all were already downloaded and viewed, and none needed fetching). All are 460x996, with no device frame and no logo. Every shot uses the same three-part layout: a caption band on top, full-bleed gameplay art in the middle and the real item tray at the bottom.

1. Captioned as an order to collect every item. A daytime fairy-forest scene (greens and browns). Three large white rings circle three copies of the same potion. The tray's selected card is that potion with a count of 3, so the rings and the tray agree and teach the mechanic without text. The counter reads 5/30. Job: teach the core loop in one glance, with the hero mechanic readable at thumbnail size.

2. A calm reassurance line saying there is no timer. A night scene of a canal bridge under a moon, string lights and lanterns. A cartoon hand taps a scroll. Found items (a frog, a wooden idol, the scroll) glow white like stickers. Small elves, a gnome, a couple on the bridge and an old reader fill the scene. Job: remove the stress objection. The switch from day to night also breaks up the row.

3. A volume claim about how many pictures there are. No UI. A grid of about 8 rounded, white-bordered scene cards, each slightly tilted. The centre card is the night scene from shot 2, larger and in front. The cards bleed off every edge. Job: show breadth and replay value, and link back to shot 2.

4. The core verb again, this time about finding hidden objects. A cross-section of a city apartment block at night, with neon, a string of bulbs and a movie-night crowd. Three rings circle three different items (a banana, a lamp, a projector), and each one appears in the tray. People, a raccoon and a hamster are caught doing things. Job: prove variety of setting and item type, and keep the mechanic present.

5. An invitation to explore the map. A sunny harbour market in terracotta and aqua. The hand taps a bowl of oranges, two more bowls glow, and the selected tray card is the oranges. Job: end on a bright, open, inviting scene.

Weak spots: shots 1 and 4 carry the same message. The map caption shows just another scene, not a map. There is no progression, collection or family-trust shot.
composition_recipe:
Proportions measured on the 460x996 shots:
- Caption band: top 13-14% of the height (bottom edge at about y 125-140).
- Gameplay art: about 67% (y 135 to 807).
- Real UI tray: bottom 19%, starting at y 807 in every gameplay shot.

Caption band:
- One caption line, optically centred at about 7% of the height.
- The line spans 65-80% of the canvas width. Cap height is about 3% of the height (about 6% of the width).
- The band's bottom edge is one soft, low wave, about 2% of the height in amplitude. It dips into the art so the art seems to rise into the band instead of being boxed.

Gameplay art:
- Full bleed. It runs under the wave and off both side edges.

Callouts:
- 2-3 white rings, each about 20-21% of the canvas width across, with a stroke of about 1% of the width and a soft drop shadow.
- The rings sit in a loose triangle (upper-left, upper-right, lower-centre). They stay at least one ring-width clear of the band and the tray.
- The circled item itself is not changed.

Hand pointer:
- About 28% of the width. It overlaps its target from below-right, so the fingertip lands on the item and the cuff points toward the thumb zone.

Tray (depth layers, back to front: art, rings and glows, hand, UI chrome):
- Real UI: a collapse chevron at bottom-left and a hint button at bottom-right with a red badge. Both sit on the art just above the tray.
- A progress counter (n/30), then a row of item cards. The fifth card is cut off at the right edge to hint that there are more.
- The selected card is always the centre (third) slot, and it always matches the item called out in the art.

Volume shot:
- Drops the tray and uses a loose, tilted grid of rounded cards (about 3-5 degree rotations, white borders, cards bleeding off every edge).
- One card, reused from an earlier shot, is enlarged and brought forward as the anchor.

Framing: no device frame, no logo and no badges. The art is always the hero, and the UI chrome proves it is real gameplay.
type_recipe:
Letterforms:
- A heavy, rounded, geometric display sans, black weight with soft terminals, in the family of chunky "friendly game" faces.
- Title case, one line, 2-4 words, ending in an exclamation mark every time.

Fill and effects:
- White fill with a dark navy outline of about 2-3 px at 460 px width, plus a small offset shadow straight down, so the text lifts off the patterned band.

Keyword colouring:
- Exactly one keyword per caption is warm sunflower yellow (about #FFD24A) with the same navy outline.
- The yellow word is either the imperative verb (Collect, Find) or the payoff noun (the time/rush pair, Pictures, Map).

Voice:
- Imperative verbs, plus one reassurance line and one volume line.
- No sentences, no punctuation beyond a single comma, no body copy anywhere.

UI type:
- In-art UI numerals (tray counts, the 5/30 counter) use a matching rounded bold in slate navy.
- In the counter the current number is dark and "/30" is lighter grey, so the typography stays in one family.
color_light_recipe:
Caption band:
- Vertical gradient from cobalt (about #3B83FC) at the top edge to sky cyan (about #4BC6FF) at the wave.
- A barely visible, same-hue pattern of organic blobs and squiggles.
- A thin, lighter rim line on the wave edge that reads as a highlight.
- The same band colour is used on every shot. It is the only constant brand colour in the set.

Scenes:
- Deliberately alternate warm/day and cool/night down the row: forest green, then night indigo with warm lantern light, then a mixed collage, then night indigo with amber windows, then sunny terracotta and aqua.
- Every shot keeps high saturation and dense, small-scale detail so it reads as rich at any size.
- Night scenes use strong warm/cool contrast: moonlit blue fields broken by amber string lights, windows and lanterns. The warm points guide the eye.

Found-state and hint effects:
- Found items get a white outer glow (sticker halo) that separates them from busy art.
- Rings are pure white with a faint dark shadow for contrast on both light and dark scenes.

Tray:
- Clean white (#FFFFFF), with pale periwinkle-grey cards.
- The selected card is tinted light blue with a slightly darker border, echoing the band blue.
- A single red notification badge is the only red in the chrome.

The hand's cuff is the same blue as the band, which ties the gesture graphic to the brand colour.
character_staging:
Characters are never mascots or posed heroes. There is no face-to-camera character, no big character cut-out and nothing breaking the frame.

People and animals are small (about 8-15% of the width) and caught mid-activity inside the scene:
- elves climbing stairs
- a gnome with a tool
- an old man reading
- a couple on a bridge
- a family watching a movie
- a raccoon eating popcorn
- a hamster in a window

They make each scene feel lived-in and full of small stories to discover, which is the same pleasure the game sells.

The only stand-in for the player is a large, friendly cartoon hand shown tapping. It is always placed on a target item and appears in two of the five shots (2 and 5). Collectible items (the frog, the wooden idol) take on character-like appeal when they get the glow treatment.
what_makes_it_work: The layout never changes (band, full-bleed art, real tray), so all five shots read as one polished system, and the art can change completely without the set looking messy.
The real UI tray is kept in 4 of 5 shots. Its counter and item cards prove this is actual gameplay, not concept art, which builds trust quietly.
Rings and tray agree. In shot 1 there are three circled potions and the selected potion card says 3. The selected tray card always matches what is called out, so the mechanic is taught with no words.
The rings are huge, about 20% of the width, so the mechanic still reads at search-result thumbnail size, where the first three shots are judged.
Two ways of highlighting (rings for targets, a white sticker glow for found items) separate the state before and after a find and make busy art scannable.
The hand pointer shows the only input (a tap), which answers the question of how you play.
Day/night alternation gives the swipe row rhythm and shows range without adding any copy.
The mid-sequence collage breaks the pattern at the right moment and makes a volume claim. It reuses the shot-2 scene as its anchor card, so the sequence feels connected.
A dedicated reassurance caption (no timer) speaks directly to relaxed and older players and removes a likely objection.
Short, one-line, two-tone captions: one yellow keyword gives the eye a single landing point, and the white-plus-navy outline stays legible on the patterned band.
transferable_to_comet_garden: Drop the device frame on at least the first three shots and go full-bleed. Crop in on the real game so the planet fills about 75-85% of the canvas width. Right now it is about 55% inside a phone frame and gets lost among dark space and chrome.

Keep the real Comet Garden HUD (throw counter, life bar, comet picker at the bottom) in every gameplay shot, in the same position, as proof of real play. It does the same job as their tray. Keep the HUD as captured and do not stage it.

Make the callouts and the HUD agree. Example: circle the three creatures that just moved in and show the in-game new-friend toast (or a friends count) above them, so the picture teaches the loop 'fling, land grows, friends arrive' without extra words.

Use our own callout shape: dotted orbit rings that reuse the game's dotted aim-line language, or a soft sparkle ring, each about 20% of the width, 2-3 per shot in a loose triangle clear of the caption and HUD.

Show the one gesture. Draw a pull-back-and-release hand in our own style, for example the kid astronaut's mitten, with the dotted aim arc running to the planet. Put it in shot 1 or 2, fingertip on the comet.

Give creatures a sticker glow (soft white or pastel outer halo) so the tiny bunny, octopus and fox read at thumbnail size against the dark sky. Stage them mid-activity (napping, waving, fishing, riding the rain cloud) and not posed.

Adopt one caption system across all 8 shots, in our own form: a band in the game's night-sky navy or violet, with faint star dust and a bottom edge shaped like a comet trail or soft cloud scallop dipping into the art. Stop changing the background colour on every shot.
Captions go to one line of 2-4 words with one accent keyword in comet orange or a sunny gradient. Lead with the verb: Fling, Grow, Meet, Collect. Shorten the current two-line captions.
Alternate biome palettes down the row for rhythm (Mossy green, then Ember red, then Frost blue, then Bramble amber), the way they alternate day and night.

Put a volume shot mid-sequence in our own shape: a spiral or orbit of round planet 'stamps' (Mossy World, Ember World, Frost Haven, Comet Haven, Bramble Rock) or a fan of Lifebook creature cards. Use the shot-1 planet as the enlarged anchor so the sequence links up.

Keep a dedicated reassurance shot aimed at parents, in our own words. Our truthful version is about no ads, grown-up-only purchases and play time grown-ups can set. That is stronger than theirs because it speaks to the buyer.
Avoid their weak spot of repeating the core-loop message. Give every shot a different job: loop, friends, fusions, sky skill, volume, homeworld, collection, parent trust.
do_not_copy: The cobalt-to-sky-blue top band with its same-hue squiggle pattern and single sine-wave bottom edge. This is their signature frame.
The exact caption treatment of white rounded-black letters with a navy outline and one sunflower-yellow keyword, in title case, always ending in an exclamation mark.
Their caption lines or near-paraphrases: the no-timer pair, the tons-of-pictures line, the explore-the-map line, the collect-all-items line and the find-hidden-objects line.
The cartoon pointing hand with a blue cuff that matches the band.
Plain white circle rings with a drop shadow as the callout style.

The white bottom tray layout: an n/30 counter over rounded item cards with count numerals, a centre card highlighted in light blue, a magnifier hint button with a red number badge, and a chevron at bottom-left.
A tilted rectangular polaroid-style grid of white-bordered scene cards as the volume shot.
Their dense, isometric, highly detailed illustration style and scene subjects (fairy forest with potions, moonlit canal bridge, city apartment movie night, sunny harbour market).

name: Seaside Escape: Merge & Story
full_sequence:
The listing has 8 screenshots, all 9:16 portrait (392x696 thumbnails, so 1242x2208-class sources). I downloaded shots 6 to 8 to shots/6443755785_6.jpg through _8.jpg. The uploaded file names show the order was changed after upload: file 08 now sits in slot 1, and file 06 comes before file 05. That suggests they test the order and moved the story hook to the front.

1. Story-hook collage (the file named 08, moved to slot 1). Three real cutscene frames are laid out as white-bordered photo cards on a periwinkle striped backdrop. The cards overlap and tilt in alternating directions by about 4 to 6 degrees, and each one keeps the full game HUD. The heroine goes from worn out, to huddled in the rain, to crying. A white thought-bubble callout gives her feeling a voice. The caption is a moral-choice question ("Help or Ignore?"). Its job is to stop the scroll with faces and emotion and to promise a story the player can take part in.

2. Core loop. A full-bleed merge board with a row of customer portraits and their orders at the top. Two green corner-bracket selectors with checkmarks show which items are being matched. The caption is an imperative verb plus a noun ("Serve Customers"). Its job is to explain the mechanic in one glance.

3. Value props. The beach merge board becomes background texture. Three chunky rounded pills are stacked in the upper middle, one each in green, blue and coral, and each is offset slightly left or right: no ads, fun, relaxing. The heroine lounges on a boat in the lower-right quadrant, overlapping both the board and the caption banner. The caption names the genre. Its job is to answer the "ads?" objection early and set a calm mood.

4. Before/after. The frame splits on a diagonal of about 8 to 10 degrees along a thin white seam. The restored, warm, busy cafe fills the top 55%. The same room below is grey and dusty, with a glowing hammer as the next action. A thick blue curved arrow with a white outline runs from the before half to the after half. The same two characters stand in both halves, so the change is easy to read. Its job is to show progress: your effort transforms the place.

5. Payoff. A finished beach plaza built around a glowing cyan aquarium-fountain centrepiece, with sparkle glints, coral, string lights and small characters spread around. Its job is to show what you get to build.

6. Reward burst. A shop window with a striped awning frames chests exploding with gems and coins. The gems fly past the window frame and pile up over the bottom edge. Its job is to promise rewards, and it is close to selling in-app purchases.

7. Event pass. A free track and a VIP track of reward tiles. A curved trail of gold tokens sweeps up from the tiles toward a progress bar, and the heroine overlaps the panel edge. Its job is to signal live events and long-term play. This is the weakest and pushiest frame.

8. Seasonal key art. A Halloween loading screen: the heroine and a child carve pumpkins in warm candlelight. The logo appears here only, top centre, with a gameplay tip above a loading bar and no caption banner. Its job is to feel fresh and brand-led. This last slot can be swapped every season without redoing the set.

Across the set: every captioned shot (1 to 7) has the same bottom banner. The first five shots tell a full arc: emotion, mechanic, reassurance, transformation, payoff. Shots 6 and 7 are about selling.
composition_recipe:
Measured on the 460x818 renders:

**Caption block**
- A full-width dome banner sits over the bottom 12 to 14% of the frame.
- Its top edge is a convex arc. It is about 86% down the frame at the centre and about 90% at the side edges, so it rises about 4% of the height in the middle.
- A thin light rim highlights the top edge, and a soft shadow falls onto the gameplay behind it.
- The caption is always one line, centred, covering 80 to 90% of the width, with a cap height of about 5 to 6% of the frame height.
- The banner never moves between shots. That is what makes seven different scenes read as one set in the gallery row.

**Hero element**
- The hero sits in the middle 60% of the frame, between the top HUD strip (about 8%) and the banner.
- Gameplay is full-bleed with no device frame. Raw HUD stays at the top and bleeds off the edges.

**Shot-specific layouts**
- Collage (shot 1): three cards, each 35 to 37% of the height. They overlap by 6 to 8%, alternate their tilt by ±4 to 6°, have a white border of about 2% of the width plus a drop shadow, and overhang the side edges slightly. The bottom card tucks under the banner.
- Value-prop shot (3): pills about 10% of the height each and 55 to 70% of the width, with gaps of about 2%. Their left edges are staggered so the stack zig-zags, and it is weighted to the upper-left third. A character fills the opposite lower-right quadrant (about 45% of the height) and overlaps the banner.
- Before/after (4): a rising diagonal seam of 8 to 10°. After is on top at about 55%, before is below. The curved arrow crosses the seam near the centre-right.

**Depth**
Five layers, back to front: backdrop or gameplay, then cards or panels, then characters, then callouts (bubbles, pills, arrows), then the banner.
